```{r}
#===============================================================================
# 01.6 LOAD UTILITY DATA FOR SCENARIO ANALYSES
#===============================================================================

# HEALTH ECONOMIC CONTEXT: Addressing Reviewer Concern About Utility Values
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Our base case uses utilities from Ramsey et al. (2000):
#   - PFS (progression-free survival) state: 0.85 (disease-free survivors, 5+ years post-diagnosis)
#   - PD (progressed disease) state:         0.65 (patients who died within 12 months)
#   - Instrument: HUI3 (Health Utilities Index Mark 3)
#   - Population: US colorectal cancer survivors
#
# REVIEWER CONCERN (Reviewer 2):
# "The PFS utility of 0.85 appears to exceed general population norms for
#  comparable age groups (60-70 years) in European countries. This may reflect:
#    1. Survivor bias (only long-term survivors were surveyed)
#    2. Response shift (cancer survivors recalibrate their quality of life expectations)
#    3. Lack of age-adjustment to country-specific population norms
#  The authors should consider adjusting utilities to population norms or
#  providing scenario analysis using more conservative values."
#
# OUR RESPONSE STRATEGY:
# We will implement a scenario analysis that:
#   1. KEEPS Ramsey (0.85, 0.65) as base case (preserves published results)
#   2. ADDS a "population norm adjusted" scenario where utilities are derived by:
#      a. Computing multipliers from mCRC literature vs UK population norms
#      b. Applying these multipliers to country- and age-specific population norms
#   3. This produces more conservative, country-specific utilities that sit
#      BELOW general population norms (as expected for cancer patients)

# DATA FILE 1: Population norm utilities by country and age band
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Source: National health surveys using EQ-5D instruments
# Countries included: Ireland, England (UK), Germany, Spain
# Age bands: 55-64, 65-74, 75+
# Columns:
#   - country:        Country name (e.g., "Ireland", "Germany", "Spain", "England (UK)")
#   - age_band:       Age range as text (e.g., "55–64", "65–74", "75+")
#   - age_midpoint:   Numeric midpoint of age band (e.g., 60, 70, 80)
#   - utility_norm:   Mean EQ-5D utility for general population in this country/age
#   - instrument_tariff: EQ-5D version and value set used (e.g., "EQ-5D-5L (UK crosswalk)")
#   - year:           Year of data collection (e.g., "2015–16", "~2014")
#   - source_short:   Short citation (e.g., "Ireland Nat'l Health Survey")
#   - citation_full:  Full bibliographic citation

df_popnorm <- read.csv("data/population_norm_utilities_by_country_age.csv",
                       stringsAsFactors = FALSE)  # stringsAsFactors = FALSE ensures country names remain as character strings, not factors

# Print first few rows to verify structure when knitting
# (Useful for sanity checking that CSV was read correctly)
cat("\n=== POPULATION NORM UTILITIES (first few rows) ===\n")
print(head(df_popnorm))
cat("\n")

# DATA FILE 2: mCRC-specific utility evidence from literature review
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Source: Systematic review of utilities in metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC)
# Studies included: Ramsey 2000, Ness 1999, Stein 2014, Färkkilä 2013, Mittmann 2009
# Purpose:
#   - Contextual comparison (where does Ramsey sit relative to other mCRC studies?)
#   - Derive "typical mCRC utility" for PFS-like and PD-like states
#   - Use these to calculate multipliers vs population norms
# Columns:
#   - study_id:        Short study identifier (e.g., "Ramsey2000", "Stein2014")
#   - country/setting: Geographic location and study type (e.g., "USA (multi-center)", "UK & Netherlands (2L trial)")
#   - line_or_state:   Disease state or treatment line (e.g., "Survivors", "Pre-progression", "Palliative care")
#   - mean_utility:    Mean utility value reported in study
#   - se_or_ci:        Standard error or confidence interval (if reported)
#   - instrument:      Utility instrument used (e.g., "HUI3", "EQ-5D-3L", "Standard Gamble")
#   - n (patients):    Sample size
#   - citation_full:   Full bibliographic citation
#   - notes:           Additional context about the study

df_mcrc_util <- read.csv("data/mCRC_Utility_Evidence_TableB.csv",
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)  # stringsAsFactors = FALSE keeps text as character

# Print first few rows to verify structure when knitting
# (Confirms that mCRC utility evidence was read correctly)
cat("\n=== mCRC UTILITY EVIDENCE (first few rows) ===\n")
print(head(df_mcrc_util))
cat("\n")

# NOTE ON DATA USAGE:
# -------------------
# - df_popnorm   → Used directly in scenario analysis to adjust utilities by country/age
# - df_mcrc_util → Used to derive multipliers and for contextual documentation
#                  (does NOT directly replace model utilities in base case)
```

```{r}
#===============================================================================
# 01.7 HELPER FUNCTION: GET POPULATION NORM UTILITY
#===============================================================================

# PURPOSE:
# --------
# Extract general population utility norm for a given country and age.
# This function looks up the appropriate row from df_popnorm based on:
#   1. Country match (exact string match, case-sensitive)
#   2. Nearest age_midpoint (finds age band closest to input age)
#
# FUNCTION DEFINITION:
get_popnorm_utility <- function(country,     # Character string: "Ireland", "Germany", "Spain", or "England (UK)"
                                 age,         # Numeric: patient age in years (e.g., 65)
                                 df_popnorm)  # Data frame: population norm utilities (loaded from CSV)
{
  # STEP 1: Filter df_popnorm to rows matching the specified country
  # -----------------------------------------------------------------
  df_country <- df_popnorm[df_popnorm$country == country, ]
  # Subset operator [condition, ] keeps only rows where condition is TRUE
  # Result: data frame with only rows for the specified country

  # STEP 2: Check if country was found; if not, fall back to England (UK)
  # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
  if (nrow(df_country) == 0) {  # nrow() counts number of rows in the filtered data frame
    # If zero rows, the country name wasn't found in df_popnorm
    warning(paste0("Country '", country, "' not found in population norms. ",
                   "Falling back to England (UK) as reference."))
    # warning() prints a message to alert user without stopping execution

    df_country <- df_popnorm[df_popnorm$country == "England (UK)", ]
    # England (UK) is used as fallback because:
    #   1. Kind et al. (1999) UK EQ-5D norms are widely cited in European CEA
    #   2. NICE (UK health technology assessment body) uses these as reference
    #   3. UK norms are generally conservative (tend to be lower than some other countries)
  }

  # STEP 3: Find age band with nearest age_midpoint to input age
  # -------------------------------------------------------------
  age_diffs <- abs(df_country$age_midpoint - age)
  # abs() takes absolute value (distance between input age and each age_midpoint)
  # Example: if age = 65 and age_midpoints are [60, 70, 80],
  #          then age_diffs = [5, 5, 15]

  nearest_idx <- which.min(age_diffs)
  # which.min() returns the INDEX (position) of the minimum value in age_diffs
  # Example: which.min([5, 5, 15]) = 1 (first occurrence of minimum value)

  # STEP 4: Extract utility_norm from the nearest age band
  # -------------------------------------------------------
  utility_norm <- df_country$utility_norm[nearest_idx]
  # Index into the utility_norm column at position nearest_idx
  # Result: single numeric value (e.g., 0.80 for England age 65-74)

  # STEP 5: Return the population norm utility
  # -------------------------------------------
  return(utility_norm)
  # This value represents average EQ-5D utility for general population
  # in the specified country and age group (NOT cancer-specific)
}

# USAGE NOTE:
# -----------
# This function will be called by get_utility_scenario() to obtain baseline
# population utility for a given country/age, which is then adjusted using
# mCRC multipliers to produce cancer-specific utilities.
```

```{r}
#===============================================================================
# 01.8 DERIVE mCRC-BASED MULTIPLIERS FROM LITERATURE VS UK POPULATION NORMS
#===============================================================================

# METHODOLOGICAL APPROACH:
# ------------------------
# Instead of using Ramsey (0.85, 0.65) to derive multipliers, we use the
# MEAN of all mCRC utilities from literature review (Table B).
#
# RATIONALE:
# 1. Ramsey is a single study (N=128 survivors, N=10 died)
# 2. Broader mCRC literature provides more robust "typical" utilities
# 3. This approach is more conservative and addresses reviewer concern
#    that Ramsey may overestimate QoL
#
# ALGEBRA:
# --------
# We compute "multipliers" that represent the RATIO of:
#   mCRC utility / general population utility (UK, age 65)
#
# For PFS-like states: mult_PFS = mean(mCRC PFS utilities) / U_ref_uk65
# For PD-like states:  mult_PD  = mean(mCRC PD utilities)  / U_ref_uk65
#
# These multipliers are expected to be < 1.0, because cancer patients have
# lower quality of life than general population.
#
# We then apply these multipliers to each country's population norms:
#   u_PFS_country = U_pop_country × mult_PFS
#   u_PD_country  = U_pop_country × mult_PD

# STEP 1: Split mCRC evidence into PFS-like and PD-like states
# -------------------------------------------------------------
# PFS-like: Survivors, pre-progression, on treatment, stable disease, NOT in palliative care
# PD-like:  Progressed, post-progression, palliative care, refractory, best supportive care

# Identify PFS-like rows using keyword search in line_or_state column
mcrc_pfs_studies <- df_mcrc_util[
  grepl("Survivor|Pre-progression|not in palliative|Metastatic disease \\(not",
        df_mcrc_util$line_or_state,
        ignore.case = TRUE),  # ignore.case = TRUE makes search case-insensitive
]
# grepl() searches for pattern in each element of line_or_state
# Returns TRUE/FALSE vector used to subset df_mcrc_util
# Example: "Survivors" → TRUE, "Palliative care" → FALSE

# Identify PD-like rows using keyword search
mcrc_pd_studies <- df_mcrc_util[
  grepl("Progressed|Post-progression|Palliative|Refractory|died|Best supportive",
        df_mcrc_util$line_or_state,
        ignore.case = TRUE),
]
# Captures studies reporting utilities for advanced/end-stage disease

# Print classification results for transparency
cat("\n=== mCRC UTILITY CLASSIFICATION ===\n")
cat("PFS-like states (n =", nrow(mcrc_pfs_studies), "):\n")
print(mcrc_pfs_studies[, c("study_id", "line_or_state", "mean_utility")])
cat("\nPD-like states (n =", nrow(mcrc_pd_studies), "):\n")
print(mcrc_pd_studies[, c("study_id", "line_or_state", "mean_utility")])
cat("\n")

# STEP 1B: DIAGNOSTIC - Check for NA utilities in matched studies
# ----------------------------------------------------------------
# This validation step checks if any matched studies have NA utility values,
# which would cause the mean() calculation to fail or return NA.

# For PFS-like studies
pfs_na_count <- sum(is.na(mcrc_pfs_studies$mean_utility))
if (pfs_na_count > 0) {
  cat("\n!!! WARNING: Found", pfs_na_count, "PFS-like studies with NA utilities !!!\n")
  cat("These studies will be excluded from mean calculation:\n")
  print(mcrc_pfs_studies[is.na(mcrc_pfs_studies$mean_utility),
                         c("study_id", "line_or_state", "mean_utility")])
  cat("\n")
}

# For PD-like studies
pd_na_count <- sum(is.na(mcrc_pd_studies$mean_utility))
if (pd_na_count > 0) {
  cat("\n!!! WARNING: Found", pd_na_count, "PD-like studies with NA utilities !!!\n")
  cat("These studies will be excluded from mean calculation:\n")
  print(mcrc_pd_studies[is.na(mcrc_pd_studies$mean_utility),
                        c("study_id", "line_or_state", "mean_utility")])
  cat("\n")
}

# STEP 1C: VALIDATION - Ensure we have valid data to work with
# -------------------------------------------------------------
# Check that we have at least one non-NA utility value for each category

pfs_valid_count <- sum(!is.na(mcrc_pfs_studies$mean_utility))
pd_valid_count <- sum(!is.na(mcrc_pd_studies$mean_utility))

if (pfs_valid_count == 0) {
  stop(paste0(
    "\n=== FATAL ERROR: No valid PFS-like utilities found ===\n\n",
    "PROBLEM:\n",
    "  Found ", nrow(mcrc_pfs_studies), " PFS-like studies, but ALL have NA utilities.\n\n",
    "LIKELY CAUSES:\n",
    "  1. CSV file has non-numeric characters in mean_utility column (e.g., '~0.45')\n",
    "  2. R read the column as 'character' type instead of 'numeric'\n",
    "  3. Encoding issues with special characters in CSV file\n\n",
    "SOLUTIONS:\n",
    "  1. Open data/mCRC_Utility_Evidence_TableB.csv\n",
    "  2. Check that mean_utility column contains only numeric values\n",
    "  3. Remove any non-numeric characters (like ~, ≈, etc.)\n",
    "  4. Ensure the CSV is saved with UTF-8 encoding\n",
    "  5. Re-run this chunk\n\n",
    "MATCHED STUDIES (with NA utilities):\n"
  ))
}

if (pd_valid_count == 0) {
  stop(paste0(
    "\n=== FATAL ERROR: No valid PD-like utilities found ===\n\n",
    "PROBLEM:\n",
    "  Found ", nrow(mcrc_pd_studies), " PD-like studies, but ALL have NA utilities.\n\n",
    "LIKELY CAUSES:\n",
    "  1. CSV file has non-numeric characters in mean_utility column (e.g., '~0.45')\n",
    "  2. R read the column as 'character' type instead of 'numeric'\n",
    "  3. Encoding issues with special characters in CSV file\n\n",
    "SOLUTIONS:\n",
    "  1. Open data/mCRC_Utility_Evidence_TableB.csv\n",
    "  2. Check that mean_utility column contains only numeric values\n",
    "  3. Remove any non-numeric characters (like ~, ≈, etc.)\n",
    "  4. Ensure the CSV is saved with UTF-8 encoding\n",
    "  5. Re-run this chunk\n\n",
    "MATCHED STUDIES (with NA utilities):\n"
  ))
}

cat("✓ Validation passed:", pfs_valid_count, "valid PFS utilities,",
    pd_valid_count, "valid PD utilities\n\n")

# STEP 2: Compute mean utilities across mCRC literature
# ------------------------------------------------------
mean_PFS_mcrc <- mean(mcrc_pfs_studies$mean_utility, na.rm = TRUE)
# mean() computes arithmetic average
# na.rm = TRUE excludes missing values from calculation
# Result: single numeric value representing "typical" PFS utility in mCRC
# Note: If ALL values are NA, mean() returns NaN (not a number)
#       If SOME values are NA, they are excluded and mean of remaining values is returned

mean_PD_mcrc <- mean(mcrc_pd_studies$mean_utility, na.rm = TRUE)
# Result: single numeric value representing "typical" PD utility in mCRC

# Print mean values for transparency
cat("\n=== MEAN mCRC UTILITIES FROM LITERATURE ===\n")
cat("Mean PFS-like utility (mCRC literature):", round(mean_PFS_mcrc, 4), "\n")
cat("  (Computed from", pfs_valid_count, "studies with valid utilities)\n")
cat("Mean PD-like utility (mCRC literature): ", round(mean_PD_mcrc, 4), "\n")
cat("  (Computed from", pd_valid_count, "studies with valid utilities)\n")
cat("\n")

# STEP 3: Get reference UK population norm at age 65
# ---------------------------------------------------
U_ref_uk65 <- get_popnorm_utility("England (UK)", 65, df_popnorm)
# Calls helper function defined above
# Returns UK EQ-5D norm for age 65-74 band (midpoint 70, but 65 is closest)
# This serves as denominator for multiplier calculation

cat("Reference UK population norm (age 65):", round(U_ref_uk65, 4), "\n\n")

# STEP 4: Calculate mCRC-based multipliers
# -----------------------------------------
mult_PFS_mcrc <- mean_PFS_mcrc / U_ref_uk65
# Multiplier for PFS state
# Interpretation: mCRC PFS utility as a PROPORTION of general population utility
# Expected: < 1.0 (cancer patients have lower QoL than general population)

mult_PD_mcrc <- mean_PD_mcrc / U_ref_uk65
# Multiplier for PD state
# Expected: << 1.0 (progressed cancer has substantially lower QoL)

# STEP 5: FINAL VALIDATION - Check if multipliers are valid
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# is.finite() returns FALSE if value is NA, NaN, Inf, or -Inf
# This prevents "missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed" errors in if statements
# Note: This should never fail now because we validated in STEP 1C above,
# but we keep it as a final safety check.

if (!is.finite(mult_PFS_mcrc)) {
  stop(paste0(
    "\n=== FATAL ERROR: mult_PFS_mcrc is not finite ===\n\n",
    "  mult_PFS_mcrc = ", mult_PFS_mcrc, "\n",
    "  mean_PFS_mcrc = ", mean_PFS_mcrc, "\n",
    "  U_ref_uk65 = ", U_ref_uk65, "\n\n",
    "This error should not occur if earlier validations passed.\n",
    "Please report this as a bug.\n"
  ))
}

if (!is.finite(mult_PD_mcrc)) {
  stop(paste0(
    "\n=== FATAL ERROR: mult_PD_mcrc is not finite ===\n\n",
    "  mult_PD_mcrc = ", mult_PD_mcrc, "\n",
    "  mean_PD_mcrc = ", mean_PD_mcrc, "\n",
    "  U_ref_uk65 = ", U_ref_uk65, "\n\n",
    "This error should not occur if earlier validations passed.\n",
    "Please report this as a bug.\n"
  ))
}

# Print multipliers for transparency
# (Safe to print now because we know they're valid)
cat("=== mCRC-BASED MULTIPLIERS ===\n")
cat("mult_PFS_mcrc (PFS multiplier):", round(mult_PFS_mcrc, 4), "\n")
cat("  Interpretation: mCRC PFS utility is", round(mult_PFS_mcrc * 100, 1), "% of UK population norm\n")
cat("mult_PD_mcrc (PD multiplier):  ", round(mult_PD_mcrc, 4), "\n")
cat("  Interpretation: mCRC PD utility is", round(mult_PD_mcrc * 100, 1), "% of UK population norm\n")
cat("\n")

# COMPARISON TO RAMSEY-BASED MULTIPLIERS (for context):
# ------------------------------------------------------
# If we had used Ramsey instead:
#   mult_PFS_ramsey = 0.85 / U_ref_uk65 ≈ 1.06 (EXCEEDS population norm!)
#   mult_PD_ramsey  = 0.65 / U_ref_uk65 ≈ 0.81
# This comparison illustrates why reviewers were concerned: Ramsey PFS > UK norms.
#
# With mCRC literature means:
#   mult_PFS_mcrc ≈ 0.80-0.95 (BELOW population norm, more realistic)
#   mult_PD_mcrc  ≈ 0.65-0.80 (substantially below norm, as expected)

# SANITY CHECK:
# -------------
# Expected multiplier ranges:
#   mult_PFS_mcrc: 0.75 - 1.00 (cancer patients may approach but rarely exceed general pop)
#   mult_PD_mcrc:  0.50 - 0.85 (progressed disease has substantial QoL decrement)
# If multipliers are outside these ranges, we should investigate further.

if (mult_PFS_mcrc > 1.05 | mult_PFS_mcrc < 0.70) {
  warning("mult_PFS_mcrc is outside expected range [0.70, 1.05]. Check data.")
}
if (mult_PD_mcrc > 0.90 | mult_PD_mcrc < 0.45) {
  warning("mult_PD_mcrc is outside expected range [0.45, 0.90]. Check data.")
}

# These multipliers are now GLOBAL VARIABLES that will be used by
# get_utility_scenario() to adjust country-specific population norms.
```

```{r}
#===============================================================================
# 01.9 HELPER FUNCTION: GET UTILITY SCENARIO
#===============================================================================

# PURPOSE:
# --------
# Return PFS and PD utilities based on selected scenario:
#   1. "ramsey_basecase" → Use Ramsey et al. (2000) values (0.85, 0.65) unchanged
#   2. "population_norm_adjusted" → Use mCRC multipliers × country/age population norms
#
# This function provides a clean interface for switching between utility sources
# while maintaining complete transparency about the methodology used.

# FUNCTION DEFINITION:
get_utility_scenario <- function(
  country,                                 # Character: "Ireland", "Germany", or "Spain"
  age,                                      # Numeric: patient age (e.g., 65)
  utility_scenario = c("ramsey_basecase",   # Scenario flag
                       "population_norm_adjusted"),
  df_popnorm,                              # Data frame: population norms
  ref_country = "England (UK)",            # Reference country for multiplier calculation
  ref_age = 65                             # Reference age for multiplier calculation
) {

  # Match utility_scenario argument to allowed values
  # --------------------------------------------------
  utility_scenario <- match.arg(utility_scenario)
  # match.arg() ensures utility_scenario is one of the allowed values
  # If not, it throws an error with a helpful message
  # This prevents typos like "ramsey_base_case" or "population_adjusted"

  # Define Ramsey base case constants
  # ----------------------------------
  ramsey_PFS <- 0.85  # Ramsey et al. (2000): disease-free survivors, 5+ years post-diagnosis
  ramsey_PD  <- 0.65  # Ramsey et al. (2000): patients who died within 12 months of survey
  # These are FIXED values that never change regardless of country/age

  #=============================================================================
  # SCENARIO 1: RAMSEY BASE CASE (NO ADJUSTMENT)
  #=============================================================================
  if (utility_scenario == "ramsey_basecase") {
    # RATIONALE FOR BASE CASE:
    # ------------------------
    # - These values are from our published analysis and have been peer-reviewed
    # - Ramsey et al. (2000) is a widely cited study in colorectal cancer CEA
    # - HUI3 (Health Utilities Index Mark 3) is a validated preference-based measure
    # - Using these values preserves continuity with existing literature
    # - All base case results will match original publication exactly

    # Return Ramsey values unchanged
    return(list(
      u_PFS       = ramsey_PFS,                    # 0.85 (PFS state utility)
      u_PD        = ramsey_PD,                     # 0.65 (PD state utility)
      method      = "Ramsey base case (no adjustment)",  # Description of method
      source      = "Ramsey et al., 2000 (HUI3, US colorectal cancer survivors)",  # Citation
      ref_country = ref_country,                   # Reference country (not used in this scenario)
      ref_age     = ref_age,                       # Reference age (not used in this scenario)
      U_ref       = NA,                            # No reference norm needed for base case
      U_pop       = NA                             # No population norm needed for base case
    ))
    # list() creates a named list for easy extraction of components
    # Example usage: result$u_PFS, result$method, etc.
  }

  #=============================================================================
  # SCENARIO 2: POPULATION NORM ADJUSTED (mCRC MULTIPLIERS)
  #=============================================================================
  if (utility_scenario == "population_norm_adjusted") {

    # HEALTH ECONOMIC THEORY: Why adjust by population norms?
    # --------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. CONTEXT-SPECIFIC VALUATION:
    #    Different countries may value health states differently due to:
    #      - Cultural differences in health expectations
    #      - Different EQ-5D value sets (UK vs German vs Spanish)
    #      - Variation in healthcare system quality and access
    #
    # 2. AGE ADJUSTMENT:
    #    Utility naturally declines with age in general population due to:
    #      - Comorbidities (arthritis, heart disease, etc.)
    #      - Physical limitations (mobility, vision, hearing)
    #      - Chronic conditions
    #    Our base case (Ramsey 0.85) doesn't account for age-related decline
    #
    # 3. CANCER-SPECIFIC DECREMENT:
    #    Instead of assuming fixed utilities, we compute:
    #      cancer utility = population norm × mCRC multiplier
    #    This approach:
    #      - Anchors utilities to realistic baseline for age/country
    #      - Applies a consistent "cancer decrement" across countries
    #      - Avoids cancer utilities exceeding population norms (illogical)

    # ALGEBRA (step-by-step):
    # -----------------------
    # At reference (UK, age 65):
    #   mult_PFS_mcrc = mean_PFS_mcrc / U_ref_uk65
    #   mult_PD_mcrc  = mean_PD_mcrc  / U_ref_uk65
    # (These were calculated globally in previous chunk)
    #
    # For target country/age:
    #   U_pop          = get_popnorm_utility(country, age, df_popnorm)
    #   u_PFS_adjusted = U_pop × mult_PFS_mcrc
    #   u_PD_adjusted  = U_pop × mult_PD_mcrc
    #
    # EXAMPLE (Ireland, age 65):
    #   U_pop_ireland    = 0.879 (Ireland EQ-5D-5L norm, age 65-74)
    #   mult_PFS_mcrc    = 0.82 / 0.80 = 1.025 (assume mean_PFS_mcrc = 0.82)
    #   u_PFS_adjusted   = 0.879 × 1.025 = 0.901
    #   mult_PD_mcrc     = 0.69 / 0.80 = 0.8625 (assume mean_PD_mcrc = 0.69)
    #   u_PD_adjusted    = 0.879 × 0.8625 = 0.758

    # STEP 1: Get reference UK population norm (already calculated globally)
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    U_ref <- U_ref_uk65
    # This was computed in previous chunk: get_popnorm_utility("England (UK)", 65, df_popnorm)
    # Typical value: ~0.80 (UK EQ-5D-3L norm for age 65-74)

    # STEP 2: Get target country/age population norm
    # -----------------------------------------------
    U_pop <- get_popnorm_utility(country, age, df_popnorm)
    # Calls helper function to look up EQ-5D norm for specified country and age
    # Examples:
    #   Ireland age 65 → 0.879
    #   Germany age 65 → 0.84
    #   Spain age 65   → 0.82

    # STEP 3: Apply mCRC multipliers to target population norm
    # ---------------------------------------------------------
    u_PFS_adjusted <- U_pop * mult_PFS_mcrc
    # Multiply population norm by mCRC PFS multiplier
    # Example: 0.879 × 1.025 = 0.901
    # Interpretation: Cancer patient in PFS has QoL that is X% of general population baseline

    u_PD_adjusted <- U_pop * mult_PD_mcrc
    # Multiply population norm by mCRC PD multiplier
    # Example: 0.879 × 0.8625 = 0.758
    # Interpretation: Cancer patient in progressed state has substantially lower QoL

    # STEP 4: Cap utilities at 1.0 (perfect health ceiling)
    # ------------------------------------------------------
    u_PFS_adjusted <- min(u_PFS_adjusted, 1.0)
    # min() ensures utility doesn't exceed 1.0 (perfect health ceiling)
    # This prevents illogical values if target country has very high norms
    # Example: if u_PFS_adjusted = 1.05, cap it at 1.0

    u_PD_adjusted <- min(u_PD_adjusted, 1.0)
    # Same capping for PD state (unlikely to exceed 1.0 but included for robustness)

    # STEP 5: Return adjusted utilities with metadata
    # ------------------------------------------------
    return(list(
      u_PFS          = u_PFS_adjusted,              # Adjusted PFS utility
      u_PD           = u_PD_adjusted,               # Adjusted PD utility
      method         = "Population norm adjustment (multiplicative, anchored on mCRC evidence)",
      source         = paste0("mCRC literature (mean utilities) scaled to ",
                              country, " age ", age, " population norms"),
      ref_country    = ref_country,                 # "England (UK)"
      ref_age        = ref_age,                     # 65
      U_ref          = U_ref,                       # UK norm at age 65 (e.g., 0.80)
      U_pop          = U_pop,                       # Target country norm (e.g., 0.879 for Ireland)
      mean_PFS_mcrc  = mean_PFS_mcrc,              # Mean PFS utility from mCRC literature
      mean_PD_mcrc   = mean_PD_mcrc,               # Mean PD utility from mCRC literature
      mult_PFS_mcrc  = mult_PFS_mcrc,              # PFS multiplier
      mult_PD_mcrc   = mult_PD_mcrc                # PD multiplier
    ))
    # This metadata-rich return allows complete transparency about:
    #   - What utilities were used
    #   - Where they came from
    #   - How they were calculated
    #   - What assumptions were made

    # ALTERNATIVE APPROACH (COMMENTED OUT FOR FUTURE USE):
    # -----------------------------------------------------
    # Instead of multiplicative scaling, we could use ABSOLUTE DECREMENT:
    #
    # decrement_PFS <- 1.0 - ramsey_PFS  # 1.0 - 0.85 = 0.15
    # decrement_PD  <- 1.0 - ramsey_PD   # 1.0 - 0.65 = 0.35
    #
    # u_PFS_adjusted <- U_pop - decrement_PFS
    # u_PD_adjusted  <- U_pop - decrement_PD
    #
    # u_PFS_adjusted <- max(u_PFS_adjusted, 0.0)  # Floor at 0
    # u_PD_adjusted  <- max(u_PD_adjusted, 0.0)
    #
    # RATIONALE FOR NOT USING ABSOLUTE DECREMENT:
    # - Assumes cancer causes a FIXED utility loss (e.g., -0.15) regardless of baseline
    # - Doesn't account for country/age differences in baseline QoL
    # - Less consistent with QALY theory (utilities are ratio-scaled, not interval-scaled)
    # - Multiplicative approach is more flexible and realistic
    #
    # We keep this code commented out in case future reviewers request it.
  }
}

# USAGE EXAMPLES:
# ---------------
# # Base case (Ramsey):
# result_ramsey <- get_utility_scenario("Ireland", 65, "ramsey_basecase", df_popnorm)
# result_ramsey$u_PFS  # Returns 0.85
# result_ramsey$u_PD   # Returns 0.65
#
# # Population norm adjusted:
# result_popnorm <- get_utility_scenario("Ireland", 65, "population_norm_adjusted", df_popnorm)
# result_popnorm$u_PFS  # Returns ~0.80-0.90 (depends on Ireland norm and mCRC multiplier)
# result_popnorm$u_PD   # Returns ~0.65-0.75 (scaled down from population norm)
```

```{r}

#===============================================================================
# COUNTRY-SPECIFIC PARAMETERS
#===============================================================================
#
# This section defines country-specific costs, WTP thresholds, and discount rates
# for Ireland, Germany, and Spain.
#
# STRATEGY:
# 1. A helper function get_country_params() returns all country-specific parameters
# 2. By default, Ireland parameters are loaded (so variables exist for downstream chunks)
# 3. To analyze a different country, manually change DEFAULT_COUNTRY below
# 4. To run all countries automatically, see the utility scenario analysis chunk
#    at the end of this document
#
#===============================================================================

# Create output directory if it doesn't exist
if (!dir.exists("output")) {
  dir.create("output", recursive = TRUE)
}


#===============================================================================
# HELPER FUNCTION: get_country_params()
#===============================================================================
#
# Returns a list of country-specific parameters for the specified country.
#
# PARAMETERS:
#   country: "Ireland", "Germany", or "Spain"
#
# RETURNS:
#   Named list with:
#     - country_name: Country identifier
#     - c_PFS_Folfox: Cost of FOLFOX per 14-day cycle
#     - c_PFS_Bevacizumab: Cost of Bevacizumab per cycle
#     - c_OS_Folfiri: Cost of FOLFIRI per cycle
#     - administration_cost: IV administration cost per cycle
#     - subtyping_test_cost: One-time RAS/BRAF subtyping test cost
#     - c_AE1: Cost of treating leukopenia (grade 3/4)
#     - c_AE2: Cost of treating diarrhea (grade 3/4)
#     - c_AE3: Cost of treating nausea/vomiting (grade 3/4)
#     - n_wtp: Willingness-to-pay threshold (€/QALY)
#     - country_discount_rate: Annual discount rate (base case)
#     - country_max_discount_rate: Annual discount rate (upper bound for sensitivity)
#     - country_min_discount_rate: Annual discount rate (lower bound for sensitivity)
#
get_country_params <- function(country) {

  if (country == "Ireland") {
    return(list(
      country_name = "Ireland",

      # 1. Cost of treatment in this country (2024 values)
      c_PFS_Folfox = 157.77,
      c_PFS_Bevacizumab = 1425.84,
      c_OS_Folfiri = 167.10,
      administration_cost = 406.50,
      subtyping_test_cost = 400,

      # 2. Cost of treating adverse events conditional on occurrence
      c_AE1 = 3485.23,  # Leukopenia
      c_AE2 = 1792.82,  # Diarrhea
      c_AE3 = 502.69,   # Nausea/vomiting

      # 3. Willingness to pay threshold
      n_wtp = 45000,

      # 4. Country-specific discount rates
      country_discount_rate = 0.04,
      country_max_discount_rate = 0.08,
      country_min_discount_rate = 0.00
    ))

  } else if (country == "Germany") {

    # Germany costs received as monthly values, converted to 14-day cycles
    return(list(
      country_name = "Germany",

      # 1. Cost of treatment in this country (2024 values)
      # Monthly costs converted to 14-day cycles: (monthly / 30) * 14
      c_PFS_Folfox = ((1406.37 / 30) * 14),
      c_PFS_Bevacizumab = ((3252.19 / 30) * 14),
      c_OS_Folfiri = ((1442.70 / 30) * 14),
      administration_cost = 1927.72,
      subtyping_test_cost = 400,

      # 2. Cost of treating adverse events conditional on occurrence
      c_AE1 = 4188.31,  # Leukopenia
      c_AE2 = 1982.68,  # Diarrhea
      c_AE3 = 1307.72,  # Nausea/vomiting

      # 3. Willingness to pay threshold
      n_wtp = 78871,

      # 4. Country-specific discount rates
      country_discount_rate = 0.03,
      country_max_discount_rate = 0.06,
      country_min_discount_rate = 0.00
    ))

  } else if (country == "Spain") {
    return(list(
      country_name = "Spain",

      # 1. Cost of treatment in this country (2024 values)
      c_PFS_Folfox = 323.39,
      c_PFS_Bevacizumab = 1399.33,
      c_OS_Folfiri = 147.31,
      administration_cost = 332.39,
      subtyping_test_cost = 400,

      # 2. Cost of treating adverse events conditional on occurrence
      c_AE1 = 5710.97,  # Leukopenia
      c_AE2 = 305.55,   # Diarrhea
      c_AE3 = 35.11,    # Nausea/vomiting

      # 3. Willingness to pay threshold
      n_wtp = 30000,

      # 4. Country-specific discount rates
      country_discount_rate = 0.03,
      country_max_discount_rate = 0.06,
      country_min_discount_rate = 0.00
    ))

  } else {
    stop(paste("Unknown country:", country,
               "\nValid options are: 'Ireland', 'Germany', 'Spain'"))
  }
}


#===============================================================================
# LOAD COUNTRY-SPECIFIC PARAMETERS
#===============================================================================
#
# Country-specific parameters are stored in separate files:
#   - params_Ireland.R
#   - params_Germany.R
#   - params_Spain.R
#
# TO CHANGE COUNTRY: Uncomment ONE of the source() lines below and comment the others
#
# Each parameter file defines:
#   - country_name: Country identifier
#   - Treatment costs (c_PFS_Folfox, c_PFS_Bevacizumab, c_OS_Folfiri, etc.)
#   - Adverse event costs (c_AE1, c_AE2, c_AE3)
#   - Willingness-to-pay threshold (n_wtp)
#   - Discount rates (country_discount_rate, country_max_discount_rate, country_min_discount_rate)
#
# IMPORTANT: All outputs will be saved with country-specific filenames to prevent
#            overwriting when running multiple countries sequentially.
#
#===============================================================================

# Uncomment ONE country (leave the others commented):
# source("params_Ireland.R")
# source("params_Germany.R")
 source("params_Spain.R")

# Print confirmation
cat("\n")
cat("================================================================================\n")
cat("COUNTRY-SPECIFIC PARAMETERS LOADED\n")
cat("================================================================================\n")
cat("Country:", country_name, "\n")
cat("WTP threshold: €", format(n_wtp, big.mark=","), " per QALY\n", sep="")
cat("Discount rate:", country_discount_rate, "(range:", country_min_discount_rate, "-", country_max_discount_rate, ")\n")
cat("================================================================================\n")
cat("\n")





# Cost Breakdowns: (Pulled from the appendix of C:\Users\Jonathan\OneDrive - Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland\COLOSSUS\Drafts\Updated Drafts 2024\Bevacizumab for Metastatic Colorectal Cancer_19_05_24_01.docx)

#   1.	Oxaliplatin:
#   o	Dosage: 85 mg/m²
# o	Patient’s BSA: 1.71 m²
# o	Cost/mg: €1.27
# o	Total dosage = Dosage per m² * BSA = 85 mg/m² * 1.71 m² = 145.35 mg
# o	Cost = Total dosage * Cost per mg = 145.35 mg * €1.27/mg = €184.59
# 2.	Leucovorin (provided twice):
#   o	Dosage: 200 mg/m²
# o	Patient’s BSA: 1.71 m²
# o	Cost/mg: €0.068
# o	Total dosage = Dosage per m² * BSA = 200 mg/m² * 1.71 m² = 342 mg
# o	Cost for one day = Total dosage * Cost per mg = 342 mg * €0.068/mg = €23.26
# o	Total cost for two days = Cost for one day * 2 = €23.26 * 2 = €46.52
# 3.	5-FU bolus (provided twice):
#   o	Dosage: 400 mg/m²
# o	Patient’s BSA: 1.71 m²
# o	Cost/mg: €0.008

# o	Cost for one day = Total dosage * Cost per mg = 684 mg * €0.008/mg = €5.47

# 4.	5-FU continuous infusion (provided twice):

# o	Cost for one day = Total dosage * Cost per mg = 1026 mg * €0.008/mg = €8.21

# We will implement a Markov model with time-dependent transition probabilities, via a parametric survival model fitted to some individual patient data for the time-to-progression (TTP) and time-to-death (TTD) for standard of care.

# A hazard ratio for the new intervention therapy vs. the standard of care will then be applied to obtain transition probabilities for the new experimental strategy.

# This also answers the question of how exactly probabilities are created in my code, the m_P_SoC is something that, when multiplied by 1, (when at the start 100% of our cohort are in the PFS state) gives us the first probability from that 100%, and the next part or row of that m_P_SoC probability is then multiplied by the proportion who are in the different states in the next row for the cohort (given their movements last time having been multiplied by m_P_SoC) which gives us the second probability multiplied by the proportion of that 1 (or 100%) in each state, and so on, and so forth, for each wave.





# Median Survival Time:

# An explanation of how best to estimate median survival time can be found here under "Estimating median survival time" https://www.emilyzabor.com/tutorials/survival_analysis_in_r_tutorial.html also saved here: C:\Users\Jonathan\OneDrive - Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland\COLOSSUS\R Code\GitHub\COLOSSUS_Model\Survival Analysis in R.pdf

# We want to calculate the median survival time WITH bevacizumab, i.e., the median PFS and OS with bev to compare it to the median PFS and OS in other studies with bevacizumab but without our chromosomal instability subtypes, so that we can make comparisons.

# Time-to-Progression (TTP):
#04 Parametric Survival Analysis itself:

# We use the 'flexsurv' package to fit several commonly used parametric survival distributions.

# The data needs to be set up to include a column for the time (in days, weeks, years, etc.,) and a status indicator whether the time corresponds to an event, i.e. progression (status = 1), or to the last time of follow up, i.e. censoring (status = 0).


# It looks like in the example, Koen is applying the flexsurvreg formula to individuals who experience progression (i.e. ~1):

head(df_TTP)

l_TTP_SoC_exp      <- flexsurvreg(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = df_TTP, dist = "exp")
l_TTP_SoC_gamma    <- flexsurvreg(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = df_TTP, dist = "gamma")
l_TTP_SoC_gompertz <- flexsurvreg(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = df_TTP, dist = "gompertz")
l_TTP_SoC_llogis   <- flexsurvreg(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = df_TTP, dist = "llogis")
l_TTP_SoC_lnorm    <- flexsurvreg(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = df_TTP, dist = "lnorm")
l_TTP_SoC_weibull  <- flexsurvreg(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = df_TTP, dist = "weibull")

```{r}

# =============================================================================
# Compare the fit numerically based on AIC and BIC
# =============================================================================
#
# AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) and BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion)
# are both measures of model fit that penalize model complexity.
# BIC applies a stronger penalty for additional parameters than AIC.
# Lower values indicate better fit.
#
# We extract both AIC and BIC from each flexsurvreg fitted model object
# to compare the candidate parametric survival distributions for TTP.
# =============================================================================

# Step 1: Extract AIC values for all candidate distributions (as before)
(v_AIC_TTP <- c(
  exp      = l_TTP_SoC_exp$AIC,
  gamma    = l_TTP_SoC_gamma$AIC,
  gompertz = l_TTP_SoC_gompertz$AIC,
  llogis   = l_TTP_SoC_llogis$AIC,
  lnorm    = l_TTP_SoC_lnorm$AIC,
  weibull  = l_TTP_SoC_weibull$AIC
))

# Step 2: Extract BIC values for all candidate distributions
# BIC is accessed via the BIC() function or directly from the flexsurvreg object
# Here we use the direct accessor for consistency with AIC extraction
(v_BIC_TTP <- c(
  exp      = BIC(l_TTP_SoC_exp),
  gamma    = BIC(l_TTP_SoC_gamma),
  gompertz = BIC(l_TTP_SoC_gompertz),
  llogis   = BIC(l_TTP_SoC_llogis),
  lnorm    = BIC(l_TTP_SoC_lnorm),
  weibull  = BIC(l_TTP_SoC_weibull)
))

# Step 3: Create a tidy data frame combining AIC and BIC for reporting
# This makes it easy to see which distribution minimizes each criterion
df_AIC_BIC_TTP <- data.frame(
  outcome      = "TTP",                           # Outcome being modeled
  distribution = names(v_AIC_TTP),                # Distribution name
  AIC          = as.numeric(v_AIC_TTP),          # AIC value
  BIC          = as.numeric(v_BIC_TTP),          # BIC value
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Step 4: Order by AIC (ascending) to show best-fitting distributions first
df_AIC_BIC_TTP <- df_AIC_BIC_TTP[order(df_AIC_BIC_TTP$AIC), ]

# Step 5: Print the table for inclusion in the knitted document
print(df_AIC_BIC_TTP)

# Step 6: Save the table as a CSV file for use in manuscript/supplement
# Write the AIC/BIC table to a CSV file
write.csv(
  df_AIC_BIC_TTP,
  file = file.path("output", "AIC_BIC_TTP.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

# Note: Weibull has the best visual and numerical fit based on AIC
# You can verify this by inspecting the printed table above

#06 Saving the survival parameters for use in the model:

# Saving the survival parameters ----

# The 'flexsurv' package return the coefficients, which need to be transformed for use in the base R functions, but that will be done when the coefficients actually are used, for the time being we will just save the survival parameters from the distribution we decide to use. 

# NB, if we are not going with Weibull then we may have to save something specific to the distribution that is not shape or scale - we can look into this if we don't use Weibull.

l_TTP_SoC_weibull
# Calling a flexsurvreg parameter like this allows you to see here that Weibull is the shape and the scale, so if we do go with another distribution we can see what it's version of shape and scale are and use these instead.

l_TTP_SoC_weibull$coefficients

coef_weibull_shape_SoC <- l_TTP_SoC_weibull$coefficients["shape"]
coef_weibull_scale_SoC <- l_TTP_SoC_weibull$coefficients["scale"]

# ============================================================================
# GAMMA DISTRIBUTION PARAMETERS FOR TTP (Time To Progression)
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC THEORY:
# In health economic modelling, we often test the robustness of our results
# to different parametric survival distribution choices. While Weibull is
# commonly used due to its flexibility (monotonically increasing or decreasing
# hazard), the gamma distribution offers additional flexibility with non-monotonic
# hazards (can increase then decrease, or vice versa).
#
# STATISTICAL BACKGROUND - GAMMA DISTRIBUTION:
# The gamma distribution for survival analysis is characterized by two parameters:
#   - shape parameter (α): Controls the shape of the hazard function
#   - rate parameter (β): Controls the scale (speed) of events
# The scale parameter is 1/rate.
#
# FLEXSURV PARAMETERIZATION:
# flexsurv fits gamma distributions and returns log(shape) and log(rate) as
# coefficients. These need to be exponentiated before use in base R functions.
#
# SURVIVAL FUNCTION FOR GAMMA:
# S(t) = 1 - F(t) where F is the gamma CDF
# In R: S(t) = pgamma(t, shape, rate, lower.tail = FALSE)
#
# WHY EXTRACT THESE NOW:
# Even though Weibull is our base case, we extract gamma parameters here so
# they're available when we want to run the gamma scenario. This follows the
# principle of "fit once, use many times" - we fit all candidate distributions
# during the survival analysis phase, then can switch between them for scenarios.
#
# THEORETICAL BACKGROUND - WHY GAMMA FOR SURVIVAL?:
# The gamma distribution is a two-parameter family with probability density:
#   f(t) = (β^α / Γ(α)) * t^(α-1) * exp(-βt)
# where α = shape, β = rate, Γ is the gamma function
#
# The hazard function for gamma is:
#   h(t) = f(t) / S(t) = (β^α * t^(α-1) * exp(-βt)) / (Γ(α, βt) / Γ(α))
# where Γ(α, βt) is the upper incomplete gamma function
#
# HAZARD BEHAVIOR:
#   - If α < 1: hazard decreases over time (like Weibull with shape < 1)
#   - If α = 1: constant hazard (exponential distribution)
#   - If α > 1: hazard increases initially, but unlike Weibull, can plateau
#                (non-monotonic behavior - this is the key advantage)
#
# CLINICAL RELEVANCE IN ONCOLOGY:
# Cancer progression risk often follows complex patterns:
#   - Early period: rapidly increasing risk as aggressive disease manifests
#   - Later period: risk may stabilize in patients who remain progression-free
# Gamma can model this "increase then plateau" pattern better than Weibull's
# strictly monotonic (always increasing or always decreasing) hazard.
#
# Extract the gamma distribution coefficients from the fitted model object
# Display the full coefficient vector for transparency and verification
l_TTP_SoC_gamma$coefficients

# Extract shape parameter (alpha) - controls the form of the hazard function
# NOTE: flexsurv returns log(shape), so we store the log-transformed value
# This will be exponentiated later when used in pgamma() function
# Higher shape values (after exp) indicate hazard that increases more steeply
coef_gamma_shape_SoC <- l_TTP_SoC_gamma$coefficients["shape"]

# Extract rate parameter (beta) - controls how quickly events occur
# NOTE: flexsurv returns log(rate), so we store the log-transformed value
# This will be exponentiated later when used in pgamma() function
# Higher rate values (after exp) indicate events happen more quickly
# (i.e., shorter expected time to progression)
coef_gamma_rate_SoC <- l_TTP_SoC_gamma$coefficients["rate"]

# Display extracted parameters for verification and documentation
# These are still on the log scale at this point
coef_gamma_shape_SoC
coef_gamma_rate_SoC

```

```{r}
#09 Saving the survival parameters for use in the model:

# Saving the survival parameters ----

# The 'flexsurv' package return the coefficients, which need to be transformed for use in the base R functions, but that will be done when the coefficients actually are used, for the time being we will just save the survival parameters from the distribution we decide to use. 

# NB, if we are not going with Weibull then we may have to save something specific to the distribution that is not shape or scale - we can look into this if we don't use Weibull.

l_TTD_SoC_weibull
# Calling a flexsurvreg parameter like this allows you to see here that Weibull is the shape and the scale, so if we do go with another distribution we can see what it's version of shape and scale are and use these instead.

l_TTD_SoC_weibull$coefficients

coef_TTD_weibull_shape_SoC <- l_TTD_SoC_weibull$coefficients["shape"]
coef_TTD_weibull_scale_SoC <- l_TTD_SoC_weibull$coefficients["scale"]

# ============================================================================
# GAMMA DISTRIBUTION PARAMETERS FOR TTD (Time To Death)
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC CONTEXT:
# Time to death (overall survival, OS) is a critical endpoint in oncology
# economic evaluations. The choice of parametric distribution for OS can
# substantially impact cost-effectiveness results, especially for:
#   1. Long-term survival extrapolation beyond trial follow-up
#   2. Calculation of life-years gained
#   3. Estimation of lifetime costs
#
# GAMMA VS. WEIBULL FOR SURVIVAL DATA:
# - Weibull: Hazard is monotonic (always increasing or always decreasing)
#     h(t) = λα(λt)^(α-1) where α is shape, λ = 1/scale
#     If α > 1: increasing hazard (worsening over time)
#     If α < 1: decreasing hazard (improving over time)
#     If α = 1: constant hazard (exponential distribution)
#
# - Gamma: Hazard can be non-monotonic (increase then plateau, etc.)
#     More flexible for complex survival patterns
#     Particularly useful when hazard initially increases but then stabilizes
#
# CLINICAL RELEVANCE FOR TIME-TO-DEATH:
# In cancer trials, mortality patterns may not follow simple monotonic hazards:
#   - Early period: high hazard due to aggressive disease progression
#   - Later period: lower hazard in long-term survivors (selected population)
#   - Plateau: some patients may achieve long-term disease control
# Gamma distribution can capture this "bathtub" or "hump-shaped" hazard
# better than Weibull in some cases.
#
# EXTRAPOLATION IMPLICATIONS:
# Choice of survival distribution has major impact on extrapolated long-term
# survival, which drives:
#   - Total QALYs gained (especially if trial follow-up is limited)
#   - Long-term treatment costs
#   - Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER)
#
# SCENARIO ANALYSIS JUSTIFICATION:
# Testing gamma as a scenario addresses structural uncertainty in our model:
#   - Are our cost-effectiveness conclusions robust to distributional choice?
#   - Does the ICER change meaningfully with a more flexible survival model?
# This is recommended by:
#   - NICE Decision Support Unit Technical Support Document 14 (survival analysis)
#   - ISPOR-SMDM Good Practice Guidelines for survival extrapolation
#   - Many HTA agencies (CADTH, PBAC, etc.)
#
# MATHEMATICAL PROPERTIES OF GAMMA FOR TTD:
# The gamma survival function is:
#   S(t) = P(T > t) = 1 - F(t) = Γ(α, βt) / Γ(α)
# where Γ(α, βt) is the upper incomplete gamma function
#
# Mean survival time: E[T] = α/β = shape/rate
# Variance: Var[T] = α/β² = shape/rate²
#
# This means:
#   - For a given mean survival, higher shape → less variability
#   - Rate parameter scales the time axis
#
# Extract the gamma distribution coefficients from the fitted model object
# Display full coefficients for transparency and model documentation
l_TTD_SoC_gamma$coefficients

# Extract shape parameter for time-to-death (overall survival)
# NOTE: flexsurv returns log(shape), stored on log scale here
# This parameter controls whether mortality risk:
#   - Decreases over time (shape < 1, after exp)
#   - Stays constant (shape = 1, after exp → exponential)
#   - Increases then plateaus (shape > 1, after exp)
# Will be exponentiated when used in pgamma() function
coef_TTD_gamma_shape_SoC <- l_TTD_SoC_gamma$coefficients["shape"]

# Extract rate parameter for time-to-death
# NOTE: flexsurv returns log(rate), stored on log scale here
# This parameter controls the overall speed of mortality events
# Higher rate (after exp) → events happen faster → shorter median survival
# Combined with shape, determines:
#   - Median survival time
#   - Long-term survival probability (tail behavior)
#   - Expected life-years
# Will be exponentiated when used in pgamma() function
coef_TTD_gamma_rate_SoC <- l_TTD_SoC_gamma$coefficients["rate"]

# Display extracted parameters for verification and model documentation
# These values are on the log scale and will need exp() transformation
coef_TTD_gamma_shape_SoC
coef_TTD_gamma_rate_SoC

```

# I don't want to mess with my original data informing transition rates in this analysis, so I clone df_TTP here

df_TTP_SOC$group <- "Chemo"
df_TTP_EXP$group <- "Chemo+Bev"

# Combine the datasets
df_combined_TTP <- rbind(df_TTP_SOC, df_TTP_EXP)
# The datasets are combined using rbind.


# To show the number at risk at specific times (0, 150, 300, 450, 600, 750, 900, 1050, 1200, 1350 days) in the risk table, you need to specify these times in the add_risktable() function. Here’s how you can modify your code to achieve this:

# Adding Risk Table Times: The add_risktable() function is modified to include the times argument, specifying the exact times at which I want to display the number at risk.

# Plotting: The combined data is plotted with ggsurvfit, using the group column to distinguish between the two sets of survival curves.
# This will create a single plot for each type of survival curve, showing both datasets on the same graph.

  labs(
    x = "Days",
    y = "Progression Free Survival Probability"

  add_risktable(times = c(0, 150, 300, 450, 600, 750, 900, 1050, 1200, 1350)) +
  theme_minimal()

# The ordering of V_names_states has an influence on the tornado diagram and the reported cost-effectiveness results.

# So, I need to ensure I correctly order V_names_states all the way through from the start.

# m_P_Exp and m_P_SoC both use v_names_states to set up the names of the rows and columns of their matrices. 

# As does m_M_SoC and m_M_Exp.

# Then m_M_SoC and  m_M_Exp use the row column names to fill in the 100% of the cohort (or 1) in PFS and the 0% of the cohort in OS and DEAD in wave 1. m_P_Exp and m_P_SoC also both use the row and column names to fill in the transition probabilities between PFS and OS, etc.,

# Then m_M_SoC and m_M_Exp are matrix multiplied by m_P_Exp and m_P_SoC:

# for(i_cycle in 1:(n_cycle-1)) {
#  m_M_SoC[i_cycle + 1, ] <- m_M_SoC[i_cycle, ] %*% m_P_SoC[ , , i_cycle]
#  m_M_Exp[i_cycle + 1, ] <- m_M_Exp[i_cycle, ] %*% m_P_Exp[ , , i_cycle]
# }

# The way this matrix multiplication works is that the value in box 1 for m_M_SoC is multiplied by the value in box 1 for m_P_SoC and so on. If box 1 for m_M_SoC and m_P_SoC is the 1 (i.e. 100% of people in the PFS state when this all starts), multiplied by the PFS state probabilities, i.e., the probability of going from the PFS state into other states like so:

#          PFS       AE1       AE2       AE3          OS        Dead

# PFS  0.974925 0.0194985 0.0194985 0.0194985 0.005074995 0.020000000

# (Ignore the AE health states, this layout is a holdover from when AE's were going to have their own health states in the Markov model).

# Then things will multiply correctly and we're multiplying PFS transition probabilities by the 100% of the cohort in the PFS state. 

# Even, if ordering v_names_states  <- c("PFS", "AE1", "AE2", "AE3", "OS", "Dead")   is not in the order as above, i.e., v_names_states  <- c("OS", "AE1", "AE2", "AE3", "PFS", "Dead") , then the m_M_SoC will have 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, because everyone still starts in the PFS state, and m_P_SoC will have  "OS", "AE1", "AE2", "AE3", "PFS", "Dead", with the right probabilities put in the right spots, so when you matrix multiply it things will multiply out fine.

# However, this is not the case for ordering costs and utilities:

# v_tc_SoC <- m_M_SoC %*% c(c_F_SoC, c_AE1, c_AE2, c_AE3, c_P, c_D)
# v_tc_Exp <- m_M_Exp %*% c(c_F_Exp, c_AE1, c_AE2, c_AE3, c_P, c_D)
# v_tu_SoC <- m_M_SoC %*% c(u_F, u_AE1, u_AE2, u_AE3, u_P, u_D)
# v_tu_Exp <- m_M_Exp %*% c(u_F, u_AE1, u_AE2, u_AE3, u_P, u_D)

# As you can see, in both cases the ordering is set manually by how we enter things in the concatenated brackets, so in the case above where ordering v_names_states  <- c("PFS", "AE1", "AE2", "AE3", "OS", "Dead") is ordered differently, i.e., v_names_states  <- c("OS", "AE1", "AE2", "AE3", "PFS", "Dead") when we matrix multiply costs and utilities by m_M_SoC  and m_M_Exp above we will be multiplying the utility of being in the progression free state u_F by the matrix of individuals in the OS state, which will clearly be a smaller number of individuals in the first few waves, and multiplying the utility of the OS state (u_P) by the larger number of individuals actually in the PFS state <- c("OS", "AE1", "AE2", "AE3", "PFS", "Dead"). We'll be doing the same thing with costs. What this will mean is more people getting the OS costs and OS utility and fewer people getting the PFS costs and the PFS utility, which will in turn have consequences for the cost-effectiveness analysis results with more OS costs and more OS utility being considered in the equation that compares costs and utilities.

# I've confirmed all of the things I say about by changing the ordering first of v_names_states, and then of the cost and utility concatenations. Changing the ordering of v_names_states did nothing to the CEA results or Tornado diagram provided I changed the ordering of utilities and costs to match this, changing the ordering of utilities and costs changed both unless I changed them to be in an order that matched the changed ordering of v_names_states.

## General setup

# Here, I think about how time from individual patient data may be changed to match the time of our cycles.

# I think the digitiser (if I am using one) will give me the time in the context of the survival curves I am digitising, i.e., time in weeks, or time in months or time in years. Otherwise if I get the data directly from Ian it will also have time in the context of the existing survival curves.

# Then I will have to set-up my time accordingly in the R code so that my cycle length is at the same level as the individual patient data.

# That is, in Koen's example:

# C:\Users\Jonathan\OneDrive - Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland\COLOSSUS\R Code\Parametric Survival Analysis\ISPOR WEBINAR Health Economic Modelling in R\ISPOR_webinar_R-master

# the data includes a column for the time (in years)
# t_cycle <- 1/4      # cycle length of 3 months (in years)                                # n_cycle <- 60       # number of cycles (total runtime 15 years)
  

# So I would have my colum for time, in the [TIME] the graph I was digitising/getting data from used.
# Then I would create my cycle length of X weeks (in [TIME] the graph I was digitising used)
# Then I would have my number of cycles that would add up to give me a total runtime of how long I want to run the model for.
# So, above Koen wanted to run the model for 15 years, but his cycles were in 3 months, or each cycle was a quarter of a year, so 60 quarters, or 60 3 month cycles, is 15 years.

# REALISE HERE THEAT P_PD ISNT THE PROBABILITY OF PROGRESSION TO DEAD, BUT OF PFS TO DEAD, OF FIRST LINE TO DEAD, BECAUSE OUR ANGIOPREDICT CURVES ONLY EVER DESCRIBE FIRST LINE TREATMENT, BE THAT FIRST LINE SOC TREATMENT OR FIRST LINE EXP TREATMENT.

# Here we define all our model parameters, so that we can call on these parameters later during our model:

t_cycle <- 14      # cycle length of 2 weeks (in [[days]] - this is assuming the survival curves I am digitising will be in [[days]] if they are in another period I will have to represent my cycle length in that period instead).                                  
n_cycle        <- 143                            
# We set the number of cycles to 143 to reflect 2,000 days from the Angiopredict study (5 Years, 5 Months, 3 Weeks, 1 Day) broken down into fortnightly cycles
v_names_cycles  <- paste("cycle", 0:n_cycle)    
# So here, we just name each cycle by the cycle its on, going from 0 up to the number of cycles there are, here 143
v_names_states  <- c("PFS", "OS", "Dead")  
# These are the health states in our model, PFS, OS, Death.
n_states        <- length(v_names_states)        
# We're just taking the number of health states from the number of names we came up with, i.e. the number of names to reflect the number of health states 

# Strategy names
v_names_strats     <- c("Standard of Care",         
                     "Experimental Treatment")
               # store the strategy names
n_str           <- length(v_names_strats)           
# number of strategies



# TRANSITION PROBABILITIES: Time-To-Transition - TTP:


# Time-dependent transition probabilities are obtained in four steps
# 1) Defining the cycle times
# 2) Obtaining the event-free (i.e. survival) probabilities for the cycle times for SoC
# 3) Obtaining the event-free (i.e. survival) probabilities for the cycle times for Exp based on a hazard ratio
# 4) Obtaining the time-dependent transition probabilities from the event-free (i.e. survival) probabilities

# 1) Defining the cycle times
(t <- seq(from = 0, by = t_cycle, length.out = n_cycle + 1))

# Here we're saying, at each cycle how many of the time periods our individual patient data is measured at have passed? Here our individual patient data is in days, so we have 0 in cycle 0, 14 (or two weeks) in cycle 1, and so on.

# Having established that allows us to obtain the transition probabilities for the time we are interested in for our cycles from this different period individual patient data, so where the individual patient data is in days and our cycles are in fortnight or half months, this allows us to obtain transition probabilities for these fortnights.

# 2) Obtaining the event-free (i.e. survival) probabilities for the cycle times for SoC
# S_FP_SoC - survival of progression free to progression, i.e. not going to progression, i.e. staying in progression free.
# Note that the coefficients [that we took from flexsurvreg earlier] need to be transformed to obtain the parameters that the base R function uses


S_FP_SoC <- pweibull(
  q     = t, 
  shape = exp(coef_weibull_shape_SoC), 
  scale = exp(coef_weibull_scale_SoC), 
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

head(cbind(t, S_FP_SoC))

#        t  S_FP_SoC
# [1,] 0.0 1.0000000
# [2,] 0.5 0.9948214
# [3,] 1.0 0.9770661
# [4,] 1.5 0.9458256
# [5,] 2.0 0.9015175
# [6,] 2.5 0.8454597


# Having the above header shows that this is probability for surviving in the F->P state, i.e., staying in this state, because you can see in time 0 100% of people are in this state, meaning 100% of people hadnt progressed and were in PFS, if this was instead about the progressed state (i.e. OS), there should be no-one in this state when the model starts, as everyone starts in the PFS state, and it takes a while for people to reach the OS state.


# 3) Obtaining the event-free (i.e. survival) probabilities for the cycle times for Experimental treatment (aka the novel therapy) based on a hazard ratio.
# So here we basically have a hazard ratio for the novel therapy that says you do X much better under the novel therapy than under standard of care, and we want to apply it to standard of care from our individual patient data to see how much improved things would be under the novel therapy.
# (NB - if we ultimately decide not to use a hazard ratio, I could probably just create my transition probabilities for the experimental therapy from individual patient data that I have digitised from patients under this novel therapy).
# Here our hazard ratio is 0.68, I can change that hazard ratio if I need to in the future.
# - note that S(t) = exp(-H(t)) and, hence, H(t) = -ln(S(t))
# that is, the survival function is the expoential of the negative hazard function, per:
# https://faculty.washington.edu/yenchic/18W_425/Lec5_survival.pdf
# and: 
# https://web.stanford.edu/~lutian/coursepdf/unit1.pdf
# Also saved here: C:\Users\Jonathan\OneDrive - Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland\COLOSSUS\R Code\Parametric Survival Analysis\flexsurv
# And to multiply by the hazard ratio it's necessary to convert the survivor function into the hazard function, multiply by the hazard ratio, and then convert back to the survivor function, and then these survivor functions are used for the probabilities.
HR_FP_Exp <- 0.68
H_FP_SoC  <- -log(S_FP_SoC)
H_FP_Exp  <- H_FP_SoC * HR_FP_Exp
S_FP_Exp  <- exp(-H_FP_Exp)

head(cbind(t, S_FP_SoC, H_FP_SoC, H_FP_Exp, S_FP_Exp))


head(cbind(t, S_FP_SoC, H_FP_SoC))


    # I want to vary my probabilities for the one-way sensitivity analysis, particularly for the tornado       plot of the deterministic sensitivity analysis. 
    
    # The problem here is that df_params_OWSA doesnt like the fact that a different probability for each       cycle (from the time-dependent transition probabilities) gives a large number of rows (say if there were 60 cycles,      two treatment strategies and a probability for each cycle we would see 122 rows). It wants the same number of       rows as      there are probabilities, i.e., it would prefer a probability of say 0.50 and then a max and a      min     around that.
    
    # To address this, I think I can apply this mean, max and min to the hazard ratios instead, knowing        that when run_owsa_det is run in the sensitivity analysis it calls the "oncologySemiMarkov_function" function to run and in this        function the hazard ratios generate the survivor function, and then these survivor functions are used      to generate the probabilities (which will be cycle dependent).
    
    # This is fine for the hazard ratio for the experimental strategy, I can just take:
    
    # HR_FP_Exp as my mean, and:
    
    # Minimum_HR_FP_Exp <- HR_FP_Exp - 0.20*HR_FP_Exp
    # Maximum_HR_FP_Exp <- HR_FP_Exp + 0.20*HR_FP_Exp
    
    # For min and max.
    
# For standard of care there was no hazard ratio, because we took these values from the survival curves     directly, and didnt vary them by a hazard ratio, like we do above.
    
# To address this, I create a hazard ratio that is exactly one.
    
    # hazard ratio

    # A measure of how often a particular event happens in one group compared to how often it happens in       another group, over time. In cancer research, hazard ratios are often used in clinical trials to           measure survival at any point in time in a group of patients who have been given a specific treatment      compared to a control group given another treatment or a placebo. A hazard ratio of one means that         there is no difference in survival between the two groups. A hazard ratio of greater than one or less      than one means that survival was better in one of the groups. https://www.cancer.gov/publications/dictionaries/cancer-terms/def/hazard-ratio

    # Thus, I can have a hazard ratio where the baseline value of it gives you the survival curves, and        thus the probabilities, from the actual survival curves we are drawing from, and where the min and max     will be 1 +/- 0.20, which will give us probabilities that are 20% higher or lower than the probabilities from the actual survival curves that we are drawing from in the parametric survival analysis to get transitions under standard of care.
    
    # To do this, I just have to add a hazard ratio to the code that creates the transition probabilities      under standard of care as below, then I can add that hazard ratio, and it's max and min, to the            deterministic sensitivity analysis and vary all the probabilities by 20%.
        

    # So here we basically have a hazard ratio that is equal to 1, so it leaves things unchanged for           patients, and we want to apply it to standard of care from our individual patient data to leave things     unchanged in this function, but allow things to change in the sensitivity analysis lower down.
      
    # Here our hazard ratio is 1, things are unchanged.

# So, first we create our hazard ratio == 1
HR_FP_SoC <- 1

# (I'm creating the below as new parameters, i.e. putting "nu" infront of them, in case keeping the name the same causes a problem for when I want to use them in the deterministic sensivity analysis, i.e., if I generate a parameter from itself - say var_name = var_name exactly, then there may be some way in which R handles code that won't let this work, or will take one parameter before the other, or something and stop the model from executing correctly).

# Then, we create our hazard function for SoC:
NU_S_FP_SoC <- S_FP_SoC
NU_H_FP_SoC  <- -log(NU_S_FP_SoC)
# Then, we multiply this hazard function by our hazard ratio, which is just 1, but which gives us the      opportunity to apply a hazard ratio to standard of care in our code and thus to have a hazard ratio for     standard of care for our one way deterministic sensitivity analysis and tornado diagram lower down in our code:
NUnu_H_FP_SoC  <- NU_H_FP_SoC * HR_FP_SoC
# Again, I was worried that with overlap when creating parameters I would have a problem with the deterministic sensivity analysis so I call it NU again to make it a "new" parameter again.
NU_S_FP_SoC  <- exp(-NUnu_H_FP_SoC)

head(cbind(t, NU_S_FP_SoC, NUnu_H_FP_SoC))



# NU_H_FP_SoC  <- -log(NU_S_FP_SoC)
# # Then, we multiply this hazard function by our hazard ratio, which is just 1, but which gives us the      opportunity to apply a hazard ratio to standard of care in our code and thus to have a hazard ratio for     standard of care for our one way deterministic sensitivity analysis and tornado diagram.

# 4) Obtaining the time-dependent transition probabilities from the event-free (i.e. survival) probabilities

# Now we can take the probability of being in the PFS state at each of our cycles, as created above, from 100% (i.e. from 1) in order to get the probability of NOT being in the PFS state, i.e. in order to get the probability of moving into the progressed state, i.e. the OS state.
 
p_PFSOS_SoC <- p_PFSOS_Exp <- rep(NA, n_cycle)

# First we make the probability of going from progression-free (F) to progression (P) blank (i.e. NA) for all the cycles in standard of care and all the cycles under the experimental strategy.

for(i in 1:n_cycle) {
  p_PFSOS_SoC[i] <- 1 - NU_S_FP_SoC[i+1] /  NU_S_FP_SoC[i]
  p_PFSOS_Exp[i] <- 1 - S_FP_Exp[i+1] / S_FP_Exp[i]
}

HR_PD_SoC <- 1

# (I'm creating the below as new parameters, i.e. putting "nu" infront of them, in case keeping the name the same causes a problem for when I want to use them in the deterministic sensivity analysis, i.e., if I generate a parameter from itself - say var_name = var_name exactly, then there may be some way in which R handles code that won't let this work, or will take one parameter before the other, or something and stop the model from executing correctly).

# Then, we create our hazard function for SoC:
NU_S_PD_SoC <- S_PD_SoC
NU_H_PD_SoC  <- -log(NU_S_PD_SoC)
# Then, we multiply this hazard function by our hazard ratio, which is just 1, but which gives us the      opportunity to apply a hazard ratio to standard of care in our code and thus to have a hazard ratio for     standard of care for our one way deterministic sensitivity analysis and tornado diagram.
NUnu_H_PD_SoC  <- NU_H_PD_SoC * HR_PD_SoC
# Again, I was worried that with overlap when creating parameters I would have a problem with the deterministic sensivity analysis so I call it NU again to make it a "new" parameter again.
NU_S_PD_SoC  <- exp(-NUnu_H_PD_SoC)

head(cbind(t, NU_S_PD_SoC, NUnu_H_PD_SoC))



# NU_H_PD_SoC  <- -log(NU_S_PD_SoC)
# # Then, we multiply this hazard function by our hazard ratio, which is just 1, but which gives us the      opportunity to apply a hazard ratio to standard of care in our code and thus to have a hazard ratio for     standard of care for our one way deterministic sensitivity analysis and tornado diagram.
# NU_H_PD_SoC  <- NU_H_PD_SoC * HR_PD_SoC
# # 
# NU_S_PD_SoC  <- exp(-NU_H_PD_SoC)
# 
# head(cbind(t, NU_S_PD_SoC, NU_H_PD_SoC))


# 4) Obtaining the time-dependent transition probabilities from the event-free (i.e. survival) probabilities

# Now we can take the probability of being in the PFS state at each of our cycles, as created above, from 100% (i.e. from 1) in order to get the probability of NOT being in the PFS state, i.e. in order to get the probability of moving into the progressed state, or the OS state.


p_PFSD_SoC <- p_PFSD_Exp <- rep(NA, n_cycle)

# First we make the probability of going from progression-free (F) to progressed to dead (D) blank (i.e. NA) for all the cycles in standard of care and all the cycles under the experimental strategy.

for(i in 1:n_cycle) {
  p_PFSD_SoC[i] <- 1 - NU_S_PD_SoC[i+1] / NU_S_PD_SoC[i]
  p_PFSD_Exp[i] <- 1 - S_PD_Exp[i+1] / S_PD_Exp[i]
}

# round(p_PFSD_SoC, digits=2)
# round(p_PFSD_Exp, digits=2)
# If I wanted to round I could apply the above, but my code already rounds my numbers.

# Then we generate our transition probability under standard of care and under the experimental treatement using survival functions that havent and have had the hazard ratio from above applied to them, respectively. [If we decide not to apply a hazard ratio for the experimental strategy going from progression to dead then neither may have a hazard ratio applied to them].


# The way this works is, you take next cycles probability of staying in this state, divide it by this cycles probability of staying in this state, and take it from 1 to get the probability of leaving this state. 

p_PFSD_SoC

p_PFSD_Exp

# Finally, now that I create transition probabilities from first-line treatment to death under SoC and the Exp treatment I can take them from the transition probabilities from first-line treatment to progression for SoC and Exp treatment, because the OS here from Angiopredict is transitioning from the first line treatment to dead, not from second line treatment to death, and once we get rid of the people who were leaving first line treatment to die in PFS, all we have left is people leaving first line treatment to progress. And then we can keep the first line treatment to death probabilities we've created from the OS curves to capture people who have left first line treatment to transition into death rather than second line treatment.

 # The below reflects the probability of going to death in the second line treatment, and I make the assumption that everyone gets the same second line treatment and give them the same probability after being under exp and under SoC to go from the second line therapy into dead.

P_OSD_SoC   <- 0.17 # Probability of dying when in OS.

# Costs and utilities  
# Basically the outcomes we are interested in coming out of this model, so we'll look at the cohorts costs over the time horizon and the quality adjusted life years in our cohort over this time horizon.

# Costs

# The costs are a particularly important part of the model, because these are the only things that differ between countries. We make the assumption, per the literature and pragmatically (because we are examining 3 different countries at once in this model), that utilities and incidence of adverse events are generalisable across countries.

# So, the best way to deal with needing 3 different sets of costs, one for each country, is likely to create a concatanated vector, where the first set of entries refers to Ireland, the second set refers to Germany and the third set refers to Spain, then when we are building a diagram or doing some analysis in the model we can have c_F_SoC[1], c_F_Exp[1] and c_P[1], referring to Ireland, and so on for Spain[3] and Germany[2].

Then I repeat this for each country I am interested in.
