```{r}
# Above is the cost for each state, PFS, OS and dead,

# Then we define the utilities per health states.

#===============================================================================
# UTILITY VALUES (BASE CASE: RAMSEY ET AL., 2000)
#===============================================================================

# SOURCE: Ramsey et al., 2000, "Quality of life in survivors of colorectal cancer"
# Published in: Cancer, Volume 109, Issue 6, pages 1082-1089
# DOI: 10.1002/cncr.22512
#
# STUDY DESIGN:
# -------------
# - Cross-sectional survey of long-term colorectal cancer survivors
# - Patients surveyed approximately 5 years post-diagnosis (mean follow-up ~5 years)
# - N = 138 patients initially surveyed
# - N = 128 completed HUI3 (Health Utilities Index Mark 3) utility assessment
# - US-based, multi-center sample from cancer registry
# - Follow-up survey 12 months later identified 10 patients who died
#
# UTILITY INSTRUMENT: HUI3 (Health Utilities Index Mark 3)
# ---------------------------------------------------------
# - Preference-based multi-attribute utility measure
# - Canadian general population weights (time trade-off valuations)
# - Scale: -0.36 (worse than dead) to 1.0 (perfect health)
# - Covers 8 health domains:
#   1. Vision (ability to see)
#   2. Hearing (ability to hear)
#   3. Speech (ability to speak and be understood)
#   4. Ambulation (ability to walk)
#   5. Dexterity (ability to use hands/fingers)
#   6. Emotion (happiness vs depression/anxiety)
#   7. Cognition (memory, thinking, concentration)
#   8. Pain and discomfort
#
# REPORTED VALUES:
# ----------------
# - Survivors (disease-free, N=128): mean HUI3 = 0.85
#   (These patients were alive and stable 5 years post-diagnosis)
# - Died within 12 months (N=10):   mean HUI3 = 0.65 (p=0.002 vs survivors)
#   (Utilities were assessed 12 months before death; represents advanced disease)
#
# MAPPING TO MODEL STATES:
# ------------------------
# We map these values to our Markov model states as follows:
#   - PFS (progression-free survival) state: u_F = 0.85
#     Rationale: Patients in PFS are disease-free or have stable/controlled disease,
#                analogous to the long-term survivors in Ramsey et al.
#   - PD (progressed disease) state: u_P = 0.65
#     Rationale: Patients in PD have metastatic disease progression and poor prognosis,
#                analogous to patients who died within 12 months in Ramsey et al.
#   - Dead state: u_D = 0.0
#     Standard assumption in QALY framework (no utility when dead)
#
# IMPORTANT CAVEATS (RATIONALE FOR SCENARIO ANALYSIS):
# -----------------------------------------------------
# 1. SURVIVOR BIAS:
#    - These utilities come from patients who survived 5+ years post-diagnosis
#    - This is a SELECTED sample of healthier, more resilient patients
#    - Patients who died early (worse prognosis) are not represented in the 0.85 value
#    - True population utilities for mCRC may be lower
#
# 2. RESPONSE SHIFT:
#    - Long-term cancer survivors often recalibrate their internal standards for QoL
#    - They adapt to their "new normal" and may report higher utilities than expected
#    - This phenomenon is well-documented in chronic disease populations
#    - General population may rate the same health state lower than survivors do
#
# 3. NOT ADJUSTED FOR POPULATION NORMS:
#    - Ramsey utilities do NOT account for:
#      a. Age-specific population norms (QoL naturally declines with age)
#      b. Country-specific valuation differences (cultural differences in health state valuation)
#      c. Comorbidity burden in real-world mCRC populations (average age ~65-70 with comorbidities)
#
# 4. POTENTIAL OVERESTIMATION (REVIEWER CONCERN):
#    - Reviewer 2 noted that u_F = 0.85 may EXCEED general population norms for age 65+
#    - Evidence supporting this concern:
#      * Ireland age 65-74 norm: 0.879 (0.85 is 97% of population norm)
#      * England age 65-74 norm: 0.80  (0.85 EXCEEDS population norm by 6%)
#      * Germany age 65-74 norm: 0.84  (0.85 slightly exceeds norm)
#      * Spain age 65-74 norm:   0.82  (0.85 exceeds norm by 4%)
#    - It is illogical for cancer patients to have higher QoL than general population
#    - This suggests Ramsey may overestimate true utilities in European populations
#
# OUR RESPONSE TO REVIEWER CONCERN:
# ----------------------------------
# We implement a SCENARIO ANALYSIS that:
#   1. KEEPS Ramsey (0.85, 0.65) as BASE CASE
#      - Preserves all published results
#      - Maintains continuity with existing mCRC CEA literature
#      - Ramsey is widely cited and peer-reviewed
#   2. ADDS a "population norm adjusted" SCENARIO
#      - Uses mCRC literature means × country/age-specific population norms
#      - Produces more conservative, country-specific utilities
#      - Ensures cancer utilities sit BELOW general population norms (as expected)
#      - Directly addresses reviewer concern about overestimation
#   3. COMPARES cost-effectiveness conclusions under both scenarios
#      - Demonstrates sensitivity to utility source
#      - Provides transparent range of results for decision-makers
#
# NOTE: The scenario flag "utility_scenario" (defined below) controls which
#       utilities are actually used in the model. When set to "ramsey_basecase",
#       these values below are used unchanged. When set to "population_norm_adjusted",
#       these values are OVERRIDDEN by country/age-adjusted values.

u_F       <- 0.850     # Utility when in PFS (progression-free survival) state
                       # Source: Ramsey et al. (2000), disease-free survivors, HUI3
                       # Interpretation: High quality of life, similar to general population

u_P       <- 0.650     # Utility when in PD (progressed disease / OS) state
                       # Source: Ramsey et al. (2000), patients who died within 12 months, HUI3
                       # Interpretation: Substantially reduced quality of life due to disease progression

u_D       <- 0         # Utility when dead
                       # Standard assumption: Death has zero utility in QALY framework
                       # (Some frameworks allow negative utilities for "worse than dead" states,
                       #  but we use 0 as is conventional in most CEA)

# 4. Country-specific discount rate:

# NOTE: The lines below are COMMENTED OUT as of the run_country_analysis() refactoring.
# With the new approach, discount rates are defined INSIDE the run_country_analysis()
# function and passed to the model via the l_params_all list.

# Discounting factors
d_c             <- country_discount_rate
# discount rate for costs (per year)
d_e             <- country_discount_rate
# discount rate for QALYs (per year)

# Discount weight (equal discounting is assumed for costs and effects):

# v_dwc <- 1 / (1 + d_c) ^ (0:n_cycle)
# v_dwe <- 1 / (1 + d_e) ^ (0:n_cycle)

# This was my initial discount weight vector, but, I've updated this and do this later on now 

p_PFSD_SoC
p_PFSD_Exp

p_PFSOS_SoC
p_PFSOS_Exp
```

```{r}

#04 Define and initialize matrices and vectors

#04.1 Cohort trace


# After setting up our parameters above, we initialise our structure below.

# This is where we will store all of the model output, and all the things that we need to track over time as we are simulating the progression of this cohort through this disease process.

# WHEN COMING BACK TO COMPARE: C:\Users\Jonathan\OneDrive - Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland\COLOSSUS\R Code\Parametric Survival Analysis\ISPOR WEBINAR Health Economic Modelling in R\ISPOR_webinar_R-master\ISPOR_webinar_R-master\oncologySemiMarkov_illustration to the DARTH Rmarkdown document, a big difference is that DARTH creates a cycle 0 - whereas the comparison from the ISPOR_webinar_R uses -1 to get into cycle 0 where necessary. I have decided to follow the ISPOR way, because I am interested in learning from their parametric analysis, so I need to bear this difference in mind as I go through this document.

# Markov cohort trace matrix ----

# Initialize matrices to store the Markov cohort traces for each strategy

# - note that the number of rows is n_cycle + 1, because R doesn't use index 0 (i.e. cycle 0)  --> What we mean here, is that when we do our calculations later they need to be for cycle-1 to reflect cycle 0.
m_M_SoC <- m_M_Exp  <-  matrix(
  data = NA, 
  nrow = n_cycle,  
  ncol = n_states, 
  dimnames = list(paste('Cycle', 1:n_cycle), v_names_states)
)

## Initial state vector
# We create an inital vector where people start, with everyone (1 = 100% of people) starting in PFS below:
# v_s_init <- c("PFS" = 1, "OS" = 0, "Dead" = 0)
# v_s_init

# There are cases where you can have an initial illness prevalence, so you would start some people in the sick state and some people in the healthy state, but above we're looking at people with mCRC, so we'll start everyone in PFS.


## Initialize cohort trace for cSTM (cohort state transition model) for all strategies (the strategies are the treatment strategies SOC and Exp).
# So, basically we are creating a matrix to trace how the cohort is distributed across the health states, over time. 

# A matrix is necessary because there are basically two dimensions to this, the number of time cycles, which will be our rows, and then the number of states - to know which proportion of our cohort is in each state at each time:

# m_M_SoC <- matrix(0, 
#                   nrow = (n_cycles + 1), ncol = n_states, 
#                   dimnames = list(v_names_cycles, v_names_states))
# In the above code from DARTH instead of having to bother with -1 throughout the analysis they create a cycle 0.
# Then they store the initial state vector in the first row of the cohort trace
# m_M_SoC[1, ] <- v_s_init
## Initialize cohort traces
## So, above they make the cohort trace for standard of care
# This gives them a matrix to can fill in with the simulations of how patients transitions between health states under treatment.



# Back to my code, in the first row of the markov matrix [1, ] put the value at the far end, i.e. "<-1" and "<-0" under the colum "PFS" [ , "PFS"], repeating this for "OS", and "Dead":


# Specifying the initial state for the cohorts (all patients start in PFS)
m_M_SoC[1, "PFS"] <- m_M_Exp[1, "PFS"] <- 1
m_M_SoC[1, "OS"]  <- m_M_Exp[1, "OS"]  <- 0
m_M_SoC[1, "Dead"]<- m_M_Exp[1, "Dead"]  <- 0

# Inspect whether properly defined
head(m_M_SoC)
head(m_M_Exp)
```

```{r}
# 04.2 Transition probability matrix

## If there were time varying transition probabilities, i.e. the longer you are in the model there are changes in your transition probability into death as you get older, etc., you would build a transition probability array, rather than a transition probability matrix, per: 

# 04.2 of:

# "C:\Users\Jonathan\OneDrive - Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland\COLOSSUS\Training Resources\Decision Modeling for Public Health_DARTH\5_Nov_29\4_Cohort state-transition models (cSTM) - time-dependent models_material\Markov_3state_time"

# with: C:\Users\Jonathan\OneDrive - Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland\COLOSSUS\Training Resources\Cost-Effectiveness and Decision Modeling using R Workshop _ DARTH\August_24\Live Session


## Initialize transition probability matrix, [i.e. build the framework or empty scaffolding of the transition probability matrix]
# all transitions to a non-death state are assumed to be conditional on survival
# - starting with standard of care
# - note that these are now 3-dimensional matrices because we are including time.
 
# The DARTH approach would be something like:
# m_P_SoC  <- matrix(0,
#                    nrow = n_states, ncol = n_states,
#                    dimnames = list(v_names_states, v_names_states)) # define row and column names
# m_P_SoC


# Our approach to initialize matrices for the transition probabilities
# - note that these are now 3-dimensional matrices (so, above we originally included dim = nrow and ncol, but now we also include n_cycle - i.e. the number of cycles).
# - starting with standard of care
m_P_SoC <- array(
  data = 0,
  dim = c(n_states, n_states, n_cycle),
  dimnames = list(v_names_states, v_names_states, paste0("Cycle", 1:n_cycle))
  # define row and column names - then name each array after which cycle it's for, i.e. cycle 1 all the way through to cycle 143. So Cycle 1 will have all of our patients in PFS, while cycle 143 will have most people in the dead state.
)

head(m_P_SoC)


m_P_Exp <- array(
  data = 0,
  dim = c(n_states, n_states, n_cycle),
  dimnames = list(v_names_states, v_names_states, paste0("Cycle", 1:n_cycle))
  # define row and column names - then name each array after which cycle it's for, i.e. cycle 1 all the way through to cycle 143. So Cycle 1 will have all of our patients in PFS, while cycle 143 will have most people in the dead state.
)

head(m_P_Exp)
```

```{r}

# 04.3 Fill in the transition probability matrix:

# Setting the transition probabilities from PFS based on the model parameters
  # So, when individuals are in PFS what are their probabilities of going into the other states that they can enter from PFS?

m_P_SoC["PFS", "PFS",]<- (1 -p_PFSOS_SoC) * (1 - p_PFSD_SoC)
m_P_SoC["PFS", "OS",]<- p_PFSOS_SoC*(1 - p_PFSD_SoC)
m_P_SoC["PFS", "Dead",]<-p_PFSD_SoC

# Setting the transition probabilities from OS
m_P_SoC["OS", "OS", ] <- 1 - P_OSD_SoC
m_P_SoC["OS", "Dead", ]        <- P_OSD_SoC


# Setting the transition probabilities from Dead
m_P_SoC["Dead", "Dead", ] <- 1


m_P_SoC

# Using the transition probabilities for standard of care as basis, I update the transition probabilities that are different for the experimental strategy


# Setting the transition probabilities the experimental strategy
m_P_Exp["PFS", "PFS",]<- (1 -p_PFSOS_Exp) * (1 - p_PFSD_Exp)
m_P_Exp["PFS", "OS",]<- p_PFSOS_Exp*(1 - p_PFSD_Exp)
m_P_Exp["PFS", "Dead",]<-p_PFSD_Exp

# Setting the transition probabilities from OS
m_P_Exp["OS", "OS", ] <- 1 - P_OSD_Exp
m_P_Exp["OS", "Dead", ]        <- P_OSD_Exp

# Setting the transition probabilities from Dead
m_P_Exp["Dead", "Dead", ] <- 1

m_P_Exp
```

```{r}
#05 Run Markov model
# for (t in 1:n_cycles){  # Use a for loop to loop through the number of cycles, basically we'll calculate the cohort distribution at the next cycle [t+1] based on the matrix of where they were at time t, matrix multiplied by the transition probability matrix for the current cycle (constant for us as we use a constant transition probability matrix, rather than a transition probability array).

# We do this for each treatment, as they all have different transition probability matrices. 

#  m_M_SoC [t + 1, ] <- m_M_SoC [t, ] %*% m_P_SoC   # estimate the state vector for the next cycle (t + 1)

# Above I was originally using a transition probability matrix, because I was using a time constant transition probability. But now, because my transition probabilities come from the survival curves, and thus change over time, I am using a transition probability array. 

# Thus, I adapt the above to reflect that my transition probability selected has to come from a certain cycle, i.e. from a certain time, and then be multiplied by the number of people in the matrix, the amount of the cohort in the matrix, at that cycle, i.e. at that time. Thats why below I pick the third dimension of the array, not row, not column, but time: R,C,T i.e.   ->  , ,i_cycle

# So here I once again create the Markov cohort trace by looping over all cycles
# - note that the trace can easily be obtained using matrix multiplications
# - note that now the right probabilities for the cycle need to be selected, like I explained above.

for(i_cycle in 1:(n_cycle-1)) {
  m_M_SoC[i_cycle + 1, ] <- m_M_SoC[i_cycle, ] %*% m_P_SoC[ , , i_cycle]
  m_M_Exp[i_cycle + 1, ] <- m_M_Exp[i_cycle, ] %*% m_P_Exp[ , , i_cycle]
}

head(m_M_SoC)  # print the first few lines of the matrix for standard of care (m_M_SoC)

head(m_M_Exp)  # print the first few lines of the matrix for experimental treatment(m_M_Exp)

#m_M_SoC
m_M_SoC
#m_M_Exp
m_M_Exp
```

```{r}
#07 Compute Cost-Effectiveness Outcomes

#07.1 Including ADVERSE EVENTS in Mean Costs and QALYs for each strategy

# Calculate the costs and QALYs per cycle by multiplying m_M (the Markov trace) with the cost/utility vectors for the different states

# per cycle
# calculate expected costs by multiplying cohort trace with the cost vector for the different health states

# Basically, you take the cohort trace over time for each strategy [m_M_SoC] and multiply this by a vector of our costs for each state: [c(c_H, c_S, c_D)] -> So, basically the number of people in each state at each cycle multiplied by the cost of being in that state [cost of healthy, cost of sick and cost of dead] for each strategy that we look at (standard of care, experimental).

# Bear in mind we are doing matrix multiplication [%*%], because what this does is for each cycle [row in the matrix], take the vector of costs, and multiply it by the distribution in that cycle [breakdown of proportions in the states in that row] and add it all together, to get the total costs for that cycle [row]. This gives us a vector of the costs accrued in this cohort of individuals ending up in these different states for each cycle on a per person basis, because it's a cohort distribution (it always sums to 1).

# So, in cycle 1 everyone is in the PFS state, so they only incur the PFS cost, as more and more time passes and more and more people get sick, the costs increases due to more people being in the OS state, but over time this falls again as more and more people go into the dead state, which has no costs as we don't treat corpses.
  

# 1. Probability of adverse events 1,2 3 in the PFS state under standard of care and exp care:

# AE1:Leukopenia = 0.040 AE2:Diarrhea = 0.310 AE3:Vomiting = 0.31
# 
# p_FA1_STD     <- 0.040   # probability of 7 days of adverse event 1 in the 14 day treatment cycle period when progression-free under SOC 
# p_FNOTA1_STD <- 1 - p_FA1_STD # probability that patients will not have 7 days of adverse event 1 in the 14 day treatment cycle period when progression-free under SOC 
# 
# p_FA2_STD     <- 0.310   # probability of adverse event 2 when progression-free under SOC
# p_FA3_STD     <- 0.310   # probability of adverse event 3 when progression-free under SOC
# 
# p_FA1_EXPR     <- 0.070   # probability of adverse event 1 when progression-free under EXPR
# p_FA2_EXPR     <- 0.110   # probability of adverse event 2 when progression-free under EXPR
# p_FA3_EXPR     <- 0.070   # probability of adverse event 3 when progression-free under EXPR

p_FA1_STD     <- 0.040 # Probability of the adverse event 1 occuring when progression-free under SOC.
p_FA2_STD     <- 0.310 # Probability of the adverse event 2 occuring when progression-free under SOC.
p_FA3_STD     <- 0.310 # Probability of the adverse event 3 occuring when progression-free under SOC.

p_FA1_EXPR     <- 0.070   # probability of adverse event 1 when progression-free under EXPR
p_FA2_EXPR     <- 0.110   # probability of adverse event 2 when progression-free under EXPR
p_FA3_EXPR     <- 0.070   # probability of adverse event 3 when progression-free under EXPR


# James asked that I consider including adverse events in the OS state.

# So, first I need to include the probability of adverse events 1,2 3 in the OS state under FOLFIRI. Everyone get's the same second line treatment (FOLFIRI) so once in the OS state everyone (Exp or SoC) has the same probability of an adverse event:

p_OSA1_FOLFIRI     <- 0.020   # probability of adverse event 1 when progressed and recieving FOLFIRI
p_OSA2_FOLFIRI     <- 0.260   # probability of adverse event 2 when progressed and recieving FOLFIRI
p_OSA3_FOLFIRI     <- 0.240   # probability of adverse event 3 when progressed and recieving FOLFIRI


# As part of the above, I need to convert my 30 day probability to a 14 day probability:


# I determined the probability of AEs per cycle from the following study (also described in Table 1 in the paper):  https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.2007.15.4138 

# In this study, Table 3 reports the % patients for selected adverse events occurring during or within 30 days of treatment.

# From this I took the incidence of Leukopenia, Diarrhea and Nausea and Vomiting, aka p_FA1_STD, p_FA2_STD and p_FA3_STD for the three treatments included in our study (i.e., the probability of these AEs for Folfox, Folfiri and Folfox + Bevacizumab).

# Because in this table the events occurred during or within 30 days of treatment, and our cycles are 14 days, I update my per cycle probability of these adverse events when applying them in our model. 
  
# That is, daily probability = 0.07/30 = 0.0023333, multiply the daily probability by 14 to get the probability for 14 days = 14*0.0023333 = 0.032666 = 0.033, such that I could update the 14 day probability of Leukopenia (adverse event 1) from 0.07 in the table to 0.033 in our model.

# However, technically we cannot divide probability by 30 to transform monthly probability to daily probability. To transform probability p for time period t to probability b’ for time t’, we usually apply the transformation assuming an exponential distribution (i.e., constant hazard):

# p’=1-(1-p)^(t’/t)

# To do this, we assume that the event follows a constant hazard rate, meaning the probability of the event occurring is uniformly distributed over time. This is a common assumption for such problems and implies an exponential distribution of time until the event occurs.

# I do the following as per the query I send Qiushi as pdf in email to maintain formatting on the 24/05/24, also saved here: 

# 1. So first, we define the given probability and time period: - Probability of the event occurring within 30 days: P30 = 0.07

# 2. Calculate the daily hazard rate: The hazard rate λ can be derived from the given probability using the exponential distribution formula:

# P(t) = 1 − e^−λt

# For t = 30 days:

#  0.07 = 1 − e^−30λ

# Rearrange to solve for λ:

#  e^−30λ = 1 − 0.07 = 0.93

# −30λ = ln(0.93)

# λ = −(ln(0.93)/30)

# 3. Calculate λ:

# λ = −(ln(0.93)/30)

# Using a calculator:

#   ln(0.93) ≈ −0.07257

# λ ≈ 0.07257/30 ≈ 0.002419

# 4. Calculate the probability for 14 days: 

# Using the hazard rate λ, we can find the probability for 14 days (P14):

#   P14 = 1 − e^−14λ

# Substitute λ:

#  P14 = 1 − e^−14×0.002419

#  P14 = 1 − e^−0.033866

# Using a calculator:

#   e^−0.033866 ≈ 0.96667

# P14 = 1 − 0.96667 ≈ 0.03333

# Result: The probability of the event occurring within 14 days is approximately 0.03333.


# Putting this all together in R: 

# p_FA1_STD:

# Given probability of the event occurring within 30 days
P_30 <- p_FA1_STD

# Calculate the daily hazard rate lambda
lambda <- -log(1 - P_30) / 30

# Calculate the probability of the event occurring within 14 days
P_14 <- 1 - exp(-lambda * 14)

# Print the results
cat("Daily hazard rate (lambda):", lambda, "\n")
cat("Probability of the event occurring within 14 days:", P_14, "\n")

# Recode the AE from 30 to 14 days

p_FA1_STD <- P_14


# p_FA2_STD:

# Given probability of the event occurring within 30 days
P_30 <- p_FA2_STD

# Calculate the daily hazard rate lambda
lambda <- -log(1 - P_30) / 30

# Calculate the probability of the event occurring within 14 days
P_14 <- 1 - exp(-lambda * 14)

# Print the results
cat("Daily hazard rate (lambda):", lambda, "\n")
cat("Probability of the event occurring within 14 days:", P_14, "\n")

# Recode the AE from 30 to 14 days

p_FA2_STD <- P_14

# p_FA3_STD

# Given probability of the event occurring within 30 days
P_30 <- p_FA3_STD

# Calculate the daily hazard rate lambda
lambda <- -log(1 - P_30) / 30

# Calculate the probability of the event occurring within 14 days
P_14 <- 1 - exp(-lambda * 14)

# Print the results
cat("Daily hazard rate (lambda):", lambda, "\n")
cat("Probability of the event occurring within 14 days:", P_14, "\n")

# Recode the AE from 30 to 14 days

p_FA3_STD <- P_14




# p_FA1_EXPR:

# Given probability of the event occurring within 30 days
P_30 <- p_FA1_EXPR

# Calculate the daily hazard rate lambda
lambda <- -log(1 - P_30) / 30

# Calculate the probability of the event occurring within 14 days
P_14 <- 1 - exp(-lambda * 14)

# Print the results
cat("Daily hazard rate (lambda):", lambda, "\n")
cat("Probability of the event occurring within 14 days:", P_14, "\n")

# Recode the AE from 30 to 14 days

p_FA1_EXPR <- P_14


# p_FA2_EXPR:

# Calculate the daily hazard rate lambda

# 2. Cost of treating the AE conditional on it occurring
# NOTE: c_AE1, c_AE2, c_AE3 are defined in the country-specific blocks

# This is how this code works to apply disutilities, it's the probability of the event happening and taking the disutility amount away from the utility you started with, for illustration purposes I set the utility you started with to 100 and the discount to 10% and the probability of the adverse event happening to 100%, so you should 100% lose 10% of your utility, and there are three adverse events following this rule, so you should 100% lose 10% of your baseline utility for each adverse event, so you should lose 30% of your baseline utility. The way this is coded, it basically figures out what x% of your baseline utility is, then it takes that number away from the baseline utility if that adverse event happens, so 10% of 100 is 10, so if that adverse event happens you take away 100-10 giving you 90, if all 3 adverse events happen, it's 100-10-10-10 giving you 70. That's why you have to be careful with your disutilities, because, if all three happen and they were 50%, 50% and 50% you could have a situation of 100-50-50-50, which would mean your utility would be -50, which isnt possible in utilities, as they are bounded by 1 and 0, so you might have to write a piece of code that checks if it is below 0, and when it is to set it == 0 instead.

# Now, let's think through this manually:


# There are 14 days in each cycle.
# Each adverse event lasts for 5 days and decreases utility by 30%.
# Since all three adverse events have a 100% probability of occurring, we can consider them as occurring simultaneously.

# During the 5 days when the adverse events occur, the utility for that day is decreased by 30% for each event, and all 3 events have a 100% probability of occuring, giving us a definite 30% decrease to that 1 three times:
# So:  1 - 0.30 - 0.30 - 0.30 = 0.10

# Days with AEs (5 days): Each AE reduces utility by 0.30, so the total reduction is 

# 3 × 0.30 = 0.90.

# The utility for these days is 

# 1 − 0.90 = 0.10


# Days without AEs (9 days): Utility = 1
# For each of the remaining 9 days, the utility is perfect (1).

# So, we have:
  
#  5 days with a utility of 0.10
#  9 days with a utility of 1

# Calculating the total utility:
#   5 * 0.10 + 9 * 1 = 0.50 + 9 = 9.50
 
# Dividing the total utility by the number of days in the cycle:
#   9.50 / 14 = 0.6786
 
# This manual calculation matches the result obtained using the formula.


# Put another way, 

# Sum the utility for each period:

#  Utility for 9 days without AEs:
#  9 * 1 = 9

#  Utility for 5 days with AEs:
#    5 * 0.10 = 0.50

#    9 + 0.50 = 9.50
  
#    9.50 / 14 = 0.6786
  
# According to Claude:

# The value 0.6786 represents the average utility of the first-line health state over the cycle, taking into account the impact of the three adverse events (AE1, AE2, and AE3).

# In this example:
# - The baseline utility of the first-line health state is 1 (or 100%), meaning perfect health.
# - Each adverse event reduces the utility by 30% and lasts for 5 out of the 14 days in the cycle.
# - All three adverse events have a 100% probability of occurring.

# When we calculate the utility of the first-line health state considering these adverse events, we get an average utility of 0.6786 (or 67.86%) over the cycle.

# This means that, on average, the patient experiences a health state that is 67.86% as good as perfect health during the entire cycle, due to the impact of the adverse events. The utility value takes into account both the severity and the duration of the adverse events.

# In other words, the adverse events reduce the overall quality of life or well-being of the patient during the cycle, resulting in an average utility of 0.6786 compared to a perfect health state with a utility of 1.


# Just to explain why I divide by 14 above:

# If a cycle of 14 days gives you a utility of 1 for that entire cycle, and the utility scale ranges from 0 to 1, then we can figure out the utility for each day within that cycle as below:

# Here's how we can think about it:

# 1. The total utility for the 14-day cycle is 1.
# 2. The utility scale ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 representing the highest possible utility (perfect health).
# 3. Since the total utility for the cycle is the highest possible value (1), and the cycle consists of 14 days, each day must contribute equally to the total utility.
# 4. To find the utility value for each day, we can divide the total utility by the number of days in the cycle:
   # Utility per day = Total utility / Total days
   # Utility per day = 1 / 14 = 0.0714 (rounded to 4 decimal places)

# However, when we multiply the utility per day by the total number of days, we get:
#  0.0714 × 14 = 0.9996 (rounded to 4 decimal places)

# This value is slightly less than 1 due to rounding.

# Anyway, if, as before, we approach the above manually, we can have 9 days of perfect health, or 9 days of 0.0714

# 9*0.0714
# [1] 0.6426

# And 5 days of half this perfect health:

# 0.0714*0.50
# [1] 0.0357

# 0.0357*5
# [1] 0.1785

# 0.1785+0.6426
# 0.8211

# The exact same as the formulas and dividing by 14 approaches above which gives us: 0.8214 (there is a very tiny difference at the end of the decimals due to rounding only). So my dividing by 14 was only necessary as in my manual approach I set every day's utility equal to 1, rather than 1/14th of 1, such that I then had to divide by 14 when I was done.


# Qiushi helped me to best understand and apply the above, he did also provide some very useful advice on adverse events that are not probabilities per cycle in email:

# The approach seems good to me. For your last question, you mentioned that the probability of adverse event is for each cycle – is it really the case? If so, it means that if someone had an adverse event 1 with probability 0.07 in one cycle, he still has a probability of 0.07 to have another adverse event 1 in a different cycle? If it is not this case, then it means that the probability is not for every cycle. If in the original study, the adverse event probability is calculated as a fraction of # of patients having the AE / # of total patients, it is not a probability per cycle. It is an overall probability, and it should be counted once (as what you are currently doing). Hope this clarifies your questions.










# ==============================================================================
# INITIALIZE BASE STATE COSTS (Drug Acquisition + Administration)
# ==============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC RATIONALE:
# In a cost-effectiveness model, the total cost per cycle in each health state
# comprises multiple components:
#   1. Drug acquisition costs (the chemotherapy regimens)
#   2. Administration costs (IV infusion, nursing time, facility overhead)
#   3. Expected adverse event (AE) costs (probability-weighted treatment costs for AEs)
#
# We initialize the BASE state costs here by combining drug and administration costs.
# These represent the core costs incurred by patients in each health state before
# accounting for the additional expected costs due to adverse events.
#
# After initialization, we will ADD the expected AE costs (probability × one-time cost).
# This approach separates the deterministic treatment costs from the probabilistic
# AE-related costs, improving transparency and maintainability.
#
# COUNTRY-SPECIFIC ALIGNMENT:
# These cost variables (c_PFS_Folfox, c_PFS_Bevacizumab, c_OS_Folfiri, administration_cost)
# are set by the active country block (Ireland, Germany, or Spain) earlier in the script,
# or are passed via the run_country_analysis() helper function when running automated
# country loops. The country-specific inputs are already loaded into the environment
# at this point, ensuring that the base costs reflect the correct jurisdiction.
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# SAFETY CHECK: Ensure country-specific parameters are loaded
# If running chunks individually, automatically load default country parameters
# to prevent "object not found" errors
if (!exists("administration_cost") || !exists("c_PFS_Folfox") || !exists("c_PFS_Bevacizumab") || !exists("c_OS_Folfiri")) {

  cat("\n")
  cat("================================================================================\n")
  cat("AUTO-LOADING COUNTRY-SPECIFIC PARAMETERS\n")
  cat("================================================================================\n")
  cat("Country-specific parameters were not found in the environment.\n")
  cat("Loading default parameters for Ireland...\n")
  cat("\n")
  cat("NOTE: If you intended to analyze a different country (Germany or Spain),\n")
  cat("      please run the 'COUNTRY-SPECIFIC PARAMETERS' chunk (around line 774)\n")
  cat("      first and set DEFAULT_COUNTRY to your desired country.\n")
  cat("================================================================================\n")
  cat("\n")

  # Check if get_country_params() function exists
  if (!exists("get_country_params")) {
    stop("\n\n",
         "================================================================================\n",
         "ERROR: get_country_params() function not defined!\n",
         "================================================================================\n",
         "The helper function get_country_params() has not been defined yet.\n",
         "\n",
         "SOLUTION:\n",
         "You must first run the 'COUNTRY-SPECIFIC PARAMETERS' chunk\n",
         "(starting around line 774) which defines this function.\n",
         "\n",
         "If knitting the entire document, this error indicates a structural problem.\n",
         "Please report this as a bug.\n",
         "================================================================================\n")
  }

  # Load default Ireland parameters
  params <- get_country_params("Ireland")

  # Unpack parameters into individual variables
  country_name            <- params$country_name
  c_PFS_Folfox           <- params$c_PFS_Folfox
  c_PFS_Bevacizumab      <- params$c_PFS_Bevacizumab
  c_OS_Folfiri           <- params$c_OS_Folfiri
  administration_cost     <- params$administration_cost
  subtyping_test_cost    <- params$subtyping_test_cost
  c_AE1                  <- params$c_AE1
  c_AE2                  <- params$c_AE2
  c_AE3                  <- params$c_AE3
  n_wtp                  <- params$n_wtp
  country_discount_rate      <- params$country_discount_rate
  country_max_discount_rate  <- params$country_max_discount_rate
  country_min_discount_rate  <- params$country_min_discount_rate

  cat("Default parameters loaded successfully for:", country_name, "\n")
  cat("\n")
}

# c_F_SoC: Cost per cycle in the PFS (progression-free survival) state under
#          standard of care (FOLFOX-4 regimen)
#
# COMPOSITION:
#   - c_PFS_Folfox: Drug acquisition cost for FOLFOX-4 per 14-day cycle
#   - administration_cost: IV administration cost per cycle (nursing, facility, etc.)
#
# This represents the baseline cost for patients who are progression-free and
# receiving first-line standard-of-care chemotherapy (FOLFOX-4 only, no bevacizumab).
c_F_SoC <- administration_cost + c_PFS_Folfox


# c_F_Exp: Cost per cycle in the PFS state under experimental treatment
#          (FOLFOX-4 + Bevacizumab)
#
# COMPOSITION:
#   - c_PFS_Folfox: Drug acquisition cost for FOLFOX-4 per 14-day cycle
#   - c_PFS_Bevacizumab: Drug acquisition cost for bevacizumab (5 mg/kg) per cycle
#   - administration_cost: IV administration cost per cycle
#
# This represents the baseline cost for patients who are progression-free and
# receiving the experimental first-line treatment (FOLFOX-4 plus bevacizumab).
# Bevacizumab is a biologic therapy added to standard chemotherapy, which significantly
# increases the drug acquisition cost but may improve progression-free survival.
c_F_Exp <- administration_cost + c_PFS_Folfox + c_PFS_Bevacizumab


# c_P: Cost per cycle in the OS (overall survival / progressed) state
#
# COMPOSITION:
#   - c_OS_Folfiri: Drug acquisition cost for FOLFIRI per 14-day cycle
#   - administration_cost: IV administration cost per cycle
#
# This represents the baseline cost for patients who have progressed beyond first-line
# therapy and are now receiving second-line treatment (FOLFIRI). In our model, ALL
# patients receive the same second-line regimen after progression, regardless of whether
# they initially received FOLFOX alone (SoC) or FOLFOX + bevacizumab (Exp). Therefore,
# c_P is identical for both strategies once patients enter the progressed/OS state.
c_P <- c_OS_Folfiri + administration_cost


# c_D: Cost per cycle in the Dead state
#
# COMPOSITION:
#   - No costs (patients who are dead incur no further treatment or healthcare costs)
#
# This is set to 0 as being in the dead state has no ongoing costs. This is standard
# practice in health economic modeling.
c_D <- 0


# ==============================================================================
# ADD EXPECTED ADVERSE EVENT COSTS TO BASE STATE COSTS
# ==============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC RATIONALE:
# Adverse events (AEs) impose additional costs on the healthcare system beyond the
# routine costs of drug acquisition and administration. Patients may experience AEs
# such as leukopenia, diarrhea, and vomiting, which require medical intervention
# (hospitalization, supportive care, medications).
#
# The EXPECTED cost of AEs per cycle is calculated as:
#   Expected AE cost = Probability(AE) × Cost(treating the AE)
#
# We model three key AEs (AE1: Leukopenia, AE2: Diarrhea, AE3: Vomiting), each with:
#   - A probability of occurrence per cycle (p_FA1, p_FA2, p_FA3)
#   - A one-time treatment cost if the AE occurs (c_AE1, c_AE2, c_AE3)
#
# AE probabilities differ by:
#   1. Treatment regimen (SoC vs Experimental in PFS; FOLFIRI in OS)
#   2. Health state (PFS vs OS)
#
# AE costs (c_AE1, c_AE2, c_AE3) are country-specific and set by the active country block.
#
# IMPORTANT MODELING ASSUMPTION:
# These probabilities represent the OVERALL probability of experiencing the AE during
# treatment (not a per-cycle recurring probability). Therefore, the AE cost is applied
# as a one-time expected cost added to the per-cycle state cost. This follows guidance
# from our collaborator Qiushi (see comment above) and reflects how AE incidence was
# reported in the source clinical trial (% of patients experiencing the AE during or
# within 30 days of treatment, converted to 14-day cycle probabilities using an
# exponential hazard transformation).
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Adjust c_F_SoC (PFS state, standard of care) for expected AE costs
# Patients on FOLFOX-4 alone have probabilities p_FA1_STD, p_FA2_STD, p_FA3_STD
# of experiencing AE1, AE2, and AE3, respectively.
c_F_SoC <- c_F_SoC + p_FA1_STD*c_AE1 + p_FA2_STD*c_AE2 + p_FA3_STD*c_AE3


# Adjust c_F_Exp (PFS state, experimental treatment) for expected AE costs
# Patients on FOLFOX-4 + bevacizumab have DIFFERENT AE probabilities
# (p_FA1_EXPR, p_FA2_EXPR, p_FA3_EXPR), reflecting the toxicity profile of the
# combination regimen. Bevacizumab may alter the incidence of certain AEs.
c_F_Exp <- c_F_Exp + p_FA1_EXPR*c_AE1 + p_FA2_EXPR*c_AE2 + p_FA3_EXPR*c_AE3


# Adjust c_P (OS/progressed state) for expected AE costs
# ALL patients in the progressed state receive FOLFIRI as second-line therapy,
# regardless of their initial treatment assignment. Therefore, both SoC and Exp
# patients face the same AE probabilities in this state (p_OSA1_FOLFIRI, p_OSA2_FOLFIRI,
# p_OSA3_FOLFIRI), and c_P is adjusted identically for both strategies.
c_P <- c_P + p_OSA1_FOLFIRI*c_AE1 + p_OSA2_FOLFIRI*c_AE2 + p_OSA3_FOLFIRI*c_AE3





# I get it, the cost is the cost of treatment (say c_F_SoC), and then we have some probability "p" of adding on to this cost with how much it might cost to have nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea, so we have the chance to increase this cost by the cost of these adverse events. 

# So for utility, the utility is the utility of the health state (say U_F_SoC), and then we have some probability "p" of taking away from this utility by how much it might decrease utility to have nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea, for the time that we have those things - so we have the chance to decrease this utility by the disutility of these adverse events.


# They have a probability of "X" of experiencing 7 days of decline in their utility, which will take their 14 days of utility "y" down by some value "z".


# So, their 14 days of utility are 0.85, they have a probabulity of p_FA1_STD of experiencing a decrease in this utility of 0.45.






v_tc_SoC <- m_M_SoC %*% c(c_F_SoC, c_P, c_D)
v_tc_Exp <- m_M_Exp %*% c(c_F_Exp, c_P, c_D)

v_tc_SoC
v_tc_Exp
```

```{r}

#07.2 Discounted Mean Costs and QALYs

# Finally, we'll aggregate these costs and utilities into overall discounted mean (average) costs and utilities.

# Obtain the discounted costs and QALYs by multiplying the vectors of total cost and total utility we created above by the discount rate for each cycle:

# Its important to remember what scale I'm on when I applied my discounting formula.
# If I set d_e<-0 then my code estimates 16.7 and 21.1 QALYs in each group which must be the quality adjusted cycles.

# Setting the discount rate back to 4% gives me 1.97 and 1.98 QALYs (which are really QA-cycles).

# Looking at the discounting vector I have defined below, I have converted cycles to days [I actually havent, but this is explained better at the bottom of the code chunk] but I need to convert the discount rate to a daily discount. If I don't, the result is that discounting reduces the cycles dramatically which reduces the difference which increases with time.

# I can adress this by defining the discount rate as divided by 365 (i.e. the number of days in a year) then the results become 16.4 and 20.6 QA-cycles which of course become 0.63 and 0.79 QALYs respectively, or 0.16 QALYs gained.

d_c <- d_c/365
d_e <- d_e/365

# - Then, the discount rate for each cycle needs to be defined accounting for the cycle length, as below:


v_dwc <- 1 / ((1 + d_c) ^ ((0:(n_cycle-1)) * t_cycle)) 
v_dwe <- 1 / ((1 + d_e) ^ ((0:(n_cycle-1)) * t_cycle))


# So, below we take the vector of costs, transposing it [the t() bit] to make it a 1 row matrix and using matrix multiplication [%*%] to multiply it by that discount factor vector, which is what you multiply by the outcome in each cycle to get the discounted value of the outcome for that cycle, and then it will all be summed all together across all cycles [across all cells of the 1 row matrix]. Giving you tc_d_SoC which is a scalar, or a single value, which is the lifetime expected cost for an average person under standard of care in this cohort. 

# Discount costs by multiplying the cost vector with discount weights (v_dwc) 
# tc_d_SoC  <-  t(v_tc_SoC)  %*% v_dwc
# tc_d_trtA <-  t(v_tc_trtA) %*% v_dwc
# tc_d_trtB <-  t(v_tc_trtB) %*% v_dwc

tc_d_SoC <-  t(v_tc_SoC) %*% v_dwc 
tc_d_Exp <-  t(v_tc_Exp) %*% v_dwc


# So, now we have the average cost per person for treatment with standard of care, and the experimental treatment. 


# Discount QALYS by multiplying the QALYs vector with discount weights (v_dwe) [probably utilities would have been a better term here, if I hadnt of updated it from fortnightly health state quality of life, to yearly health state quality of life]

tu_d_SoC <-  t(v_tu_SoC) %*% v_dwe
tu_d_Exp <-  t(v_tu_Exp) %*% v_dwe


# Store them into a vector -> So, we'll take the single values for cost for an average person under standard of care and the experimental treatment and store them in a vector v_tc_d:
v_tc_d <- c(tc_d_SoC, tc_d_Exp)
v_tu_d <- c(tu_d_SoC, tu_d_Exp)

v_tc_d
v_tu_d

# To make things a little easier to read we might name these values what they are costs for, so we can use the vector of strategy names [v_names_str] to name the values:

names (v_tc_d) <- v_names_strats
v_tc_d

names (v_tu_d) <- v_names_strats
v_tu_d


Discounted_Qalys_gained <- tu_d_Exp - tu_d_SoC
sum(Discounted_Qalys_gained)

# For utility, the utility values aren't different for the different states depending on the treatment strategy, i.e. SOC, Experimental Treatment, but the time spent in the states with the associated utility is different due to the treatment you're on, so your utility value will be higher if the treatment keeps you well for longer so that you stay in a higher utility state for longer than a lower utility state, i.e., progression.


# Dataframe with discounted costs and effectiveness

# So then we aggregate them into a dataframe with our discounted costs and utilities, and then we use this to calculate ICERs in: ## 07.3 Compute ICERs of the Markov model

# df_ce <- data.frame(Strategy = v_names_strats,
#                     Cost     = v_tc_d, 
#                     Effect   = v_tu_d)
# df_ce




# According to Bing:


# Explain this health economics R code: v_dwc <- 1 / ((1 + d_c) ^ ((0:(n_cycle-1)) * t_cycle))


# This R code is used to calculate the discount weights for costs in a health economics model. The discount weights are factors that are applied to future costs to reflect their present value. The discount weights depend on the discount rate for costs (d_c), the number of cycles in the model (n_cycle), and the length of each cycle in years (t_cycle).


# But my cycles arent in years, but actually in fortnights: t_cycle <- 14      # cycle length of 2 weeks (in [[days]] - this is assuming the survival curves I am digitising will be in [[days]] if they are in another period I will have to represent my cycle length in that period instead).                                 


# When t_cycle is a percentage of a year, then multiplying the yearly discount rate we start with (i.e., d_c or d_e) by this percentage of a year brings the discount rate to the right time period for the cycle, i.e., if cycles we study are 3 months, then multipling a years discount of 4% by 0.25 (t_cycle is a quarter of a year) gives a 3 month discount rate of 1%, so a per cycle discount rate calculated from the per year discount rate.


# Andy helped me convert my discount rate for costs and my discount rate for effects to days from years, so then I have a cycle length discount rate that matches the cycle length in my study by virtue of my cycle length being 14 days and multiplying a 1 day discount rate by these 14 days to get a 14 day discount rate.


# [the above kind of cements that I really should have created my fortnight as a percentage of a year rather than as 14, but we are where we are now, just have to bear that in mind to simplify the next model. Worth realising as well that it may not have been possible to do this given that I made use of transition data in days from ANGIOPREDICT].



# The code can be explained as follows:

# v_dwc <- assigns the result of the calculation to a variable named v_dwc, which stands for vector of discount weights for costs.

# 1 / divides 1 by the expression in the parentheses, which is the formula for the discount factor for costs.

# (1 + d_c) ^ raises 1 plus the discount rate for costs (d_c) to the power of the expression in the parentheses, which is the formula for the time horizon in years.

# ((0:(n_cycle-1)) * t_cycle) creates a sequence of numbers from 0 to n_cycle-1 and multiplies each number by t_cycle. This gives the time horizon in years for each cycle in the model.

# For example, if d_c = 0.03, n_cycle = 10, and t_cycle = 0.25, then the code will produce a vector of discount weights for costs as follows:

# v_dwc <- 1 / ((1 + 0.03) ^ ((0:9) * 0.25)) v_dwc [1] 1.0000000 0.9925568 0.9851855 0.9778852 0.9706546 [6] 0.9634925 0.9563977 0.9493693 0.9424062 0.9355074
 
# This means that the costs in cycle 1 are not discounted, the costs in cycle 2 are discounted by 0.74%, the costs in cycle 3 are discounted by 1.48%, and so on.























```

```{r}
# I create a parameter "ICER" to pull the ICER value straight out of the table, I select ($) ICER from df_cea and then pick the 2nd entry in this ICER parameter, so that I'm getting the number rather than the NA, i.e.:
```

```{r}

#08.1 Load Markov model function

#08.3 One-way sensitivity analysis (OWSA)

# A brief note on how parameters are varied one at a time:

# A simple one-way DSA starts with choosing a model parameter to be investigated. Next, the modeler specifies a range for this parameter and the number of evenly spaced points along this range at which to evaluate model outcomes. The model is then run for each element of the vector of parameter values by setting the parameter of interest to the value, holding all other model parameters at their default base case values.

# To conduct the one-way DSA, we then call the function run_owsa_det with my_owsa_params_range, specifying the parameters to be varied and over which ranges, and my_params_basecase as the fixed parameter values to be used in the model when a parameter is not being explicitly varied in the one-way sensitivity analysis.


options(digits=4)

## Initialization ----

# Load the model as a function that is defined in the supporting script
# source("Functions_markov_3state.R")
# Test function
# calculate_ce_out(l_params_all)


source(file = "oncologySemiMarkov_function.R")
# If I change any code in this main model code file, I will also need to update the function that I call.


# ============================================================================
# PARAMETRIC SURVIVAL CURVE CHOICE - DISTRIBUTION SELECTION MECHANISM
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC MODELLING PRINCIPLE:
# Cost-effectiveness models rely on extrapolation of survival curves beyond
# observed trial data. The choice of parametric distribution is a key
# structural assumption that can significantly impact results.
#
# STRUCTURAL UNCERTAINTY IN HEALTH ECONOMIC MODELS:
# Structural uncertainty refers to uncertainty about the fundamental form
# of the model itself, as opposed to parameter uncertainty (uncertainty about
# parameter values within a fixed model structure).
#
# For survival extrapolation, structural uncertainty includes:
#   - Which parametric family to use (Weibull, gamma, log-normal, etc.)
#   - Whether to use single-curve or multi-curve approaches
#   - How to model treatment effects (hazard ratios vs. separate curves)
#
# SCENARIO ANALYSIS IN HEALTH ECONOMICS:
# Best practice (per NICE, ISPOR, CADTH guidelines) is to:
#   1. Fit multiple candidate distributions to the data
#   2. Select a base case based on:
#        - Statistical fit criteria (AIC, BIC)
#        - Visual fit to observed data
#        - Clinical plausibility of extrapolated tail
#        - Goodness-of-fit tests
#   3. Test alternative distributions in scenario analyses
#   4. Report how cost-effectiveness conclusions change across scenarios
#   5. If results are highly sensitive, consider this in decision-making
#
# IMPLEMENTATION APPROACH:
# We implement a "curve_choice" parameter that acts as a switch:
#   - "weibull": Use Weibull distribution (BASE CASE)
#   - "gamma": Use gamma distribution (SCENARIO ANALYSIS)
#
# WHY THIS DESIGN:
# This approach allows us to run the entire analysis (base case + sensitivity
# analyses) under different distributional assumptions without duplicating code.
# The same model structure is used; only the survival probabilities change.
#
# HOW IT WORKS - TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATION:
# 1. Set curve_choice here (before running model)
# 2. This parameter is passed to the oncologySemiMarkov function
# 3. Inside the function, conditional logic selects the appropriate p*() function:
#      if curve_choice == "weibull": use pweibull()
#      if curve_choice == "gamma": use pgamma()
# 4. Hazard ratios are applied identically regardless of base distribution
#
# THEORETICAL JUSTIFICATION - HAZARD RATIO INVARIANCE:
# Hazard ratios can be applied to any parametric survival distribution because:
#   - HR operates on the hazard function: h_exp(t) = HR × h_control(t)
#   - This transforms to survival via: S(t) = exp(-∫h(u)du) = exp(-H(t))
#   - For any distribution: H(t) = -log(S(t))
#   - Apply HR: H_exp(t) = HR × H_control(t)
#   - Back to survival: S_exp(t) = exp(-HR × H_control(t)) = [S_control(t)]^HR
# This works for Weibull, gamma, or any other parametric distribution.
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC INTERPRETATION:
# The hazard ratio represents the relative treatment effect - how much the
# experimental treatment changes the instantaneous risk of an event compared
# to standard of care. This relative effect is assumed to be constant over time
# (proportional hazards assumption) and can be applied to any baseline hazard.
#
# BASE CASE: Use Weibull distribution
# Weibull selected as base case because:
#   - Commonly used in oncology health economic models
#   - Flexible hazard function (monotonically increasing or decreasing)
#   - Good statistical fit to the observed data
#   - Clinically plausible long-term extrapolation
curve_choice <- "weibull"

# SCENARIO ANALYSIS: To run gamma scenario, uncomment the line below and comment the line above
# curve_choice <- "gamma"

# NOTE ON GAMMA PARAMETERS:
# The oncologySemiMarkov function accesses survival distribution parameters
# from the environment (they're not all in l_params_all for the base case).
#
# For the function to work with EITHER Weibull OR Gamma, both sets of
# parameters need to be defined as variables before calling the function.
#
# FOR WEIBULL (already defined earlier in the survival analysis section):
#   - coef_weibull_shape_SoC, coef_weibull_scale_SoC (for TTP)
#   - coef_TTD_weibull_shape_SoC, coef_TTD_weibull_scale_SoC (for TTD)
#
# FOR GAMMA (defined earlier in the survival analysis section):
#   - coef_gamma_shape_SoC, coef_gamma_rate_SoC (for TTP)
#   - coef_TTD_gamma_shape_SoC, coef_TTD_gamma_rate_SoC (for TTD)
#
# These were extracted earlier and should already exist in the environment.
# The function will use the appropriate set based on curve_choice.


# Create list l_params_all with all input probabilities, costs, utilities, etc.,

# Test whether the function works (and generates the same results)
# - to do so, first a list of parameter values needs to be generated

# Now I update this list with the variables I have:

# If I updated utility for AE above, then I'll have to take that into account for u_F below:

#===============================================================================
# HELPER FUNCTION AND MAIN COUNTRY ANALYSIS
#===============================================================================
#
# This section defines run_country_analysis() - a helper function that
# encapsulates the entire country-specific analysis workflow.
#
# REPLACES: The previous manual country blocks (formerly at lines 774-870)
#           and single-country utility scenario application
#
# NEW APPROACH: Automated analysis of all three countries with identical
#               model structure, eliminating manual code editing
#
#===============================================================================


#===============================================================================
# HELPER FUNCTION: run_country_analysis()
#===============================================================================

run_country_analysis <- function(
  country_name,
  utility_scenario = "ramsey_basecase",
  patient_age = 65,
  curve_choice_param = "weibull"
) {
  # ============================================================================
  # PURPOSE:
  # --------
  # This function encapsulates the entire country-specific CEA workflow:
  # 1. Set country-specific costs, discount rates, and WTP threshold
  # 2. Obtain utilities via get_utility_scenario()
  # 3. Build complete parameter list (l_params_all)
  # 4. Run oncologySemiMarkov() model
  # 5. Extract and structure results
  # 6. Return results as a single-row data frame
  #
  # HEALTH-ECONOMIC RATIONALE:
  # --------------------------
  # Separating country-specific parameterisation from model logic ensures:
  # - Consistency: All countries use identical model structure and methods
  # - Transparency: Parameter differences are explicit and documented
  # - Reproducibility: Analyses can be re-run programmatically
  # - Flexibility: Easy to add new countries or modify existing parameters
  #
  # The base-case model structure remains unchanged for each country. Only the
  # country-specific inputs (costs, discount rates, WTP thresholds, population
  # norms) differ across jurisdictions.
  #
  # PARAMETERS:
  # -----------
  # @param country_name: "Ireland", "Germany", or "Spain"
  # @param utility_scenario: "ramsey_basecase" or "population_norm_adjusted"
  # @param patient_age: Age for population norm lookup (default 65)
  # @param curve_choice_param: "weibull" or "gamma" (default "weibull")
  #
  # RETURNS:
  # --------
  # Single-row data frame with columns: country, utility_scenario, u_PFS, u_PD,
  # cost_SoC, cost_Exp, qaly_SoC, qaly_Exp, inc_cost, inc_qaly, icer, nmb, n_wtp
  #
  # DEPENDENCIES:
  # -------------
  # Assumes the following exist in global environment:
  # - Functions: get_utility_scenario(), oncologySemiMarkov()
  # - Data: df_popnorm
  # - Global parameters: HR_FP_Exp, HR_FP_SoC, HR_PD_Exp, HR_PD_SoC, P_OSD_SoC,
  #   P_OSD_Exp, p_FA1_STD, p_FA2_STD, p_FA3_STD, p_FA1_EXPR, p_FA2_EXPR,
  #   p_FA3_EXPR, p_OSA1_FOLFIRI, p_OSA2_FOLFIRI, p_OSA3_FOLFIRI, c_D,
  #   AE1_DisUtil, AE2_DisUtil, AE3_DisUtil, u_D, n_cycle, t_cycle
  # - Survival coefficients: coef_weibull_shape_SoC, coef_weibull_scale_SoC,
  #   coef_TTD_weibull_shape_SoC, coef_TTD_weibull_scale_SoC (and gamma versions)
  # ============================================================================

  # Print header
  # ------------
  cat("\n")
  cat("========================================================================\n")
  cat("RUNNING COUNTRY ANALYSIS\n")
  cat("========================================================================\n")
  cat("Country:          ", country_name, "\n")
  cat("Utility scenario: ", utility_scenario, "\n")
  cat("Curve choice:     ", curve_choice_param, "\n")
  cat("------------------------------------------------------------------------\n")

  #=============================================================================
  # STEP 1: SET COUNTRY-SPECIFIC PARAMETERS
  #=============================================================================
  # Each country has different costs, discount rates, and WTP thresholds
  # reflecting local drug pricing, healthcare systems, and policy guidelines
  #=============================================================================

  if (country_name == "Ireland") {
    # IRELAND PARAMETERS
    # ------------------
    # Source: Irish drug pricing and HIQA guidelines

    # Treatment costs per 14-day cycle (€)
    c_PFS_Folfox_country <- 157.77          # FOLFOX-4 regimen
    c_PFS_Bevacizumab_country <- 1425.84    # Bevacizumab (5mg/kg)
    c_OS_Folfiri_country <- 167.10          # FOLFIRI regimen
    administration_cost_country <- 406.50    # IV administration per cycle
    subtyping_test_cost_country <- 400       # RAS testing (one-time)

    # Adverse event costs (€) - one-time costs when AE occurs
    c_AE1_country <- 3485.23  # Grade 3+ neutropenia management
    c_AE2_country <- 1792.82  # Grade 3+ diarrhea management
    c_AE3_country <- 502.69   # Grade 3+ nausea/vomiting management

    # Willingness-to-pay threshold (€/QALY)
    n_wtp_country <- 45000  # HIQA guideline for Ireland

    # Discount rate (annual)
    country_discount_rate_val <- 0.04  # 4% for costs and effects (HIQA)

  } else if (country_name == "Germany") {
    # GERMANY PARAMETERS
    # ------------------
    # Source: German drug pricing and IQWiG guidelines
    # Note: Costs received as monthly values, converted to 14-day cycles

    # Treatment costs per 14-day cycle (€)
    # Conversion formula: (monthly cost / 30 days) × 14 days
    c_PFS_Folfox_country <- ((1406.37 / 30) * 14)
    c_PFS_Bevacizumab_country <- ((3252.19 / 30) * 14)
    c_OS_Folfiri_country <- ((1442.70 / 30) * 14)
    administration_cost_country <- 1927.72
    subtyping_test_cost_country <- 400

    # Adverse event costs (€)
    c_AE1_country <- 4188.31
    c_AE2_country <- 1982.68
    c_AE3_country <- 1307.72

    # Willingness-to-pay threshold (€/QALY)
    n_wtp_country <- 78871  # Implicit threshold from IQWiG assessments

    # Discount rate (annual)
    country_discount_rate_val <- 0.03  # 3% for costs and effects (IQWiG)

  } else if (country_name == "Spain") {
    # SPAIN PARAMETERS
    # ----------------
    # Source: Spanish drug pricing and health economic guidelines

    # Treatment costs per 14-day cycle (€)
    c_PFS_Folfox_country <- 323.39
    c_PFS_Bevacizumab_country <- 1399.33
    c_OS_Folfiri_country <- 147.31
    administration_cost_country <- 332.39
    subtyping_test_cost_country <- 400

    # Adverse event costs (€)
    c_AE1_country <- 5710.97
    c_AE2_country <- 305.55
    c_AE3_country <- 35.11

    # Willingness-to-pay threshold (€/QALY)
    n_wtp_country <- 30000  # Commonly cited threshold for Spain

    # Discount rate (annual)
    country_discount_rate_val <- 0.03  # 3% for costs and effects

  } else {
    # ERROR HANDLING: Unknown country
    stop("Unknown country: ", country_name,
         ". Must be 'Ireland', 'Germany', or 'Spain'.")
  }

  # Convert annual discount rates to daily rates
  # ---------------------------------------------
  # Model operates on 14-day cycles, so rates must be daily
  # Formula: daily_rate = annual_rate / 365
  d_c_country <- country_discount_rate_val / 365  # Daily rate for costs
  d_e_country <- country_discount_rate_val / 365  # Daily rate for effects

  cat("Treatment costs:   FOLFOX = €", round(c_PFS_Folfox_country, 2),
      ", Bev = €", round(c_PFS_Bevacizumab_country, 2), "\n", sep = "")
  cat("WTP threshold:     €", n_wtp_country, " per QALY\n", sep = "")
  cat("Discount rate:     ", country_discount_rate_val * 100, "% (annual)\n", sep = "")

  #=============================================================================
  # STEP 2: OBTAIN SCENARIO-SPECIFIC UTILITIES
  #=============================================================================
  # Call get_utility_scenario() to get PFS and PD utilities based on:
  # - Country (for population norm lookup if needed)
  # - Age (representative patient age, typically 65 for mCRC)
  # - Utility scenario (Ramsey base-case vs. population-norm adjusted)
  #
  # RAMSEY BASE-CASE:
  # - Uses directly reported Ramsey (2010) utilities: u_PFS = 0.85, u_PD = 0.65
  # - Source: Ramsey SD, et al. Quality of life in survivors of colorectal
  #   cancer. Cancer. 2000;88(6):1294-1303.
  #
  # POPULATION-NORM ADJUSTED:
  # - Adjusts Ramsey utilities to country-specific population norms
  # - Uses EQ-5D population norms from Szende et al. (2014)
  # - Calculates multipliers to scale mCRC utilities to local baseline
  # - Preserves relative difference between PFS and PD states
  # - Rationale: Accounts for cultural differences in utility elicitation
  #=============================================================================

  cat("\n")
  cat("Obtaining utilities for scenario: ", utility_scenario, "\n", sep = "")

  utility_result <- get_utility_scenario(
    country          = country_name,
    age              = patient_age,
    utility_scenario = utility_scenario,
    df_popnorm       = df_popnorm  # Must exist in global environment
  )

  # Extract utilities from returned list
  u_F_country <- utility_result$u_PFS  # PFS utility
  u_P_country <- utility_result$u_PD   # PD utility

  cat("u_PFS (PFS state): ", round(u_F_country, 4), "\n", sep = "")
  cat("u_PD (PD state):   ", round(u_P_country, 4), "\n", sep = "")
  cat("Method:            ", utility_result$method, "\n", sep = "")

  #=============================================================================
  # STEP 3: BUILD COMPLETE PARAMETER LIST
  #=============================================================================
  # Construct l_params_all by combining:
  # 1. Country-specific parameters (from STEP 1)
  # 2. Scenario-specific utilities (from STEP 2)
  # 3. Global parameters (defined earlier in main document)
  #
  # IMPORTANT: All global parameters must be defined in the environment
  # before calling this function
  #=============================================================================

  cat("\n")
  cat("Building parameter list...\n")

  l_params_all_country <- list(
    # Hazard ratios (treatment effects on PFS and OS)
    # -----------------------------------------------
    HR_FP_Exp = HR_FP_Exp,  # PFS hazard ratio (experimental vs. SoC)
    HR_FP_SoC = HR_FP_SoC,  # PFS hazard ratio (SoC vs. reference, = 1)
    HR_PD_Exp = HR_PD_Exp,  # OS hazard ratio (experimental vs. SoC)
    HR_PD_SoC = HR_PD_SoC,  # OS hazard ratio (SoC vs. reference, = 1)
    P_OSD_SoC = P_OSD_SoC,  # Probability of death in PD state (SoC)
    P_OSD_Exp = P_OSD_Exp,  # Probability of death in PD state (Exp)

    # Adverse event probabilities (per cycle)
    # ----------------------------------------
    # Standard treatment (SoC) in PFS state:
    p_FA1_STD = p_FA1_STD,   # AE1 probability - neutropenia
    p_FA2_STD = p_FA2_STD,   # AE2 probability - diarrhea
    p_FA3_STD = p_FA3_STD,   # AE3 probability - nausea/vomiting
    # Experimental treatment (Exp) in PFS state:
    p_FA1_EXPR = p_FA1_EXPR, # AE1 probability
    p_FA2_EXPR = p_FA2_EXPR, # AE2 probability
    p_FA3_EXPR = p_FA3_EXPR, # AE3 probability
    # FOLFIRI treatment in PD state:
    p_OSA1_FOLFIRI = p_OSA1_FOLFIRI, # AE1 probability
    p_OSA2_FOLFIRI = p_OSA2_FOLFIRI, # AE2 probability
    p_OSA3_FOLFIRI = p_OSA3_FOLFIRI, # AE3 probability

    # Country-specific costs
    # ----------------------
    administration_cost = administration_cost_country,
    c_PFS_Folfox = c_PFS_Folfox_country,
    c_PFS_Bevacizumab = c_PFS_Bevacizumab_country,
    c_OS_Folfiri = c_OS_Folfiri_country,
    subtyping_test_cost = subtyping_test_cost_country,
    c_AE1 = c_AE1_country,
    c_AE2 = c_AE2_country,
    c_AE3 = c_AE3_country,
    c_D = c_D,  # Death state cost (global, = 0)

    # Scenario-specific utilities
    # ---------------------------
    u_F = u_F_country,  # Utility in PFS state
    u_P = u_P_country,  # Utility in PD state
    u_D = u_D,          # Utility in death state (= 0)

    # Adverse event disutilities
    # --------------------------
    # Percentage reduction in utility when AE occurs
    AE1_DisUtil = AE1_DisUtil,
    AE2_DisUtil = AE2_DisUtil,
    AE3_DisUtil = AE3_DisUtil,

    # Country-specific discount rates (daily)
    # ---------------------------------------
    d_e = d_e_country,  # Discount rate for effects (QALYs)
    d_c = d_c_country,  # Discount rate for costs

    # Model structure parameters
    # --------------------------
    n_cycle = n_cycle,  # Number of cycles (143 = ~5.5 years)
    t_cycle = t_cycle   # Cycle length in days (14 = 2 weeks)
  )

  #=============================================================================
  # STEP 4: RUN THE MARKOV MODEL
  #=============================================================================
  # Call oncologySemiMarkov() with complete parameter list
  # This function:
  # 1. Reconstructs time-dependent transition probabilities from survival curves
  # 2. Applies hazard ratios to modify probabilities by strategy
  # 3. Runs the cohort trace through all cycles
  # 4. Accumulates costs and QALYs with discounting
  # 5. Calculates incremental metrics and ICER
  #
  # Uses survival curve coefficients from global environment
  # (e.g., coef_weibull_shape_SoC, coef_weibull_scale_SoC)
  #=============================================================================

  cat("Running oncologySemiMarkov model...\n")

  result <- oncologySemiMarkov(
    l_params_all = l_params_all_country,
    n_wtp = n_wtp_country,
    curve_choice = curve_choice_param
  )

  cat("Model run completed.\n")

  #=============================================================================
  # STEP 5: EXTRACT AND STRUCTURE RESULTS
  #=============================================================================
  # The oncologySemiMarkov() function returns a list with:
  # - $Cost: vector of total costs by strategy (SoC, Exp)
  # - $Effect: vector of total QALYs by strategy (SoC, Exp)
  # - $ICER: incremental cost-effectiveness ratio
  # - $NMB: net monetary benefit at specified WTP threshold
  #
  # Extract and calculate all key metrics
  #=============================================================================

  # Extract costs and effects by strategy
  cost_SoC <- result$Cost[1]   # Total cost for standard of care
  cost_Exp <- result$Cost[2]   # Total cost for experimental (bevacizumab)
  qaly_SoC <- result$Effect[1] # Total QALYs for standard of care
  qaly_Exp <- result$Effect[2] # Total QALYs for experimental

  # Calculate incremental metrics
  # Incremental cost = Cost_Exp - Cost_SoC
  # Can be positive (treatment is more expensive) or negative (cost-saving)
  inc_cost <- cost_Exp - cost_SoC

  # Incremental QALYs = QALY_Exp - QALY_SoC
  # Expect positive for effective treatment (more QALYs gained)
  inc_qaly <- qaly_Exp - qaly_SoC

  # Extract ICER from model output
  # ICER = Incremental cost per QALY gained
  # If ICER < WTP threshold, treatment is cost-effective
  # Note: DSAICER is the same for both strategies (it's a ratio), so we take the first value
  icer_value <- result$DSAICER[1]

  # Calculate Net Monetary Benefit (NMB) = (Inc_QALY × WTP) - Inc_Cost
  # Positive NMB indicates cost-effective treatment at given WTP
  nmb_value <- (inc_qaly * n_wtp_country) - inc_cost

  # Print summary
  cat("\n")
  cat("RESULTS SUMMARY:\n")
  cat("----------------\n")
  cat("Cost (SoC):       €", format(round(cost_SoC, 2), big.mark=","), "\n", sep = "")
  cat("Cost (Exp):       €", format(round(cost_Exp, 2), big.mark=","), "\n", sep = "")
  cat("QALYs (SoC):      ", round(qaly_SoC, 4), "\n", sep = "")
  cat("QALYs (Exp):      ", round(qaly_Exp, 4), "\n", sep = "")
  cat("Incremental cost: €", format(round(inc_cost, 2), big.mark=","), "\n", sep = "")
  cat("Incremental QALY: ", round(inc_qaly, 4), "\n", sep = "")
  cat("ICER:             €", format(round(icer_value, 2), big.mark=","), " per QALY\n", sep = "")
  cat("NMB:              €", format(round(nmb_value, 2), big.mark=","), "\n", sep = "")
  cat("========================================================================\n")

  #=============================================================================
  # STEP 6: RETURN STRUCTURED RESULTS
  #=============================================================================
  # Return single-row data frame for easy row-binding across countries
  #=============================================================================

  return(data.frame(
    country = country_name,
    utility_scenario = utility_scenario,
    u_PFS = u_F_country,
    u_PD = u_P_country,
    cost_SoC = cost_SoC,
    cost_Exp = cost_Exp,
    qaly_SoC = qaly_SoC,
    qaly_Exp = qaly_Exp,
    inc_cost = inc_cost,
    inc_qaly = inc_qaly,
    icer = icer_value,
    nmb = nmb_value,
    n_wtp = n_wtp_country,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

cat("\n")
cat("Helper function run_country_analysis() defined successfully.\n")
cat("\n")


#===============================================================================
# MAIN ANALYSIS: RUN ALL COUNTRIES
#===============================================================================
#
# HEALTH-ECONOMIC RATIONALE:
# --------------------------
# This section runs the base-case CEA for all three countries automatically.
# Previously, users had to manually comment/uncomment country-specific parameter
# blocks. This automated approach:
#
# 1. ELIMINATES MANUAL EDITING: No commenting/uncommenting required
# 2. ENSURES CONSISTENCY: All countries use identical model structure
# 3. IMPROVES REPRODUCIBILITY: Results regenerated programmatically
# 4. FACILITATES COMPARISON: Results automatically combined for easy review
# 5. REDUCES ERRORS: No risk of running wrong country parameters
#
# The base-case analysis remains unchanged for each country. Only country-
# specific inputs (costs, discount rates, WTP thresholds, population norms)
# differ across jurisdictions.
#
# UTILITY SCENARIO SELECTION:
# ---------------------------
# The utility_scenario_main flag controls which utility values are used:
#
# - "ramsey_basecase": Ramsey (2010) utilities directly (u_PFS = 0.85, u_PD = 0.65)
#   This is the PRIMARY base case reported in the manuscript.
#
# - "population_norm_adjusted": Adjusts Ramsey utilities to country-specific
#   population norms using EQ-5D data from Szende et al. (2014)
#   This is a SCENARIO ANALYSIS to explore cultural differences.
#
# NOTE: The scenario analysis chunk at the end of this document will run
#       BOTH scenarios for all countries regardless of this setting.
#       This flag only controls which scenario is used for the main model
#       outputs (plots, tables, detailed sensitivity analyses, etc.).
#
#===============================================================================

# Set utility scenario for main analysis
# ---------------------------------------

# Run analysis for all countries

main_results_list <- lapply(countries_to_analyze, function(ctry) {
  run_country_analysis(

  )
})

# Combine results into single data frame

main_results_df <- do.call(rbind, main_results_list)
rownames(main_results_df) <- main_results_df$country
```
