# A one-way sensitivity analysis (OWSA) can be defined by specifying the names of the parameters that are to be incuded and their minimum and maximum values.


# We create a dataframe containing all parameters we want to do the sensitivity analysis on, and the min and max values of the parameters of interest 
# "min" and "max" are the mininum and maximum values of the parameters of interest.


# options(scipen = 999) # disabling scientific notation in R

df_params_OWSA <- data.frame(
  pars = c("HR_FP_Exp", "HR_FP_SoC", "HR_PD_SoC", "HR_PD_Exp", "P_OSD_SoC", "P_OSD_Exp", "p_FA1_STD", "p_FA2_STD", "p_FA3_STD", "p_FA1_EXPR", "p_FA2_EXPR", "p_FA3_EXPR", "p_OSA1_FOLFIRI", "p_OSA2_FOLFIRI", "p_OSA3_FOLFIRI", "administration_cost", "c_PFS_Folfox", "c_PFS_Bevacizumab", "c_OS_Folfiri", "subtyping_test_cost", "c_AE1", "c_AE2", "c_AE3", "d_e", "d_c", "u_F", "u_P", "AE1_DisUtil", "AE2_DisUtil", "AE3_DisUtil"),   # names of the parameters to be changed
  min  = c(Minimum_HR_FP_Exp, Minimum_HR_FP_SoC, Minimum_HR_PD_SoC, Minimum_HR_PD_Exp, Minimum_P_OSD_SoC, Minimum_P_OSD_Exp, Minimum_p_FA1_STD, Minimum_p_FA2_STD, Minimum_p_FA3_STD, Minimum_p_FA1_EXPR, Minimum_p_FA2_EXPR, Minimum_p_FA3_EXPR, Minimum_p_OSA1_FOLFIRI, Minimum_p_OSA2_FOLFIRI, Minimum_p_OSA3_FOLFIRI, Minimum_administration_cost, Minimum_c_PFS_Folfox, Minimum_c_PFS_Bevacizumab, Minimum_c_OS_Folfiri, Minimum_subtyping_test_cost, Minimum_c_AE1, Minimum_c_AE2, Minimum_c_AE3, Minimum_d_e, Minimum_d_c, Minimum_u_F, Minimum_u_P, Minimum_AE1_DisUtil, Minimum_AE2_DisUtil, Minimum_AE3_DisUtil),         # min parameter values
  max  = c(Maximum_HR_FP_Exp, Maximum_HR_FP_SoC, Maximum_HR_PD_SoC, Maximum_HR_PD_Exp, Maximum_P_OSD_SoC, Maximum_P_OSD_Exp, Maximum_p_FA1_STD, Maximum_p_FA2_STD, Maximum_p_FA3_STD, Maximum_p_FA1_EXPR, Maximum_p_FA2_EXPR, Maximum_p_FA3_EXPR, Maximum_p_OSA1_FOLFIRI, Maximum_p_OSA2_FOLFIRI, Maximum_p_OSA3_FOLFIRI, Maximum_administration_cost, Maximum_c_PFS_Folfox, Maximum_c_PFS_Bevacizumab, Maximum_c_OS_Folfiri, Maximum_subtyping_test_cost, Maximum_c_AE1,  Maximum_c_AE2, Maximum_c_AE3, Maximum_d_e, Maximum_d_c, Maximum_u_F, Maximum_u_P, Maximum_AE1_DisUtil, Maximum_AE2_DisUtil, Maximum_AE3_DisUtil)          # max parameter values
)


# I made sure the names of the parameters to be varied and their mins and maxs are in the same order in all the brackets above in order to make sure that the min and max being applied are the min and the max of the parameter I want to consider a min and a max for.



# The OWSA is performed using the run_owsa_det function


# This function runs a deterministic one-way sensitivity analysis (OWSA) on a given function that produces outcomes. rdrr.io/github/DARTH-git/dampack/src/R/run_dsa.R

DSAICER  <- run_owsa_det(

# run_owsa_det: https://rdrr.io/github/DARTH-git/dampack/man/run_owsa_det.html

  # We need to make sure we consistently use "DSAICER" throughout, or else the function will present with an error saying "DSAICER" not found.  
   
# Arguments:
  
  params_range     = df_params_OWSA,     # dataframe with parameters for OWSA

# params_range	
# data.frame with 3 columns of parameters for OWSA in the following order: "pars", "min", and "max".
# The number of samples from this range is determined by nsamp. 
# "pars" are the parameters of interest and must be a subset of the parameters from params_basecase.


# Details
# params_range
 
# "pars" are the names of the input parameters of interest. These are the parameters that will be varied in the deterministic sensitivity analysis. variables in "pars" column must be a subset of variables in params_basecase
 

  
  params_basecase  = l_params_all,       # list with all parameters

# params_basecase	

# a named list of basecase values for input parameters needed by FUN, the user-defined function. So, I guess it takes the values that the parameters are equal to in l_params_all as the base case, so if cost is generated equal to 1,000 it'll take that as the base case, and then take the min and the max around this from the data.frame we created above.

# To conduct the one-way DSA, we then call the function run_owsa_det with my_owsa_params_range, specifying the parameters to be varied and over which ranges, and my_params_basecase as the fixed parameter values to be used in the model when a parameter is not being explicitly varied in the one-way sensitivity analysis. https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dampack/vignettes/dsa_generation.html

  nsamp            = 100,                # number of parameter values

# nsamp	

# number of sets of parameter values to be generated. If NULL, 100 parameter values are used -> I think Eva Enns said these are automatically evenly spaced out values of the parameters.

# Additional inputs are the number of equally-spaced samples (nsamp) to be used between the specified minimum and maximum of each range, the user-defined function (FUN) to be called to generate model outcomes for each strategy, the vector of outcomes to be stored (must be outcomes generated by the data frame output of the function passed in FUN), and the vector of strategy names to be evaluated.

# cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dampack/vignettes/dsa_generation.html

  FUN              = oncologySemiMarkov, # function to compute outputs

# FUN	
# function that takes the basecase in params_basecase and runs the analysis in the function... to produce the outcome of interest. The FUN must return a dataframe where the first column are the strategy names and the rest of the columns must be outcomes.
#  

 outcomes         = c("DSAICER"),           # output to do the OWSA on

# string vector with the outcomes of interest from FUN produced by nsamp
# This basically tells run_owsa_det what the name of the outcome of interest from the function we fed it is. Here our function previously had NMB, i.e., the net monetary benefit.

#  outcomes         = c("NMB"),           # output to do the OWSA on

# outcomes	

  strategies       = v_names_strats,       # names of the strategies

# If I went back to trying to produce one ICER for the tornado diagram I would replace the above with this and similarly update my function per the commented code therein:  strategies       = "Experimental Treatment",       # names of the strategies


# strategies
# Set it equal to a vector of strategy names. The default NULL will use strategy names in FUN (  strategies = NULL,)
# Here that's "Standard of Care" and "Experimental Treatment".

  progress = TRUE,

# progress	
# TRUE or FALSE for whether or not function progress should be displayed in console, i.e., like 75% complete, 100%, etc.,

# The input progress = TRUE allows the user to see a progress bar as the DSA is conducted. When many parameters are being varied, nsamp is large, and/or the user-defined function is computationally burdensome, the DSA may take a noticeable amount of time to compute and the progress display is recommended.
# cran.r-project.org/web/packages/dampack/vignettes/dsa_generation.html


  n_wtp            = n_wtp               # extra argument to pass to FUN to specify the willingness to pay
)

# Value
# A list containing dataframes with the results of the sensitivity analyses. The list will contain a dataframe for each outcome specified. List elements can be visualized with plot.owsa, owsa_opt_strat and owsa_tornado from dampack

# Basically, run_owsa_det creates the above.

# Also, each owsa object returned by run_owsa_det is a data frame with four columns: parameter, strategy, param_val, and outcome_val. For each row, param_val is the value used for the parameter listed in parameter and outcome_val is the value of the specified outcome for the strategy listed in strategy. 

# So, OWSA_NMB shows a row is created for each sampling of the parameter value from min to max, so 100 rows per parameter (because nsamp = 100,), and the outcome value associated with a parameter value of this size is displayed under outcome_val.

# You can see how this works by putting the below into the console.

# OWSA_NMB

# Or just DSAICER for DSAICER.

# Resources on this available here:


# https://rdrr.io/github/DARTH-git/dampack/man/run_owsa_det.html (also saved here: C:\Users\Jonathan\OneDrive - Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland\COLOSSUS\Training Resources\sensitivity analysis help files\rdrr-io-github-DARTH-git-dampack-man-run_owsa_det-html.pdf)


# This link is pretty good for showing that the OWSA can be run across a variety of outcomes outcomes = c("Cost", "QALY", "LY", "NMB"), and then you can pick which of the OWSA outcomes you'd like to focus on and build tornado diagrams, etc., from that:

# "Because we have defined multiple parameters in my_owsa_params_range, we have instructed run_owsa_det to execute a series of separate one-way sensitivity analyses and compile the results into a single owsa object for each requested outcome. When only one outcome is specified run_owsa_det returns a owsa data frame. When more than one outcome is specified, run_owsa_det returns a list containing one owsa data frame for each outcome. To access the owsa object corresponding to a given outcome, one can select the list item with the name “owsa_”. For example, the owsa object associated with the NMB outcome can be accessed as l_owsa_det$owsa_NMB."

# Change the values in the 'parameter' column

# I use the mutate() function from the dplyr package to change the values of the parameter column in my DSAICER data frame based on conditions.

# First I look at DSAICER before any changes to learn the variable names and see what it looks like before:

DSAICER

# Then I change the values in the 'parameter' column

DSAICER <- DSAICER %>%
  mutate(parameter = case_when(
    parameter == "P_OSD_SoC" ~ "Prob Second Line Death - SoC",
    parameter == "P_OSD_Exp" ~ "Prob Second Line Death - Exp",
    parameter == "p_FA1_STD" ~ "Prob Leukopenia - SoC",
    parameter == "p_FA2_STD" ~ "Prob Diarrhea - SoC",
    parameter == "p_FA3_STD" ~ "Prob Nausea - SoC",
    parameter == "p_FA1_EXPR" ~ "Prob Leukopenia - Exp",
    parameter == "p_FA2_EXPR" ~ "Prob Diarrhea - Exp",
    parameter == "p_FA3_EXPR" ~ "Prob Nausea - Exp",
    parameter == "p_OSA1_FOLFIRI" ~ "Prob Leukopenia - Second Line",
    parameter == "p_OSA2_FOLFIRI" ~ "Prob Diarrhea - Second Line",
    parameter == "p_OSA3_FOLFIRI" ~ "Prob Nausea - Second Line",
    parameter == "administration_cost" ~ "Administration Cost",
    parameter == "c_PFS_Folfox" ~ "Folfox Cost",
    parameter == "c_PFS_Bevacizumab" ~ "Bevacizumab Cost",
    parameter == "c_OS_Folfiri" ~ "Folfiri Cost",
    parameter == "c_AE1" ~ "Leukopenia Cost",
    parameter == "c_AE2" ~ "Diarrhea Cost",
    parameter == "c_AE3" ~ "Nausea Cost",
    parameter == "subtyping_test_cost" ~ "Subtyping Test Cost",
    parameter == "u_F" ~ "Utility First Line",
    parameter == "u_P" ~ "Utility Second Line",
    parameter == "AE1_DisUtil" ~ "Leukopenia Disutility",
    parameter == "AE2_DisUtil" ~ "Diarrhea Disutility",
    parameter == "AE3_DisUtil" ~ "Nausea Disutility",
    parameter == "d_c" ~ "Cost Discount Rate",
    parameter == "d_e" ~ "Utility Discount Rate",
    parameter == "HR_PD_SoC" ~ "Prob First Line - Death SoC",
    parameter == "HR_FP_SoC" ~ "Prob First - Second Line SoC",
    parameter == "HR_PD_Exp" ~ "HR First Line - Death Bev",
    parameter == "HR_FP_Exp" ~ "HR First - Second Line Bev",
    TRUE ~ parameter  # I keep the original value if none of the above conditions are met
  ))

# In this code, case_when() is used inside mutate() to change the values of the parameter column based on multiple conditions. The format is condition ~ new_value. If none of the conditions are met, the original value is kept (TRUE ~ parameter).


# The tilde symbol (~) is used in R as a binary infix operator to separate the left-hand side and the right-hand side in a model formula. In the context of the mutate() function and the case_when() function from the dplyr package, it’s used to separate conditions from their corresponding values.

# Here’s how it works:

# mutate(df, new_column = case_when(
#   condition1 ~ value1,
#   condition2 ~ value2,
#   TRUE ~ parameter
# ))

# In this code, ~ separates each condition (condition1, condition2, etc.) from its corresponding value (value1, value2, etc.). If a condition is met (i.e., it evaluates to TRUE), the corresponding value is used. If none of the conditions are met, the parameter value is used (specified by TRUE ~ parameter).

# So, in the context of my code, parameter == "HR_FP_Exp" ~ "Hazard Ratio First to Second Line Treatment Bev" means “if parameter equals HR_FP_Exp, use Hazard Ratio First to Second Line Treatment Bev”.

# In the context of my code, TRUE ~ parameter serves as a default case in the case_when() function.

# That is, in this code, each condition is checked in order. If condition1 is TRUE, value1 is used. If condition2 is TRUE, value2 is used. If none of the conditions are TRUE, then the TRUE ~ parameter line is executed. Since TRUE is always TRUE, this line serves as a catch-all or default case.

# So, TRUE ~ parameter means “if none of the above conditions are met, keep the original value of parameter”. This ensures that the values of parameter that don’t meet any of the specified conditions remain unchanged.

# I look at DSAICER again to see how the above has changed my parameter names:

DSAICER


# If I want to change the bottom of the tornado diagram to say "ICER" instead of the default "Outcome" then I need to remember that: 

# owsa_tornado either return a ggplot object plot or a data frame with ranges of parameters for which each strategy is optimal - per: https://rdrr.io/github/DARTH-git/dampack/man/owsa_tornado.html


# Thus, to change the label at the bottom of the tornado plot from "outcome" to "ICER", I need to modify the ggplot object returned by the owsa_tornado function. Since owsa_tornado returns a ggplot object, I can use standard ggplot2 functions to modify the plot.

# We can address the labelling by accessing the plot object owsa_tornado returns, which is a ggplot object. The labs function can be used to modify the labels post-generation.

# How I previously generated the tornado plot:
# owsa_tornado(owsa = DSAICER, txtsize = 11)

# ============================================================================
# STEP 1: CREATE BASE TORNADO PLOT WITH AXIS LIMITS
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC PURPOSE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Generate a tornado plot showing how each parameter's uncertainty affects the
# ICER (Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio). The tornado plot is a standard
# tool in health economic sensitivity analysis that visually displays which
# parameters have the greatest influence on cost-effectiveness conclusions.
#
# WHAT IS A TORNADO PLOT?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A tornado plot is a type of bar chart where:
# - Each horizontal bar represents one parameter from the model
# - The bar shows the range of ICER values as that parameter varies across
#   its uncertainty range (typically ±20% or between min/max plausible values)
# - Parameters are sorted by their impact on the outcome (most influential at top)
# - The shape resembles a tornado, widest at the top and narrowing downward
#
# WHY USE AXIS LIMITS?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Setting axis limits (ylim) serves two purposes:
# 1. STANDARDIZATION: Allows comparison across countries by using consistent scales
# 2. FOCUS: Zooms in on the decision-relevant range around key WTP thresholds
#
# However, limits can also:
# - Hide important extreme values if set too narrow
# - Create misleading impressions of parameter influence
# Therefore, we create BOTH a limited and unlimited version for comparison
#
# MODELING APPROACH:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Use dampack's owsa_tornado() function with the DSAICER one-way sensitivity
# analysis results generated previously. Apply axis limits of €100,000-€400,000
# to capture the typical decision space for Ireland, Germany, and Spain.

# Generate the tornado plot using owsa_tornado function from dampack
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# FUNCTION: owsa_tornado()
#   - owsa: the one-way sensitivity analysis results (DSAICER object)
#   - txtsize: base text size for labels (11pt is readable for publication)
#   - ylim: axis limits in euros (€100,000 to €400,000)
#
# IMPORTANT: Despite the parameter name "ylim", this actually controls the
# HORIZONTAL axis (ICER values) because tornado plots are rotated 90 degrees.
# This is a quirk of the owsa_tornado() function implementation.
#
# Health economic interpretation: We're constraining the visualization to show
# ICERs within the €100k-€400k range, which spans typical WTP thresholds for
# the three countries analyzed (Ireland: €45k, Germany: €78.9k, Spain: €30k)
tornado_plot <- owsa_tornado(
  owsa = DSAICER,      # OWSA results containing all parameter variations
  txtsize = 11,         # Text size for parameter labels
  ylim = c(100000, 350000)  # ICER range to display (€100k to €400k)
)

# NOTE: Alternative approach (commented out below)
# If you wanted different limits, you could specify them as follows:
# Reference: https://rdrr.io/github/DARTH-git/dampack/man/owsa_tornado.html
#
# tornado_plot <- owsa_tornado(
#   owsa = DSAICER,
#   txtsize = 11,
#   ylim = c(0, 500000)  # Wider range: €0 to €500,000
# )

# ============================================================================
# STEP 2: FIX AXIS LABELS (SWAP ICER AND OUTCOME LABELS)
# ============================================================================
#
# TECHNICAL CHALLENGE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The owsa_tornado() function creates a HORIZONTAL tornado plot (bars extend
# left-right rather than up-down). Due to this 90-degree rotation:
#
# - What appears as the HORIZONTAL axis (showing ICER values) is technically
#   the Y-AXIS in ggplot2's internal coordinate system
# - What appears as the VERTICAL axis (showing parameter names) is technically
#   the X-AXIS in ggplot2's internal coordinate system
#
# This means axis labels are SWAPPED from what you'd intuitively expect!
#
# SOLUTION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# To set the label for the horizontal ICER axis (what viewers see as x-axis),
# we must modify the Y-AXIS label in ggplot2's labs() function.
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC VALUE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Proper axis labeling is critical for interpretation:
# - "ICER" clearly indicates this is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio
# - Helps readers understand the outcome being analyzed
# - Essential for publication quality figures
#
# IMPLEMENTATION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Use ggplot2's labs() function to modify axis labels
# The + operator adds layers to the ggplot object (standard ggplot2 syntax)

# Modify the axis label to display "ICER"
# ----------------------------------------
# IMPORTANT: We use labs(y = "ICER") NOT labs(x = "ICER") because the plot
# is rotated. The visual horizontal axis is ggplot2's y-axis.
#
# labs() is ggplot2's function for modifying plot labels:
#   - y: label for y-axis (which is visually the horizontal ICER axis here)
#   - x: label for x-axis (which would be the vertical parameter axis)
#
# Health economic interpretation: Clearly labeling the outcome measure ensures
# readers understand we're examining cost-effectiveness, not just costs or effects
tornado_plot <- tornado_plot + labs(y = "ICER")

# ============================================================================
# STEP 3: CREATE DYNAMIC TITLE WITH COUNTRY NAME
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC PURPOSE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Each country analysis uses different:
# - Treatment costs
# - Healthcare system costs
# - Willingness-to-pay thresholds
# - Discount rates
#
# Therefore, the tornado plot results are COUNTRY-SPECIFIC. The title must
# clearly indicate which country's analysis is shown to avoid confusion.
#
# IMPLEMENTATION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Use paste() to concatenate "Tornado Plot" with the country_name variable.
# The country_name[1] extracts the first element in case country_name is a vector.

# Create descriptive title including country context
# ---------------------------------------------------
# paste() combines text strings:
#   - "Tornado Plot": describes what type of visualization this is
#   - country_name[1]: inserts the active country (e.g., "Ireland")
#   - Result: "Tornado Plot Ireland"
#
# The [1] subscript ensures we extract only the first element of country_name.
# This is defensive programming in case country_name is accidentally a vector.
#
# Health economic interpretation: Providing country context is essential because
# cost-effectiveness is country-specific due to different costs and WTP thresholds
plot_title <- paste("Tornado Plot", country_name[1])

# ============================================================================
# STEP 4: APPLY TITLE AND ADJUST ALIGNMENT
# ============================================================================
#
# PROFESSIONAL FORMATTING REQUIREMENTS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Publication-quality figures require:
# 1. CENTERED TITLE: Standard practice in academic journals
# 2. ALIGNED AXIS LABELS: Proper vertical centering of axis text
# 3. CONSISTENT THEME: Professional appearance across all figures
#
# GGPLOT2 THEME SYSTEM:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# ggplot2's theme() function controls all non-data plot elements:
# - Text size, font, color
# - Alignment and positioning
# - Background colors
# - Grid lines
#
# Two key elements we're adjusting:
# - plot.title: the main title at the top of the plot
# - axis.title.y: the y-axis label (which is visually the horizontal ICER axis)
#
# ALIGNMENT PARAMETERS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# hjust (horizontal justification):
#   - 0 = left-aligned
#   - 0.5 = centered
#   - 1 = right-aligned
#
# vjust (vertical justification):
#   - 0 = bottom-aligned
#   - 0.5 = centered
#   - 1 = top-aligned
#
# For axis labels, vjust controls how far the label is from the axis line.
# A value of 0.25 provides a small offset for readability.

# Add title and apply professional formatting
# --------------------------------------------
# This single line of code performs three operations (chained with +):
#
# 1. ggtitle(plot_title): Adds the title we created above
#
# 2. theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)): Centers the title
#    - plot.title: selects the title element
#    - element_text(): function for modifying text properties
#    - hjust = 0.5: centers the title horizontally
#
# 3. theme(axis.title.y = element_text(vjust = 0.25)): Adjusts y-axis label
#    - axis.title.y: selects the y-axis label (visual horizontal axis for ICER)
#    - vjust = 0.25: positions label with slight offset from axis
#
# Health economic value: Professional presentation enhances credibility and
# ensures the analysis is taken seriously by decision-makers and peer reviewers
tornado_plot <- tornado_plot +
  ggtitle(plot_title) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),       # Center the title
    axis.title.y = element_text(vjust = 0.25)     # Adjust y-axis label position
  )

# NOTE: If we wanted perfect vertical centering of the axis label, we could
# use vjust = 0.5 instead of 0.25. The 0.25 value provides a small offset
# that often looks better visually by giving the label breathing room from
# the axis tick labels.

# ============================================================================
# STEP 5: SAVE HIGH-RESOLUTION TORNADO PLOT
# ============================================================================
#
# PUBLICATION REQUIREMENTS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Academic journals typically require:
# - High resolution: 300-600 DPI (dots per inch) minimum
# - Specific dimensions: Often 8" width for full-page figures
# - Common formats: PNG, TIFF, or EPS
#
# We use 600 DPI for maximum quality, suitable for:
# - Print publication
# - High-resolution displays
# - Zooming without pixelation
#
# FILE NAMING CONVENTION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Format: Tornado_Diagram_<Country>.png
# Examples:
#   - Tornado_Diagram_Ireland.png
#   - Tornado_Diagram_Germany.png
#   - Tornado_Diagram_Spain.png
#
# This naming convention:
# - Clearly describes the content ("Tornado_Diagram")
# - Includes country context for organization
# - Uses consistent format for easy batch processing
#
# IMPLEMENTATION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Use ggplot2's ggsave() function for high-quality output

# Save the tornado plot as a high-resolution PNG file
# ----------------------------------------------------
# ggsave() parameters:
#   - filename: paste() constructs "Tornado_Diagram_<Country>.png"
#   - plot: specify which ggplot object to save (tornado_plot)
#   - width: 8 inches (standard full-page width)
#   - height: 4 inches (appropriate for tornado plot aspect ratio)
#   - dpi: 600 dots per inch (high resolution for publication)
#
# paste() with sep="" concatenates strings with no separator:
#   - "Tornado_Diagram_"
#   - country_name[1] (e.g., "Ireland")
#   - ".png"
#   - Result: "Tornado_Diagram_Ireland.png"
#
# Health economic value: High-resolution outputs ensure visual details
# (parameter labels, axis values) are crisp and readable in publications
ggsave(
  file.path("output", paste("Tornado_Diagram_", country_name[1], ".png", sep = "")),
  plot = tornado_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 4,
  dpi = 600  # High resolution for publication quality
)

# Close all open graphics devices
# --------------------------------
# R can have multiple graphics devices open simultaneously. This while loop
# ensures all devices are properly closed after saving, preventing:
# - Memory leaks
# - File locking issues
# - Conflicts with subsequent plots
#
# dev.list() returns a list of open devices (NULL if none are open)
# dev.off() closes the current device
# The loop continues until dev.list() returns NULL
while (!is.null(dev.list())) dev.off()

# NOTE: Alternative approach (commented out below)
# The older png() / dev.off() workflow is less flexible than ggsave():
# png(paste("Tornado_Diagram_", country_name[1], ".png", sep = ""))
# print(tornado_plot)  # Would need to explicitly print the plot
# dev.off()
#
# ggsave() is preferred because it:
# - Automatically detects file format from extension
# - Handles sizing and resolution more intuitively
# - Doesn't require explicit print() calls

# TECHNICAL NOTE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The [1] subscript in country_name[1] is defensive programming that ensures
# we extract only the first element of the country_name vector. This prevents
# errors if country_name is accidentally defined as a multi-element vector.
#
# If country_name is guaranteed to be a single string, the [1] is not strictly
# necessary, but it's a good practice for robust code.

# ============================================================================
# STEP 6: CREATE UNLIMITED VERSION FOR COMPARISON
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC RATIONALE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# As mentioned earlier, setting axis limits can:
# - BENEFIT: Standardize comparisons and focus on decision-relevant ranges
# - RISK: Hide extreme parameter values or truncate important information
#
# BEST PRACTICE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Create TWO versions of the tornado plot:
# 1. LIMITED version (above): Focused view with standardized axis (€100k-€400k)
# 2. UNLIMITED version (below): Full view showing all data without truncation
#
# This allows analysts to:
# - Compare the two versions to ensure limits aren't hiding critical information
# - Use the limited version for cross-country comparisons (consistent scales)
# - Use the unlimited version to see the full range of parameter influence
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC VALUE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Transparency in sensitivity analysis is essential. Providing both versions
# demonstrates that we're not hiding inconvenient results and allows reviewers
# to verify that our chosen limits are appropriate.

# Generate unlimited tornado plot (no axis limits)
# -------------------------------------------------
# DIFFERENCE FROM ABOVE: No ylim parameter
# This allows the plot to automatically scale to fit all data points
# The function will choose appropriate axis limits based on data range
#
# Health economic interpretation: This shows the TRUE range of parameter
# influence without artificial constraints. Some parameters may have much
# larger effects than visible in the limited version.
unlimited_tornado_plot <- owsa_tornado(
  owsa = DSAICER,      # Same OWSA results as before
  txtsize = 11          # Same text size for consistency
  # NO ylim parameter - let the plot scale automatically
)

# Apply the same axis label fix as before
# ----------------------------------------
# Must modify y-axis label to change the visual horizontal axis (due to rotation)
unlimited_tornado_plot <- unlimited_tornado_plot + labs(y = "ICER")

# Create identical title (without "unlimited" suffix for now)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# We use the same title format for consistency. Some users prefer to add
# "- Unlimited Scale" to the title to distinguish the versions, but here
# we rely on the filename to differentiate them.
plot_title <- paste("Tornado Plot", country_name[1])

# Apply identical formatting (centered title, adjusted axis label)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# Use the same theme settings to ensure visual consistency between the two
# versions. The only difference should be the axis limits, not the styling.
unlimited_tornado_plot <- unlimited_tornado_plot +
  ggtitle(plot_title) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title.y = element_text(vjust = 0.25)
  )

# Save the unlimited version with descriptive filename
# -----------------------------------------------------
# FILE NAMING: "Unlimited_Tornado_Diagram_<Country>.png"
# The "Unlimited_" prefix clearly distinguishes this from the limited version
#
# IMPORTANT: Use identical dimensions and resolution (width=8, height=4, dpi=600)
# to ensure fair comparison between limited and unlimited versions
#
# Health economic value: Consistent dimensions and resolution allow side-by-side
# comparison of the two versions without visual bias from different sizes
ggsave(
  file.path("output", paste("Unlimited_Tornado_Diagram_", country_name[1], ".png", sep = "")),
  plot = unlimited_tornado_plot,
  width = 8,      # Same as limited version
  height = 4,     # Same as limited version
  dpi = 600       # Same high resolution
)

# Close all graphics devices
# ---------------------------
while (!is.null(dev.list())) dev.off()

# ============================================================================
# SUMMARY: HIGH-RESOLUTION OUTPUT SETTINGS
# ============================================================================
#
# DPI (DOTS PER INCH) EXPLANATION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# DPI controls image resolution and quality:
#
# - 72-96 DPI: Screen viewing (low quality, not suitable for print)
# - 150-300 DPI: Basic print quality
# - 600 DPI: High-quality print, professional publication standard
#
# We use 600 DPI because:
# 1. JOURNAL REQUIREMENTS: Many journals require 300+ DPI for figures
# 2. FUTURE-PROOFING: High-resolution originals can be downsampled if needed,
#    but low-resolution images cannot be upsampled without quality loss
# 3. DETAILED ANALYSIS: Allows zooming to read small parameter labels clearly
# 4. PROFESSIONALISM: Demonstrates attention to quality and detail
#
# FILE SIZE IMPLICATIONS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Higher DPI = larger file sizes:
# - 72 DPI: ~50-100 KB
# - 300 DPI: ~500 KB - 1 MB
# - 600 DPI: ~2-4 MB
#
# For modern systems, the extra file size is negligible compared to the
# benefit of having publication-quality outputs.
#
# CONSISTENCY ACROSS BOTH VERSIONS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Both the limited and unlimited tornado plots use:
# - Width: 8 inches (standard page width)
# - Height: 4 inches (appropriate for horizontal tornado plots)
# - DPI: 600 (high resolution)
#
# This ensures fair comparison between the two versions.

# ============================================================================
# AT THIS POINT WE HAVE CREATED TWO TORNADO PLOT OUTPUTS:
# ============================================================================
#
# 1. Tornado_Diagram_<Country>.png
#    - Axis limits: €100,000 to €400,000
#    - Purpose: Standardized view for cross-country comparison
#    - Use case: Focus on decision-relevant ICER range
#
# 2. Unlimited_Tornado_Diagram_<Country>.png
#    - Axis limits: Automatic (based on data)
#    - Purpose: Full view of all parameter influences
#    - Use case: Verify no important information is hidden by axis limits
#
# NEXT STEPS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# After generating these plots, you should:
# 1. Visually compare both versions to verify axis limits are appropriate
# 2. Check that parameter labels are fully visible and not truncated
# 3. Verify the most influential parameters match clinical expectations
# 4. Consider whether any parameters show surprisingly large or small effects
# 5. Use these plots to communicate sensitivity analysis results to stakeholders


# Plotting the outcomes of the OWSA in a tornado plot
# - note that other plots can also be generated using the plot() and owsa_opt_strat() functions


# owsa_tornado(
#   DSAICER,
#   return = c("data"),
#   txtsize = 12,
#   min_rel_diff = 0,
#   col = c("full", "bw"),
#   n_y_ticks = 8,
#   ylim = NULL,
#   ybreaks = NULL
# )


# owsa_tornado(DSAICER,
# 
# min_rel_diff = 0.05)

# For owsa objects that contain many parameters that have minimal effect on the parameter of interest, you may want to consider producing a plot that highlights only the most influential parameters. Using the min_rel_diff argument, you can instruct owsa_tornado to exclude all parameters that fail to produce a relative change in the outcome below a specific fraction.
