## 08.2.1 Top 10 Most Influential Parameters - Simplified Tornado Plots

```{r}

# ============================================================================
# SECTION PURPOSE: CREATE SIMPLIFIED TORNADO PLOTS (TOP 10 PARAMETERS ONLY)
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC RATIONALE FOR THIS ANALYSIS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# In cost-effectiveness analysis, tornado plots are a key tool for communicating
# parameter uncertainty and identifying research priorities. However, when many
# parameters are included (as in our model with 30 parameters), the full tornado
# plot can become:
#
# 1. VISUALLY CLUTTERED: Too many bars make it hard to see which parameters
#    truly matter for decision-making
#
# 2. DIFFICULT TO INTERPRET: Decision-makers and reviewers may struggle to
#    identify the key drivers of cost-effectiveness
#
# 3. UNSUITABLE FOR PUBLICATION: Journal space is limited; a focused plot
#    is more effective than a comprehensive but cluttered one
#
# By focusing on the TOP 10 most influential parameters, we achieve several
# health economic objectives:
#
# a) IMPROVED COMMUNICATION: Stakeholders can quickly identify which parameters
#    have the largest impact on the ICER, facilitating informed discussion
#
# b) RESEARCH PRIORITIZATION: Parameters with large influence on cost-effectiveness
#    should be prioritized for:
#    - Additional data collection
#    - Expert elicitation
#    - Further validation studies
#    - Threshold analysis
#
# c) VALUE OF INFORMATION ANALYSIS: High-impact parameters are candidates for
#    Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI) analysis to determine whether
#    additional research to reduce their uncertainty would be cost-effective
#
# d) TRANSPARENCY: By showing which assumptions matter most, we increase the
#    transparency and credibility of the analysis
#
# e) BEST PRACTICE ALIGNMENT: This approach aligns with ISPOR-SMDM guidelines
#    for good practices in model-based economic evaluation, which emphasize
#    clear communication of uncertainty
#
# MODELING APPROACH AND METHODOLOGY:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Our approach follows these steps:
#
# STEP 1: Calculate each parameter's "impact" on ICER
#         Impact = Range of ICER values when parameter varies from min to max
#
# STEP 2: Rank all parameters by absolute impact (largest first)
#
# STEP 3: Select the top 10 most influential parameters
#
# STEP 4: Filter the OWSA results to include only these top 10
#
# STEP 5: Calculate sensible axis limits based on the ICER range for top 10
#
# STEP 6: Generate tornado plots with dampack's owsa_tornado() function
#
# STEP 7: Add appropriate labels, titles, and footnotes
#
# STEP 8: Save high-resolution plots for publication
#
# This methodology preserves the full OWSA results (all 30 parameters) while
# creating publication-ready visualizations focused on the most important inputs.
#
# TECHNICAL NOTE ON OWSA STRUCTURE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The DSAICER object created by run_owsa_det() is a data frame with structure:
#   - parameter: name of the parameter being varied
#   - strategy: the strategy being evaluated
#   - param_val: the value of the parameter in this sample
#   - outcome_val: the resulting ICER at this parameter value
#
# For each parameter, there are nsamp=100 rows showing how ICER changes as
# the parameter moves from its minimum to maximum value, holding all other
# parameters at their base-case values.
#
# ============================================================================


# ============================================================================
# STEP 1: CALCULATE PARAMETER IMPACT ON ICER
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC CONCEPT - PARAMETER INFLUENCE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# In sensitivity analysis, we want to identify which parameters have the
# greatest influence on our cost-effectiveness conclusion. A parameter is
# "influential" if small changes in its value lead to large changes in the ICER.
#
# WHY THIS MATTERS IN HEALTH ECONOMICS:
# - High-impact parameters represent key uncertainties in the decision problem
# - They determine whether an intervention appears cost-effective or not
# - Reducing uncertainty in these parameters (through research) has high value
# - They should be the focus of probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA)
# - They may warrant scenario analysis or threshold analysis
#
# MATHEMATICAL DEFINITION OF IMPACT:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# For each parameter p, we define its impact as:
#
#   Impact(p) = max(ICER_p) - min(ICER_p)
#
# Where:
#   - max(ICER_p) = highest ICER when p varies across its range
#   - min(ICER_p) = lowest ICER when p varies across its range
#
# This measures the total swing in cost-effectiveness attributable to
# uncertainty in parameter p.
#
# EXAMPLE INTERPRETATION:
# If the impact of "Bevacizumab cost" is €50,000 per QALY, this means:
# - When Bev cost is at its minimum, ICER might be €150,000/QALY
# - When Bev cost is at its maximum, ICER might be €200,000/QALY
# - The uncertainty in Bev cost creates a €50,000/QALY uncertainty in ICER
# - This is a HIGH impact - Bev cost is a critical parameter
#
# MODELING APPROACH:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We use dplyr to group the OWSA results by parameter and calculate summary
# statistics for each parameter's influence on ICER.

# Use the dplyr package to manipulate the OWSA results data frame
# This allows us to group rows by parameter and calculate statistics
library(dplyr)

# Group the OWSA results by parameter name
# For each parameter, we will calculate summary statistics
# The group_by function creates groups based on unique parameter values
parameter_impacts <- DSAICER %>%
  # Group all rows by the 'parameter' column
  # This means subsequent operations will be performed separately for each parameter
  # Health economic interpretation: We're analyzing each input parameter independently
  group_by(parameter) %>%

  # Calculate summary statistics for each parameter group
  # The summarise function creates one row per parameter with our calculated metrics
  summarise(
    # Calculate the minimum ICER value for this parameter
    # This occurs when the parameter is at one extreme of its range
    # Health economic interpretation: Best-case ICER scenario for this parameter
    min_icer = min(outcome_val),

    # Calculate the maximum ICER value for this parameter
    # This occurs when the parameter is at the other extreme of its range
    # Health economic interpretation: Worst-case ICER scenario for this parameter
    max_icer = max(outcome_val),

    # Calculate the range = difference between max and min
    # This is the total "swing" in ICER caused by this parameter's uncertainty
    # Health economic interpretation: The parameter's influence on cost-effectiveness
    # Modeling interpretation: The width of the tornado bar for this parameter
    impact = max_icer - min_icer,

    # Calculate the absolute value of impact
    # We use absolute value because we only care about magnitude, not direction
    # Some parameters increase ICER (positive impact), others decrease it (negative)
    # For ranking purposes, we want the largest magnitude regardless of direction
    # Health economic interpretation: The size of uncertainty this parameter creates
    abs_impact = abs(impact)
  ) %>%

  # Sort the parameters by absolute impact, largest first
  # This puts the most influential parameters at the top of our data frame
  # Health economic interpretation: Ranking parameters by research priority
  # Modeling interpretation: Ordering for selection of top N parameters
  arrange(desc(abs_impact))

# Display the parameter impacts table in the console
# This allows us to review which parameters are most influential
# Health economic value: Transparent reporting of sensitivity analysis results
# Practical use: Helps us verify that our top 10 selection makes clinical sense
print("Parameter Impacts on ICER (sorted by influence):")
print(parameter_impacts)

# The output will show a table like:
# parameter                          min_icer  max_icer  impact    abs_impact
# Bevacizumab Cost                   120000    200000    80000     80000
# HR First - Second Line Bev         140000    180000    40000     40000
# ...etc

# ============================================================================
# STEP 2: SELECT TOP 10 MOST INFLUENTIAL PARAMETERS
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC RATIONALE FOR TOP 10 SELECTION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We select exactly 10 parameters as a balance between:
#
# COMPREHENSIVENESS: Showing enough parameters to give a complete picture
# of model uncertainty and validate that we've captured key drivers
#
# PARSIMONY: Not overwhelming the reader with too many parameters, most of
# which may have minimal influence on the decision
#
# PRACTICAL UTILITY: 10 parameters is manageable for:
# - Discussion in a manuscript (can describe each one)
# - Presentation slides (fits on one readable chart)
# - Value of information analysis (computationally feasible)
# - Threshold analysis (can explore each parameter)
#
# PRECEDENT: The top 10 approach is commonly used in health economic publications
# and is consistent with guidelines from ISPOR and NICE
#
# MODELING APPROACH:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We use dplyr's slice() function to take the first 10 rows from our
# already-sorted parameter_impacts data frame, then extract just the parameter
# names into a character vector.

# Take the first 10 rows from parameter_impacts
# Remember: parameter_impacts is already sorted by abs_impact (largest first)
# So this gives us the 10 parameters with the highest absolute impact
# Health economic interpretation: These are our 10 highest research priorities
top10_parameters <- parameter_impacts %>%

  # The slice function selects rows by position
  # slice(1:10) means "take rows 1 through 10"
  # Since our data is sorted by impact (descending), these are the top 10
  # Modeling interpretation: Filtering to the most influential subset
  slice(1:10) %>%

  # The pull function extracts a single column as a vector
  # pull(parameter) gives us just the parameter names, not the whole data frame
  # This creates a character vector like: c("Bevacizumab Cost", "HR First - Second Line Bev", ...)
  # Health economic interpretation: Creating our focused parameter list
  # Modeling interpretation: Preparing the filter vector for subsetting DSAICER
  pull(parameter)

# Display the top 10 parameter names for review
# This is important for validation: do these parameters make clinical sense?
# For example, we'd expect to see treatment costs, key hazard ratios, and
# important utilities in the top 10 for an oncology model
# Health economic value: Allows face validity check of results
print("Top 10 Most Influential Parameters:")
print(top10_parameters)

# Example output might be:
# [1] "Bevacizumab Cost"
# [2] "HR First - Second Line Bev"
# [3] "Folfox Cost"
# [4] "Prob First - Second Line SoC"
# [5] "Utility First Line"
# ... etc

# ============================================================================
# STEP 3: FILTER OWSA RESULTS TO TOP 10 PARAMETERS ONLY
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC PURPOSE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We now create a subset of our OWSA results that includes only the top 10
# most influential parameters. This filtered dataset will be used to generate
# the simplified tornado plot.
#
# This subset maintains all the detail of the original OWSA (100 samples per
# parameter showing how ICER changes), but focuses only on the parameters that
# matter most for the cost-effectiveness decision.
#
# MODELING APPROACH:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We use dplyr's filter() function to keep only rows where the parameter name
# is in our top10_parameters vector.

# Filter the DSAICER data frame to include only top 10 parameters
# The filter function keeps rows that meet a specified condition
# The %in% operator checks if a value is in a vector
# Health economic interpretation: Focusing our analysis on key uncertainties
DSAICER_top10 <- DSAICER %>%

  # Keep only rows where the parameter column matches one of our top 10
  # The %in% operator returns TRUE if parameter is in top10_parameters vector
  # This will keep all 200 rows per parameter (100 samples × 2 strategies)
  # Health economic interpretation: Retaining full detail for influential parameters
  # Modeling interpretation: Subsetting the data frame for focused visualization
  filter(parameter %in% top10_parameters)

# Verify we have the expected number of rows
# With 10 parameters, 100 samples each (nsamp=100), and 2 strategies, we expect 2000 rows
# Note: run_owsa_det() returns rows for BOTH strategies (Folfox and Bevacizumab)
# Even though ICER is the same ratio for both, dampack stores it per-strategy
# The run_owsa_det() function from dampack returns data for both strategies (Folfox and Bevacizumab), even though the ICER value is the same for both (since ICER is a ratio comparing the two).
# This is a data quality check to ensure our filtering worked correctly
# Health economic value: Ensuring data integrity before visualization
# Modeling value: Catching any potential errors in the filtering process
print(paste("Number of rows in DSAICER_top10:", nrow(DSAICER_top10)))
print(paste("Expected rows: 10 parameters × 100 samples × 2 strategies = 2000"))

# If the numbers don't match, something went wrong in our filtering
# This could indicate:
# - Fewer than 10 unique parameters in the original OWSA (unlikely)
# - The parameter names don't match between our filter and the data
# - Some other data processing error

# ============================================================================
# STEP 4: SET FIXED AXIS LIMITS FOR CONSISTENT TORNADO PLOT COMPARISON
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC RATIONALE FOR FIXED AXIS LIMITS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# For multi-country comparative analysis, using consistent axis scales across
# all tornado plots is critical for valid visual comparison. Fixed limits allow:
#
# COMPARABILITY: Identical axis scales enable direct visual comparison across
#                countries and analyses
# CONTEXT: A fixed €200k-€400k range provides appropriate policy context since
#          it spans well beyond all three countries' WTP thresholds
# FOCUS: Constraining the range to policy-relevant ICERs improves readability
# STANDARDIZATION: Consistent scaling is a best practice for comparative CEA
#
# In health economic reporting, when comparing across countries or scenarios,
# we must ensure that:
# - Visual comparisons are valid (same scales)
# - The range encompasses the decision-relevant ICER values
# - The magnitude of parameter influence can be compared across analyses
# - The chosen range is justified and transparent
#
# FIXED RANGE APPROACH:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We set axis limits to a fixed €100k-€400k range for all tornado plots:
#
# 1. Lower bound: €100,000 per QALY
# 2. Upper bound: €400,000 per QALY
# 3. Range spans all country WTP thresholds (Ireland: €45k, Germany: €78.9k, Spain: €30k)
# 4. Focuses on clinically and policy-relevant ICER values
#
# This ensures:
# - Direct visual comparability across all analyses
# - Policy-relevant context for decision-makers
# - Consistent presentation standards
# - Transparent and reproducible approach
#
# MODELING APPROACH:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We set ylim_top10 to a fixed vector c(100000, 400000) rather than
# calculating data-driven limits.

# Set fixed axis limits for consistent ICER range visualization
# We're constraining the visualization to show ICERs within the €100k-€400k range
# This provides a standardized comparison scale across all tornado plots
# Health economic interpretation: We're establishing a consistent scale that:
# 1. Spans well beyond the WTP thresholds for all three countries analyzed:
#    - Ireland: €45,000
#    - Germany: €78,871
#    - Spain: €30,000
# 2. Focuses on the clinically and policy-relevant ICER range
# 3. Enables direct visual comparison across different analyses
# Modeling interpretation: Setting explicit ylim bounds for owsa_tornado
# Note: "ylim" is the parameter name in owsa_tornado, but due to horizontal
# orientation, this actually controls the ICER axis (which appears horizontal/x)
ylim_top10 <- c(100000, 350000)

# Display the fixed limits being used
# This transparency is important for reproducibility and validation
# Health economic value: Transparent reporting of visualization decisions
# Practical value: Ensures consistency across all tornado plot outputs
print(paste("Fixed ICER axis limits:", ylim_top10[1], "to", ylim_top10[2]))

# Expected output:
# "Fixed ICER axis limits: 100000 to 400000"

# ============================================================================
# STEP 5: CREATE TORNADO PLOT FOR TOP 10 PARAMETERS
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC PURPOSE OF TORNADO PLOTS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Tornado plots (also called tornado diagrams) are a standard tool in health
# economic evaluation for visualizing one-way sensitivity analysis results.
#
# KEY FEATURES OF TORNADO PLOTS:
# 1. Bars are sorted by magnitude of impact (creating a "tornado" shape)
# 2. Each bar shows the range of outcome values for one parameter
# 3. Bar length represents the parameter's influence on the outcome
# 4. Allows quick visual comparison of parameter importance
#
# INTERPRETATION GUIDANCE:
# - LONG BARS = high-impact parameters that strongly influence cost-effectiveness
# - SHORT BARS = low-impact parameters with minimal effect on the decision
# - Parameters at the top (longest bars) are research priorities
# - If bars cross a threshold (e.g., willingness-to-pay), the parameter can
#   change the cost-effectiveness decision
#
# DAMPACK'S OWSA_TORNADO FUNCTION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The owsa_tornado() function from the dampack package creates publication-quality
# tornado plots following health economic best practices. It automatically:
# - Sorts parameters by impact (largest at top)
# - Creates horizontal bars showing min-to-max range
# - Labels parameters clearly
# - Allows customization of text size, colors, axis limits
#
# FUNCTION PARAMETERS WE'RE USING:
# - owsa: The OWSA results data frame (we use our top 10 subset)
# - txtsize: Base text size for labels (11 pt is readable)
# - ylim: Axis limits (fixed at €100k-€400k for cross-country comparability)
#
# Note on axis naming: Due to horizontal orientation, "ylim" in the function
# actually controls the ICER axis (which displays horizontally).

# Load the dampack package if not already loaded
# dampack provides functions for decision-analytic modeling
# Health economic value: Standardized tools for CEA visualization
library(dampack)

# Create the tornado plot using the owsa_tornado function
# This generates a ggplot2 object that we can further customize
# Health economic interpretation: Visualizing parameter influence for communication
tornado_plot_top10 <- owsa_tornado(

  # Specify the OWSA results to plot
  # We use our filtered dataset with only top 10 parameters
  # This ensures the plot is focused and readable
  # Health economic interpretation: Showing only the most influential uncertainties
  # Modeling interpretation: Passing the subsetted data frame to the plotting function
  owsa = DSAICER_top10,

  # Set the base text size for parameter labels
  # 11 points is large enough to read clearly but small enough to fit 10 labels
  # This affects parameter names, axis labels, and tick marks
  # Health economic interpretation: Ensuring accessibility of visualization
  # Practical consideration: Must balance readability with space constraints
  txtsize = 11,

  # Apply our fixed axis limits (€100k-€400k for cross-country comparability)
  # This ensures consistent scaling across all country analyses
  # ylim is a two-element vector: c(minimum, maximum)
  # Health economic interpretation: Standardized bounds for valid comparison
  # Modeling interpretation: Controlling the range of the ICER axis
  # Important: In owsa_tornado's horizontal layout, ylim controls the outcome (ICER)
  # axis, even though it appears horizontally on the page
  ylim = ylim_top10
)

# At this point, tornado_plot_top10 is a ggplot object
# We can modify it further using standard ggplot2 functions
# This is one of the strengths of dampack - it returns standard ggplot objects
# that can be customized as needed

# ============================================================================
# STEP 6: CUSTOMIZE PLOT LABELS AND TITLE
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC IMPORTANCE OF CLEAR LABELING:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# In health economic reporting, figures must be self-explanatory and accessible.
# Good practice requires:
#
# 1. CLEAR AXIS LABELS: Readers should immediately know what is being plotted
#    - Not just "Outcome" but "ICER (€ per QALY)"
#    - Include units (€, QALY, years, etc.)
#
# 2. DESCRIPTIVE TITLES: The title should indicate:
#    - What type of analysis this is (tornado plot / one-way sensitivity)
#    - What it shows (top 10 parameters only)
#    - Which country/population it applies to
#
# 3. PROFESSIONAL FORMATTING: Center-aligned titles, appropriate spacing
#
# GGPLOT2 CUSTOMIZATION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Since owsa_tornado returns a ggplot object, we can use standard ggplot2
# functions to customize it:
# - labs() for labels and titles
# - theme() for formatting and positioning
# - + operator to add layers to the plot

# Load ggplot2 if not already loaded
# ggplot2 is the graphics package underlying dampack's plots
# Health economic value: Industry-standard, publication-quality graphics
library(ggplot2)

# Add clear axis labels
# In owsa_tornado's horizontal layout:
# - Parameters are on the y-axis (vertical, on the left)
# - ICER values are on the x-axis (horizontal, at the bottom)
# Therefore we use labs(x = ...) to label the outcome axis and labs(y = ...) for parameters
# Health economic interpretation: Making the outcome variable and parameters explicit
tornado_plot_top10 <- tornado_plot_top10 +

  # The labs function adds or modifies labels
  # x = sets the x-axis label (this is the outcome/ICER axis in horizontal tornado plots)
  # y = sets the y-axis label (this is the parameter axis)
  # Health economic best practice: Clear, simple labels
  # Modeling interpretation: Labeling both axes
  labs(y = "ICER (€ per QALY)", x = "Parameter")

# Create a descriptive title that includes:
# 1. What it is: "Tornado Plot"
# 2. What it shows: "Top 10 Most Influential Parameters"
# 3. Context: Country name
# The paste function concatenates strings
# country_name[1] extracts the first element of the country_name vector
# We use [1] to ensure we get a single value, not a vector
# Health economic interpretation: Providing full context for the analysis
# Practical value: Allows readers to immediately know what they're looking at
plot_title_top10 <- paste(
  "Tornado Plot - Top 10 Most Influential Parameters (",
  country_name[1],
  ")",
  sep = ""  # sep="" means no separator between the pasted elements
)

# Add the title to the plot and center it
# Also adjust the positioning of axis labels
# The ggtitle function adds a title
# The theme function controls non-data elements of the plot
tornado_plot_top10 <- tornado_plot_top10 +

  # Add the title we created
  # ggtitle is a shortcut for labs(title = ...)
  # Health economic interpretation: Making the plot self-contained
  ggtitle(plot_title_top10) +

  # Customize the appearance using theme
  # theme controls all non-data display (text, backgrounds, spacing, etc.)
  theme(
    # Center the title horizontally
    # plot.title refers to the main title we just added
    # element_text allows us to modify text properties
    # hjust = 0.5 means horizontal justification at 50% (centered)
    # hjust = 0 would be left-aligned, hjust = 1 would be right-aligned
    # Health economic best practice: Centered titles are standard in publications
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),

    # Adjust the vertical position of the x-axis label
    # axis.title.x refers to the x-axis label ("ICER (€ per QALY)")
    # vjust controls vertical justification (positioning)
    # vjust = 0.25 moves it slightly up from default position
    # This creates better visual spacing between the axis and the label
    # Health economic consideration: Professional appearance for publication
    axis.title.x = element_text(vjust = 0.25)
  )

# At this point, tornado_plot_top10 is fully labeled and formatted
# It shows:
# - Top 10 parameters only (readable, focused)
# - Clear ICER axis label with units
# - Descriptive title with country context
# - Professional formatting

# ============================================================================
# STEP 7: ADD FOOTNOTE WITH ABBREVIATIONS
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC RATIONALE FOR ABBREVIATION FOOTNOTES:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# In health economic models, we often use abbreviations for:
# - Clinical terms (SoC = Standard of Care)
# - Statistical concepts (HR = Hazard Ratio)
# - Treatment names (Bev = Bevacizumab)
# - Model states (PFS = Progression-Free Survival)
#
# ACCESSIBILITY REQUIREMENT:
# Best practice in scientific communication requires that:
# 1. Figures should be self-contained (understandable without reading the full paper)
# 2. All abbreviations should be defined where they are used
# 3. Readers from different backgrounds should be able to interpret the figure
#
# This is particularly important for:
# - Journal reviewers who may skim the paper
# - Policy makers who may only look at key figures
# - International readers who may not know country-specific abbreviations
# - Interdisciplinary audiences (clinicians, economists, statisticians)
#
# GGPLOT2 CAPTION FUNCTIONALITY:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We use the labs() function to add a caption (footnote) at the bottom of the plot.
# The theme() function controls the appearance and positioning of this caption.

# Create a text string explaining the key abbreviations
# We use paste to concatenate multiple lines of text
# The \n character creates a line break (new line)
# Health economic interpretation: Making the plot accessible to all readers
# Practical consideration: Include only abbreviations that actually appear in the plot
abbreviations_caption <- paste(
  # First line: Define the most important abbreviations
  # These are the clinical and statistical terms likely to appear in parameter names
  "Abbreviations: HR = Hazard Ratio; Prob = Probability; SoC = Standard of Care;",

  # Second line: Define treatment-specific abbreviations
  "Exp = Experimental (Bevacizumab); Bev = Bevacizumab.",

  # Third line: Explain the selection criterion and why only 10 are shown
  # This adds transparency about our methodology
  # The \n at the start creates a line break for visual separation
  "\nParameters ranked by absolute impact on ICER. Only top 10 shown for clarity."
)

# Add the caption to the plot and control its formatting
# The labs function can add multiple types of labels including captions
# The theme function controls the caption's appearance
tornado_plot_top10 <- tornado_plot_top10 +

  # Add the caption using the labs function
  # caption = sets the footnote text at the bottom of the plot
  # Health economic interpretation: Ensuring self-contained, accessible figures
  labs(caption = abbreviations_caption) +

  # Customize the caption appearance using theme
  theme(
    # Control the text properties of the caption
    # plot.caption refers to the caption we just added
    # element_text allows us to modify text properties
    plot.caption = element_text(
      # Left-align the caption text
      # hjust = 0 means horizontal justification at 0% (left edge)
      # This is standard for footnotes - they're typically left-aligned
      # Health economic convention: Footnotes are left-aligned in academic publications
      hjust = 0,

      # Use smaller text size for the caption
      # size = 8 is smaller than the main plot text (which is 11)
      # This visually distinguishes the footnote from the main content
      # Standard practice: Footnotes are smaller than body text
      size = 8
    ),

    # Control where the caption is positioned
    # plot.caption.position can be "panel" (within plotting area) or "plot" (below everything)
    # "plot" means the caption appears below the entire plot including axes
    # This is standard for figure footnotes in publications
    # Health economic best practice: Captions go at the bottom, outside the plot area
    plot.caption.position = "plot"
  )

# Now tornado_plot_top10 is complete with:
# - Top 10 parameters only
# - Clear axis labels with units
# - Descriptive title with country
# - Footnote explaining abbreviations
# - Professional formatting throughout

# ============================================================================
# STEP 8: CREATE OUTPUT FOLDER AND SAVE THE PLOT
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC RATIONALE FOR ORGANIZED OUTPUT STRUCTURE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# In health economic modeling projects, organized file management is critical for:
#
# 1. REPRODUCIBILITY: Others must be able to find and use your outputs
# 2. VERSION CONTROL: Keep model outputs separate from code and inputs
# 3. COLLABORATION: Team members need a clear, consistent folder structure
# 4. REGULATORY SUBMISSION: Agencies require well-organized supporting materials
# 5. ARCHIVING: Outputs must be findable months or years later
#
# BEST PRACTICE FOLDER STRUCTURE:
# - /code or /R: R scripts and Rmd files
# - /data or /inputs: Input data files
# - /output or /results: Generated outputs (plots, tables, CSVs)
# - /docs: Documentation and manuscripts
#
# By saving outputs to an "output/" folder, we:
# - Keep the repository root clean
# - Make it easy to find all results in one place
# - Enable .gitignore rules to exclude outputs if needed
# - Follow standard project organization conventions
#
# MODELING APPROACH:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We use base R's file system functions to:
# 1. Construct the full file path for our plot
# 2. Save the plot with ggsave at high resolution

# Construct the full file path for our plot
# file.path() joins path components with the correct separator for the OS
# This is more robust than paste() because it handles Windows vs. Unix paths
# paste0() concatenates strings with no separator
# tolower() converts the country name to lowercase for consistent filenames
# Health economic interpretation: Creating organized, findable output files
# Practical value: Lowercase filenames avoid case-sensitivity issues
filename_top10 <- file.path(
  # First argument: the folder name
  # All files will be saved in the "output" folder
  "output",

  # Second argument: the filename
  # We construct this dynamically using the country name
  # paste0 concatenates without spaces: "tornado_top10_ireland.png"
  # tolower ensures consistent lowercase filenames (ireland, germany, spain)
  # Health economic best practice: Descriptive filenames that indicate content
  paste0("tornado_top10_", tolower(country_name[1]), ".png")
)

# Display the filename for confirmation
# This transparency helps with debugging and reproducibility
# Users can see exactly where the file will be saved
# Health economic value: Transparent reporting of outputs
print(paste("Saving top 10 tornado plot to:", filename_top10))

# Save the plot to a PNG file
# ggsave is ggplot2's function for saving plots to files
# It handles multiple formats (PNG, PDF, JPEG, etc.) and resolution settings
# Health economic importance: Publication-quality outputs for manuscripts
ggsave(
  # First argument: the filename (including path)
  # This is where the file will be saved
  # Example: "output/tornado_top10_ireland.png"
  filename_top10,

  # Specify which plot object to save
  # plot = identifies which ggplot object to export
  # We use our fully customized tornado_plot_top10 object
  # Health economic interpretation: Saving our publication-ready visualization
  plot = tornado_plot_top10,

  # Set the width of the plot in inches
  # 8 inches is standard for a full-width figure in a two-column journal
  # This provides enough space for parameter names and the tornado bars
  # Health economic consideration: Standard figure width for publications
  width = 8,

  # Set the height of the plot in inches
  # 6 inches accommodates 10 parameter labels with good spacing
  # This is taller than our previous 4-inch plots because we have a caption
  # The extra height ensures the caption is readable and not cramped
  # Health economic consideration: Adequate space for all elements
  height = 6,

  # Set the resolution in dots per inch (DPI)
  # 600 DPI is high resolution, suitable for publication
  # Journal requirements typically range from 300-600 DPI
  # Higher DPI means sharper text and clearer graphics
  # Health economic best practice: Publication-quality resolution
  # Practical consideration: 600 DPI ensures acceptance by any journal
  dpi = 600
)

# Close any open graphics devices
# R can have multiple graphics devices open simultaneously
# dev.list() returns a list of open devices (NULL if none)
# !is.null() checks if there are any open devices
# dev.off() closes the current device
# This while loop closes all open devices to free memory
# Health economic value: Clean environment for reproducibility
# Practical value: Prevents graphics device errors in subsequent plots
while (!is.null(dev.list())) dev.off()

# Print confirmation message
# This provides feedback that the save operation completed
# Health economic value: Transparent workflow documentation
print(paste("Top 10 tornado plot saved successfully as:", filename_top10))

# At this point we have:
# - Saved high-resolution PNG of top 10 tornado plot
# - Filename: output/tornado_top10_<country>.png (e.g., output/tornado_top10_ireland.png)

# ============================================================================
# STEP 9: CREATE SECOND TORNADO PLOT VERSION (KEPT FOR CONSISTENCY)
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC NOTE ON DUPLICATE VERSIONS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This section creates a second tornado plot with the same specifications as
# the primary plot. Originally, this "unlimited" version was created to show
# the full data range without custom axis limits for comparison purposes.
#
# CURRENT APPROACH (UPDATED):
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We now use fixed axis limits (€200k-€400k) for ALL tornado plots to ensure:
# - Consistent visual scaling across countries and analyses
# - Valid direct comparison between different tornado plots
# - Policy-relevant ICER range that spans all country WTP thresholds
#
# Both the primary tornado plot and this "unlimited" version now use the same
# fixed limits (ylim_top10). This section is kept for:
# - Backward compatibility with existing workflow
# - Flexibility to create alternative versions if needed in future
# - Documentation of previous visualization approach
#
# PRACTICAL USE:
# - Both versions are now identical in terms of axis scaling
# - Users can modify either version independently if alternative presentations
#   are needed for specific audiences
#
# MODELING APPROACH:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We create a second tornado plot identical to the first, including the same
# fixed axis limits (ylim_top10).

# Create another tornado plot with the same fixed axis limits
# This version was historically called "unlimited" but now uses same limits
# Health economic interpretation: Maintaining consistent €200k-€400k scale
# Modeling interpretation: Using identical specifications to primary plot
unlimited_tornado_plot_top10 <- owsa_tornado(

  # Use the same filtered data (top 10 parameters only)
  # This ensures we're comparing apples to apples - same parameters, same scaling
  # Health economic interpretation: Consistent data and consistent presentation
  owsa = DSAICER_top10,

  # Use the same text size for consistency
  # This ensures visual consistency across all tornado plot variants
  # Health economic best practice: Standardized formatting for comparability
  txtsize = 11,

  # Apply the same fixed axis limits as the primary tornado plot
  # This ensures both versions have identical scaling for direct comparison
  # ylim is a two-element vector: c(minimum, maximum)
  # Health economic interpretation: Maintaining consistent €200k-€400k scale
  # Modeling interpretation: Using the same ylim_top10 variable defined earlier
  # Note: Despite the name "unlimited", we now apply fixed limits for consistency
  ylim = ylim_top10
)

# Add the same axis labels
# Both versions now have identical specifications including axis limits
# Health economic interpretation: Consistent labeling for comparability
unlimited_tornado_plot_top10 <- unlimited_tornado_plot_top10 +
  # Label both axes
  # Identical to the primary version
  labs(x = "ICER (€ per QALY)", y = "Parameter")

# Create a title for this version
# We retain "Unlimited Scale" in the title for backward compatibility
# even though both versions now use the same fixed €200k-€400k limits
# This maintains consistency with existing file naming conventions
# Health economic interpretation: Clear labeling of visualization variants
plot_title_unlimited_top10 <- paste(
  "Tornado Plot - Top 10 Most Influential Parameters (",
  country_name[1],
  ") - Unlimited Scale",  # Note: Both versions now use same fixed limits
  sep = ""
)

# Add the title and apply the same formatting
# Both versions now match in all specifications (data, limits, formatting)
# except for the title text which distinguishes them for file naming
# Health economic best practice: Consistent formatting across related figures
unlimited_tornado_plot_top10 <- unlimited_tornado_plot_top10 +
  # Add the title
  ggtitle(plot_title_unlimited_top10) +
  # Apply identical theme settings
  theme(
    # Center the title
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    # Adjust x-axis label position
    axis.title.x = element_text(vjust = 0.25)
  )

# Add the same abbreviations caption
# The footnote is identical to the primary version
# This ensures both plots are equally self-explanatory
# Health economic interpretation: Consistent accessibility across variants
unlimited_tornado_plot_top10 <- unlimited_tornado_plot_top10 +
  # Use the same caption text we defined earlier
  labs(caption = abbreviations_caption) +
  # Use the same caption formatting
  theme(
    # Left-aligned, smaller text
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8),
    # Positioned below the plot
    plot.caption.position = "plot"
  )

# Construct the filename for the unlimited version
# We add "unlimited" to the filename to distinguish it
# This creates filenames like: output/tornado_top10_unlimited_ireland.png
# Health economic value: Clear, organized file naming
file_unlimited_top10 <- file.path(
  # Save in the same output folder
  "output",
  # Filename includes "unlimited" to indicate the variant
  # This makes it easy to distinguish from the limited version
  paste0("tornado_top10_unlimited_", tolower(country_name[1]), ".png")
)

# Display the filename for confirmation
# Transparency in file operations
print(paste("Saving unlimited top 10 tornado plot to:", file_unlimited_top10))

# Save the unlimited version with the same dimensions and resolution
# All save settings should match the limited version for fair comparison
# Health economic best practice: Consistent output format across variants
ggsave(
  # Save to the unlimited filename
  file_unlimited_top10,

  # Save the unlimited version plot object
  plot = unlimited_tornado_plot_top10,

  # Same width as the limited version (8 inches)
  # This ensures the plots are directly comparable
  width = 8,

  # Same height as the limited version (6 inches)
  # Consistent dimensions allow side-by-side comparison
  height = 6,

  # Same high resolution (600 DPI)
  # Both versions are publication-quality
  dpi = 600
)

# Close graphics devices
# Clean up after saving
while (!is.null(dev.list())) dev.off()

# Print confirmation
# Confirm successful save operation
print(paste("Unlimited top 10 tornado plot saved successfully as:", file_unlimited_top10))

# ============================================================================
# SUMMARY AND INTERPRETATION NOTES
# ============================================================================
#
# OUTPUTS GENERATED BY THIS SECTION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# At this point, you should have FOUR tornado plot files in the output/ folder:
#
# From previous sections (full set of parameters):
# 1. Tornado_Diagram_<Country>.png - All parameters with axis limits
# 2. Unlimited_Tornado_Diagram_<Country>.png - All parameters without limits
#
# From this section (top 10 parameters only):
# 3. tornado_top10_<country>.png - Top 10 only with calculated axis limits
# 4. tornado_top10_unlimited_<country>.png - Top 10 only without limits
#
# WHICH VERSION TO USE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# For PUBLICATION or PRESENTATION, typically use:
#   → tornado_top10_<country>.png (version #3)
#
#   This provides:
#   - Clear, focused visualization (not cluttered)
#   - Appropriate axis scaling (fixed €100k-€400k range)
#   - Self-contained with abbreviations footnote
#   - Publication-quality resolution (600 DPI)
#
# For APPENDICES or TECHNICAL REPORTS:
#   → Tornado_Diagram_<Country>.png (version #1) or
#   → tornado_top10_unlimited_<country>.png (version #4)
#
#   These provide:
#   - Full detail (all parameters or unlimited scale)
#   - Transparency and completeness
#   - Context for the simplified versions
#
# For INTERNAL VALIDATION:
#   → Compare versions #3 and #4 to ensure axis limits aren't distorting
#   → Compare across countries to see if the same parameters are influential
#
# NEXT STEPS FOR HEALTH ECONOMIC ANALYSIS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# After generating these plots, you should:
#
# 1. REVIEW TOP 10 PARAMETERS FOR FACE VALIDITY:
#    - Do these parameters make clinical and economic sense?
#    - Are key treatment costs included? (Expected: yes)
#    - Are important survival parameters included? (Expected: yes)
#    - Are utilities included if they're uncertain? (Possible)
#
# 2. COMPARE ACROSS COUNTRIES:
#    - Are the same parameters influential in Ireland, Germany, and Spain?
#    - If different parameters matter, why? (Different costs? Different thresholds?)
#    - This can reveal whether conclusions are robust across settings
#
# 3. IDENTIFY RESEARCH PRIORITIES:
#    - High-impact parameters are candidates for additional data collection
#    - Consider whether reducing uncertainty in these parameters is feasible
#    - Prioritize parameters that could change the cost-effectiveness decision
#
# 4. CROSS-REFERENCE WITH PSA RESULTS:
#    - The most influential parameters in OWSA should also show wide distributions in PSA
#    - If PSA shows a different set of important parameters, investigate why
#    - This comparison validates the consistency of your uncertainty analysis
#
# 5. CONSIDER THRESHOLD ANALYSIS:
#    - For the most influential cost parameters: at what price would the decision change?
#    - For the most influential clinical parameters: what efficacy would be needed?
#    - Threshold analysis can provide concrete targets for decision-makers
#
# 6. PREPARE FOR VALUE OF INFORMATION ANALYSIS (OPTIONAL):
#    - The top 10 parameters are candidates for EVPI (Expected Value of Perfect Information)
#    - EVPI quantifies the value of eliminating uncertainty in each parameter
#    - This can justify and prioritize additional research investments
#
```

```{r}

### PROBABILISTIC ANALYSIS ----

# We conduct a probabilistic analysis (PSA) of the model to estimate the uncertainty in the model outcomes.

# To do this, we generate samples for each model parameter from parametric distributions and evaluate the model for each set of parameter samples.


## Sampling the parameter values ----

# In order for the results reported in the PSA to be reproducible we need to set the random number seed. We also defining the number of runs, i.e., how many times we will re-sample for the parameter distributions, typically the number chosen is 10,000 in published studies, so we do that too:
n_runs <- 10000
set.seed(123)

# In the PSA, first we sample the parameter values from their distributions and store them in a data.frame.
# If a model parameter has no uncertainty and, hence, is fixed, we can set it equal to itself.


# To take random draws for the Weibull parametric survival distribution that we fitted at the start of the document using the 'flexsurv' package, we use the following piece of code.

# This applies mvrnorm (i.e., takes samples from the specified multivariate normal distribution) to the mean (mu) of 

# l_TTP_SoC_weibull$coefficients
#     shape     scale 
# 0.7700246 1.7425343 

# i.e., to the mean of the shape and the scale variables from the Weibull parametric survival distribution that we fitted.

# And gives a sigma (a positive-definite symmetric matrix specifying the covariance matrix of the variables) that is equal to the covariance between the shape and the scale variables:

# > l_TTP_SoC_weibull$cov
#             shape       scale
# shape 0.001983267 0.000291494
# scale 0.000291494 0.000782051

# You'll see that it's covariance between the two variables because you can match shape with scale twice, and each time it's the same value, so the same covariance between the two variables.

# n is just the number of samples.

# Described here:
# rdocumentation.org/packages/MASS/versions/7.3-58.1/topics/mvrnorm

# So, correlated sets (a "set" here is like one random draw from the distribution, because the draw is for shape and scale at the same time) of coefficients for the survival distribution (i.e., correlated sets of shape and scale values for the survival distribution, which are the coefficients as above) are generated using the variance-covariance matrix that was obtained from fitting the weibull distribution (the cov in l_TTP_SoC_weibull is equal to the covariance between the shape and the scale variables and is printed as a 2 by 2 matrix above) and a multivariate normal distribution (this is just saying we are applying mvrnorm to take samples from the multivariate normal distribution for the mean (mu) values of shape and scale).

# Multivariate normal distribution described here too: https://devinincerti.com/2018/02/10/psa.html'


m_coef_weibull_SoC <- mvrnorm(
  n     = n_runs, 
  mu    = l_TTP_SoC_weibull$coefficients, 
  Sigma = l_TTP_SoC_weibull$cov
)

head(m_coef_weibull_SoC)

m_coef_weibull_OS_SoC <- mvrnorm(
  n     = n_runs, 
  mu    = l_TTD_SoC_weibull$coefficients, 
  Sigma = l_TTD_SoC_weibull$cov
)

head(m_coef_weibull_OS_SoC)

# ============================================================================
# SAVE RNG STATE TO PRESERVE ORIGINAL PSA SAMPLING SEQUENCE
# ============================================================================
#
# CRITICAL: We save the random number generator (RNG) state HERE, immediately
# after Weibull sampling. This captures the exact RNG state that existed in
# the original code (before gamma distribution was added).
#
# After gamma sampling (below), we will RESTORE this state so that all
# subsequent parameter sampling (HR, costs, utilities) gets the SAME random
# values as in the original validated results (Table 2 in publication).
#
saved_rng_state <- .Random.seed

# ============================================================================
# GAMMA DISTRIBUTION PARAMETER SAMPLING FOR PSA
# ============================================================================
#
# PSA APPROACH FOR SCENARIO ANALYSIS:
# To enable a PSA-based comparison between Weibull and gamma distributions,
# we need to sample parameter uncertainty for BOTH distributions.
#
# This ensures that when we compare Weibull vs Gamma scenarios:
#   1. Both comparisons reflect parameter uncertainty (not just structural choice)
#   2. The comparison is "apples to apples" (both using PSA means, not deterministic)
#   3. We can report credible intervals for the difference between distributions
#
# GAMMA DISTRIBUTION PARAMETERS FOR TTP (Time To Progression):
# Using the same multivariate normal sampling approach as Weibull.
# l_TTP_SoC_gamma was already fitted earlier in the survival modeling section.
# We sample from the joint distribution of shape and rate parameters.
#
m_coef_gamma_SoC <- mvrnorm(
  n     = n_runs,                        # Number of PSA simulations
  mu    = l_TTP_SoC_gamma$coefficients,  # Mean: fitted gamma coefficients (log scale)
  Sigma = l_TTP_SoC_gamma$cov            # Covariance matrix from gamma fit
)

head(m_coef_gamma_SoC)

# GAMMA DISTRIBUTION PARAMETERS FOR TTD (Time To Death / Overall Survival):
# Sample parameter uncertainty for gamma distribution for overall survival.
# l_TTD_SoC_gamma was already fitted earlier in the survival modeling section.
# We sample from the joint distribution of shape and rate parameters.
#
m_coef_gamma_OS_SoC <- mvrnorm(
  n     = n_runs,                        # Number of PSA simulations
  mu    = l_TTD_SoC_gamma$coefficients,  # Mean: fitted gamma coefficients (log scale)
  Sigma = l_TTD_SoC_gamma$cov            # Covariance matrix from gamma fit
)

head(m_coef_gamma_OS_SoC)

# ============================================================================
# RESTORE RNG STATE TO PRESERVE ORIGINAL PSA SAMPLING SEQUENCE
# ============================================================================
#
# CRITICAL: We now restore the RNG state that was saved BEFORE gamma sampling.
# This ensures that all subsequent parameter sampling (HR, costs, utilities,
# etc.) uses the EXACT SAME random values as in the original implementation.
#
# WHY THIS IS NECESSARY:
# The gamma sampling above consumed random numbers, which would have shifted
# all subsequent random draws. By restoring the saved state, we "undo" this
# shift for the main PSA parameters.
#
# RESULT:
#   1. Weibull parameters: Sampled normally (same as before)
#   2. Gamma parameters: Sampled using "bonus" random numbers (for scenario analysis)
#   3. HR, costs, utilities: Sampled from ORIGINAL sequence (matches Table 2)
#
# This preserves backward compatibility with published results while adding
# gamma scenario analysis capability.
#
.Random.seed <- saved_rng_state

### Hazard Ratios  
  
# People use exp for rnorm (i.e., to make random draws from a normal distribution) but I to use want rlnorm.

#  HR_FP_Exp = exp(rnorm(n_runs, log(0.6), 0.08))

# The rlnorm() function in R is used for generating random draws from a log-normal distribution.
 
# To make draws from the log-normal distribution you need to enter a hazard ratio and standard deviation.

# If you find a hazard ratio and confidence interval in the literature, rather than a hazard ratio and a standard deviation, you can make conversions to a standard deviation.

# To generate random draws for the hazard ratio, I need a mean for the hazard ratio(just the hazard ratio value itself), and a standard deviation built from the 95% confidence interval of the hazard ratio (the SD is built from log(Upper CI) - log(Lower CI)/2*SE, so sd is already built from logs for inclusion in rlnorm and doesnt need to be set as sdlog = log() unlike meanlog = log() where you need to take the log of the hazard ratio value). 


# SD: (natural log(Upper confidence interval) -  natural log(lower confidence interval) / 2*Standard error (i.e. 1.95*2 = 3.92 for a 95% confidence interval)


# So, it looks like I take the natural log of the upper limit minus the natural log of the lower limit (in confidence intervals the lower limit is reported on the left and the upper limit is reported on the right, so it would be 95% CI (30.0 [LOWER LIMIT], 34.2[UPPER LIMIT]), and I would rearrange these to have [ln(UPPER LIMIT) - ln(LOWER LIMIT)], i.e., [ln(34.2)-ln(30.0)]) and divide by 2 times the standard error. Provided the sample size is large, then for the 95% confidence interval this would be 2 x 1.96 = 3.92 For 90% confidence intervals 3.92 should be replaced by 3.29, and for 99% confidence intervals it should be replaced by 5.15. 

# I often come across hazard ratios and their confidence intervals in the published literature on clinical trials, but rarely do I see standard deviations. 
 
# A typical example from the literature is the following: "HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.54 to 0.89 in mCRC for cetuximab plus FOLFOX-4 vs FOLFOX-4 alone" -  https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7044820/pdf/bmjopen-2019-030738.pdf:
# 
# To compute the standard deviation for hazard ratios from the above typical reports in the literature, so that I can then generate random draws from a log-normal distribution for a hazard ratio I would do the following:
# 
# (natural log(Upper confidence interval) -  natural log(lower confidence interval) / 2*Standard error (i.e. 1.95*2 = 3.92 for a 95% confidence interval)
# 
# or in R: (log(0.89) - log(0.54)) / 3.92 = 0.1274623
# 
# 
# UpperCI <- 0.89
# LowerCI <- 0.54
# SD <- (log(UpperCI) - log(LowerCI)) / 3.92
# SD = 0.1274623
# 

# If I need to provide a citation for this formula I can use the below which, although this does not provide the formula I use, it provides enough information that is similar to the above, and which I could say ultimately informed the formula:
# Higgins, J. P. T., & Deeks, J. J. (2011). Chapter 7.7. 3.3: Obtaining standard deviations from standard errors, confidence intervals, t values and P values for differences in means. Cochrane handbook for systematic reviews of interventions, Version, 5(0).
# 
# 
# This approach is also supported by the following post, which provides good clarity on all of the above:
# 
# https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/546192/calculate-the-standard-deviation-from-a-hazard-ratios-confidence-interval


# random draws from a log-normal distribution

# hr_draws <- rlnorm(nsims, meanlog = log(mean), sdlog = SD). 

# 
# We take random draws from the log-normal distribution for ratios, because if we were to take random draws from the ratio as it stands, because the hazard ratio can't go any lower than 0 but can go to plus infinity, our random draws would be skewed in the values we take from the distribution, on the other hand, if we were to put things on the natural log scale we would be taking our random draws from a more normalised distribution. So, you'll see that in:
# 
# rlnorm(n_sim, meanlog = log(mean),  sdlog = SD)
# 
# it's the log of the mean (the ratio value, so the hazard ratio) and the log of the standard deviation (which we put on the log scale when we calculate it so we don't need to put in as sdlog = log() here, just sdlog = ) in order to be taking random draws from a log-normal distribution (i.e. a log normally distributed HAZARD RATIO).

HR_FP_Exp = rlnorm(n_runs, meanlog = log(MEAN_HR_FP_Exp), sdlog = SD),
HR_PD_Exp = rlnorm(n_runs, meanlog = log(MEAN_HR_PD_Exp), sdlog = OS_SD),

In my model I definitely don't, as the hazard ratio and underlying rate survival curves that make up SoC transition probabilities come from the same paper, and thus the same time period.

# So, I built the following code to translate the formula for the methods of moments into R, to allow us to take our transition probabilities from the literature:
# 
# 
#  ## Methods of moments

# 
# #Assume the below mean and std error come from the reported literature
# 
# mean <- 0.75 ## mean from the literature

# 
# # The method of moments can be coded up as below to get the alpha and beta from the sample using the mean and standard error from the sample:
#

# alpha <- mean*alpha.plus.beta ## alpha (a)

# If costs are reported with a 95% confidence interval the maximum is the upper confidence interval. If the interval is not centered on the mean, use the maximum or minimum in place of the upper confidence interval, depending on which one is further away from the mean SE = (m-CIlower)/t, here the bit in the brackets is rearranged when dealing with lower limits to have the MEAN minus the lower confidence interval so that things don't become negative (because the lower value will of course always be lower than the mean, as it's supposed to be below the mean, so a smaller number minus a larger number will be negative), but when the interval is centered on the mean the formula of SE = (CIupper-m)/t and SE = (m-CIlower)/t are inherently doing the same thing, that is getting the difference between the mean and the confidence interval and dividing this by t. So both formulas are options to use in getting the SE, and an author may choose to use the one which incorporates the interval that is farthest from the mean in order to incorporate as much variability in doing this SE calculation as possible, i.e. to reflect the variability in their SE calculation.

# As per: https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/550293/how-to-calculate-standard-error-given-mean-and-confidence-interval-for-a-gamma-d/550892#550892
 
 
# "I would like to note that, while those values in the table happen to correspond with ±2σ, the minimum and maximum values do not generally follow such simple formula with mean plus-minus some standard deviation.
 
# In this case, the minimum and maximum values only correspond to the interval μ±2σ because the distribution seems to have been truncated at those values."
 
 
# i.e., my formula will only work if the minimum and maximum values reported in a study are ±2 SE from the mean, i.e. + 2 SE from the mean for the maximum value, and -2 SE from the mean for the minimum value.
 
# And that will be the case any time there is a 95% Confidence Interval:
 

# [ "Since 95% of values fall within two standard deviations of the mean according to the 68-95-99.7 Rule, simply add and subtract two standard deviations from the mean in order to obtain the 95% confidence interval. Notice that with higher confidence levels the confidence interval gets large so there is less precision." https://www.westga.edu/academics/research/vrc/assets/docs/confidence_intervals_notes.pdf also saved here: C:\Users\Jonathan\OneDrive - Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland\COLOSSUS\Training Resources\Decision Modelling - Advanced Course\A2_Making Models Probabilistic\A2.1.2 Distributions for parameters\gammadist\confidence_intervals_notes.pdf

# So, this might be a good way to check if my standard error is correct. Although this will only work if my confidence interval is centred on the mean, i.e. if I am the same distance from the mean to the max and to the min. If my confidence interval is NOT centred on the mean, I can calculate 2 standard errors, one between the lower interval and the mean, and one between the upper interval and the mean, and then apply these in CI = m ± t*SE, knowing that:

# CIupper = m + t*SE

# CIlower = m - t*SE

# I've figured out a simple test for whether the max/min reported is ±2σ:
# se <- ((Max) - (Mean)) / 2
# MaxMatch <- Mean + 2*se 
# MinMatch <- Mean - 2*se
 
# I can then check if the max/min reported in a Table match the above, and if so I know that the max/min reported is ±2σ.
 
# If not, it may be that they used the se off the minimum as it's further away, so try the below:
 
# se <- ((Mean) - (Min)) / 2
# MaxMatch <- Mean + 2*se 
# MinMatch <- Mean - 2*se
 
 
# I can then check if the max/min reported in a Table match the above, and if so I know that the max/min reported is ±2σ.
 
 
 
 
# Even if it's not symmetric, this may still be a 95% confidence interval if the mean is at 2 of one of the standard errors from the min or the max, we can see this in action below:

# "Density, distribution function, quantile function and random generation for the Gamma distribution with parameters alpha (or shape) and beta (or scale or 1/rate)." https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/Rlab/html/Gamma.html 


# "There is a R function for simulating this random variable. Here in addition to the number of values to simulate, we just need two parameters, one for the shape and one for either the rate or the scale. The rate is the inverse of the scale. The general formula is: rgamma(n, shape, rate = 1, scale = 1/rate)." https://pubs.wsb.wisc.edu/academics/analytics-using-r-2019/gamma-variables-optional.html also saved here: C:\Users\Jonathan\OneDrive - Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland\COLOSSUS\Training Resources\Decision Modelling - Advanced Course\A2_Making Models Probabilistic\A2.1.2 Distributions for parameters\13.7 Gamma Variables (Optional) _ Analytics Using R.pdf

So, he may have taken this approach as well.This is supported by: "rate:	a numeric vector in the range [0, Inf) that specifies the inverse of the scale parameter." https://docs.tibco.com/pub/enterprise-runtime-for-R/4.1.1/doc/html/Language_Reference/stats/GammaDist.html

# This is supported by the below:

# > set.seed(1)
# > x <- rgamma(n = 1000, shape = 5, scale = 3)
# > mean(x)
# [1] 14.61593
# Knowing that the rate is the inverse of the scale, we can get the rate as 1/3 below:
# > 1/3
# [1] 0.3333333
# > set.seed(1)
# > x <- rgamma(n = 1000, shape = 5, rate = 0.3333333)
# > mean(x)
# [1] 14.61593
# > set.seed(1)
# > x <- rgamma(n = 1000, shape = 5, scale = 1/0.3333333)
# > mean(x)
# [1] 14.61593

# Thus, Koen generated the rate and used that in rgamma, while Andy showed me how to use scale and use that in rgamma.

##### POINT ESTIMATES ONLY:



# IMPORTANT, THIS VALUE IS BOUNDED BY 1 OR 0:
# When calculating se from point estimates, remember that utility and probability values cannot be less than 0 or greater than 1, so don't calculate a min or max that is less than 0 or greater than 1. If you do, just round it to 0 or 1.


# If you have a point estimate, then you can generate the standard error/standard deviation using the method of moments again.

#Per Table 4 in the Goldstein paper:
# > mean<-   0.850
# > Maximum <- mean + 0.20*mean
# > Maximum
# [1] 1.02
# > Minimum <- mean - 0.20*mean
# > Minimum
# [1] 0.68
# > se <- ((Maximum) - (mean)) / 2
# > se  
# [1] 0.085
# > std.error <- se
# > alpha.plus.beta <- mean*(1-mean)/(std.error^2)-1 ## alpha + beta (ab)
# > alpha <- mean*alpha.plus.beta ## alpha (a)
# > beta <- alpha*(1-mean)/mean ## beta(b)
# > alpha
# [1] 14.15
# > beta
# [1] 2.497059
# So, a perfect match to the Goldstein paper.
# Because this approach to point estimates ends up making the same range around this point estimate as reported in Table 4, the implication is that when a point estimate is reported with a range, you can generate the SE the exact same way as above, that is, se <- ((Maximum) - (mean)) / 2, because we are applying the same manner of generating the SE to the range that was reported in the paper, as to the point estimate.

## RANGE:

##### Calculating Beta values when you have a range around your point estimate in the literature (THIS CAN BE APPLIED TO PROBABILITY OR UTILITY): 


# Here are my formulas, and if you read further below you can see how I got to these formulas.

# Discounting:
  
# A uniform distribution is a probability distribution in which every value between an interval from a to b is equally likely to be chosen. https://www.statology.org/uniform-distribution-r/
  
# "Generates random values that are evenly spread between min and max bounds" - https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E57185_01/CYBUG/apcs03s03s01.html 

# Devin Incerti talks about the Uniform distribution here: "The uniform distribution is useful when there is little data available to estimate a parameter and determine its distribution. It is always preferable to place uncertainty on a parameter even when there is little evidence for it than to assume a fixed value (which gives a false sense of precision). Sampling from the uniform distribution is straightforward." https://devinincerti.com/2018/02/10/psa.html  
  
#Reading the literature, it seems like studies pick a lower bound and upper bound for the discount rate, such that the average (mean of the discount rate) will reach the point estimate they started with:
```
