```{r}
# ============================================================================
# PSA-BASED GAMMA DISTRIBUTION SCENARIO ANALYSIS - COUNTRY-SPECIFIC
# ============================================================================
#
# This analysis runs for whichever country is active (uncommented) in the
# country parameter blocks. Results will be labeled with the active country name.
#
# **CRITICAL METHODOLOGICAL NOTE - PSA-BASED COMPARISON:**
# This section implements a PROBABILISTIC sensitivity analysis comparing
# Weibull and gamma distributions. Both scenarios are evaluated using the
# SAME PSA framework (n_runs simulations with parameter uncertainty).
#
# This ensures:
#   1. The comparison reflects BOTH parameter AND structural uncertainty
#   2. Results are reported as PSA means (not single deterministic values)
#   3. We can quantify uncertainty via 95% credible intervals
#   4. The comparison is methodologically consistent with the main PSA results
#   5. Alignment with reviewer request to treat PSA as the "base case"
#
# SCENARIO ANALYSIS RATIONALE:
# This section implements a scenario analysis where we test the impact of
# using the gamma distribution instead of Weibull for survival extrapolation.
# This addresses structural uncertainty in our cost-effectiveness model.
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC IMPORTANCE:
# The choice of parametric survival distribution can substantially affect:
#   1. Long-term survival extrapolation (beyond observed trial data)
#   2. Total life-years (QALYs) gained by the intervention
#   3. Lifetime treatment costs
#   4. The resulting cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER)
#
# If the ICER is highly sensitive to distributional choice, this indicates
# structural uncertainty that may affect decision-making. HTA agencies often
# request scenario analyses exploring alternative distributions.
#
# PSA-BASED IMPLEMENTATION APPROACH:
# We will:
#   1. Run FULL PSA with curve_choice = "weibull" (n_runs simulations)
#   2. Calculate PSA means and 95% CrIs for Weibull scenario
#   3. Run FULL PSA with curve_choice = "gamma" (n_runs simulations)
#   4. Calculate PSA means and 95% CrIs for Gamma scenario
#   5. Compare PSA-based results (means and CrIs) between distributions
#   6. Interpret the sensitivity of our conclusions to distributional choice
#
# **WHY PSA-BASED INSTEAD OF DETERMINISTIC?**
# - Aligns with reviewer feedback to treat PSA as effective base case
# - Provides credible intervals around the distributional comparison
# - Ensures internal consistency: main results are PSA-based, so scenario
#   analysis should be PSA-based too
# - More transparent about combined parameter + structural uncertainty
#
# NOTE: This analysis will run for whichever country is active (uncommented)
# in the country parameter blocks at the start of the file. The output filename
# will automatically include the active country name.

# ============================================================================
# STEP 1: RUN FULL PSA WITH WEIBULL DISTRIBUTION
# ============================================================================
#
# **PSA APPROACH:**
# We run the model n_runs times (e.g., 10,000 simulations), each time sampling
# parameter values from their uncertainty distributions. This gives us a
# distribution of costs and QALYs under Weibull, not just a single point estimate.
#
# df_PA_input already contains Weibull parameters sampled for all n_runs iterations
#
cat("Running PSA for WEIBULL distribution (", country_name, ")...\n", sep = "")
cat("Number of simulations:", n_runs, "\n\n")

# Create data frames to store PSA results for Weibull scenario
# These will hold costs and QALYs for each PSA simulation
df_c_weibull <- df_e_weibull <- data.frame(
  SoC = rep(NA, n_runs),  # Standard of Care
  Exp = rep(NA, n_runs)   # Experimental treatment
)

# PSA LOOP FOR WEIBULL:
# For each PSA iteration, run the model with curve_choice = "weibull"
# Each iteration uses a different row of df_PA_input (different parameter samples)
for(i_run in 1:n_runs){
  # Run model with Weibull distribution for this PSA iteration
  # curve_choice = "weibull" tells the function to use pweibull() for survival
  l_out_temp <- oncologySemiMarkov(
    l_params_all = df_PA_input[i_run, ],  # Parameter values for this iteration
    n_wtp        = n_wtp,                  # Willingness-to-pay threshold
    curve_choice = "weibull"               # Use Weibull distribution
  )

  # Store costs and QALYs for this iteration
  df_c_weibull[i_run, ] <- l_out_temp$Cost    # Costs for SoC and Exp
  df_e_weibull[i_run, ] <- l_out_temp$Effect  # QALYs for SoC and Exp

  # Display progress every 10% of simulations
  if(i_run %% (n_runs/10) == 0) {
    cat('\r', paste(round(i_run/n_runs * 100, 0), "% done (Weibull PSA)", sep = " "))
  }
}
cat("\n")

# CALCULATE PSA SUMMARY STATISTICS FOR WEIBULL:
# For each strategy, calculate mean and 95% credible intervals
#
# Mean costs and QALYs (expected values across all PSA simulations)
weibull_cost_soc_mean <- mean(df_c_weibull$SoC)
weibull_cost_exp_mean <- mean(df_c_weibull$Exp)
weibull_qaly_soc_mean <- mean(df_e_weibull$SoC)
weibull_qaly_exp_mean <- mean(df_e_weibull$Exp)

# Calculate incremental outcomes (mean of differences = difference of means)
weibull_inc_cost_psa <- weibull_cost_exp_mean - weibull_cost_soc_mean
weibull_inc_qaly_psa <- weibull_qaly_exp_mean - weibull_qaly_soc_mean

# Calculate ICER from PSA means (not mean of ICERs, which would be misleading)
weibull_icer_psa <- weibull_inc_cost_psa / weibull_inc_qaly_psa

# Calculate Net Monetary Benefit distribution for Weibull
weibull_incremental_costs <- df_c_weibull$Exp - df_c_weibull$SoC
weibull_incremental_qalys <- df_e_weibull$Exp - df_e_weibull$SoC
weibull_incremental_nmb <- (weibull_incremental_qalys * n_wtp) - weibull_incremental_costs

# Calculate 95% credible intervals for incremental outcomes
weibull_inc_cost_lower <- quantile(weibull_incremental_costs, probs = 0.025)
weibull_inc_cost_upper <- quantile(weibull_incremental_costs, probs = 0.975)
weibull_inc_qaly_lower <- quantile(weibull_incremental_qalys, probs = 0.025)
weibull_inc_qaly_upper <- quantile(weibull_incremental_qalys, probs = 0.975)
weibull_inc_nmb_mean <- mean(weibull_incremental_nmb)
weibull_inc_nmb_lower <- quantile(weibull_incremental_nmb, probs = 0.025)
weibull_inc_nmb_upper <- quantile(weibull_incremental_nmb, probs = 0.975)

# Display Weibull PSA results
cat("\n=======================================================\n")
cat("WEIBULL PSA RESULTS (", country_name, ") - PSA-BASED\n", sep = "")
cat("=======================================================\n")
cat("Number of simulations:", n_runs, "\n\n")
cat("Mean Costs:\n")
cat("  SoC: €", round(weibull_cost_soc_mean, 2), "\n")
cat("  Exp: €", round(weibull_cost_exp_mean, 2), "\n\n")
cat("Mean QALYs:\n")
cat("  SoC:", round(weibull_qaly_soc_mean, 4), "\n")
cat("  Exp:", round(weibull_qaly_exp_mean, 4), "\n\n")
cat("Incremental Cost (Mean): €", round(weibull_inc_cost_psa, 2),
    " [95% CrI: €", round(weibull_inc_cost_lower, 2), " to €", round(weibull_inc_cost_upper, 2), "]\n")
cat("Incremental QALYs (Mean):", round(weibull_inc_qaly_psa, 4),
    " [95% CrI:", round(weibull_inc_qaly_lower, 4), "to", round(weibull_inc_qaly_upper, 4), "]\n")
cat("ICER (from PSA means): €", round(weibull_icer_psa, 2), " per QALY\n")
cat("Incremental NMB (Mean): €", round(weibull_inc_nmb_mean, 2),
    " [95% CrI: €", round(weibull_inc_nmb_lower, 2), " to €", round(weibull_inc_nmb_upper, 2), "]\n")
cat("=======================================================\n\n")


# ============================================================================
# STEP 2: RUN FULL PSA WITH GAMMA DISTRIBUTION
# ============================================================================
#
# **PSA APPROACH:**
# Now we run the SAME PSA (same n_runs, same parameter samples from df_PA_input),
# but with curve_choice = "gamma" instead of "weibull".
#
# This ensures the comparison isolates STRUCTURAL uncertainty (Weibull vs Gamma)
# while keeping PARAMETER uncertainty constant across both scenarios.
#
cat("Running PSA for GAMMA distribution (", country_name, ")...\n", sep = "")
cat("Number of simulations:", n_runs, "\n\n")

# Create data frames to store PSA results for Gamma scenario
df_c_gamma <- df_e_gamma <- data.frame(
  SoC = rep(NA, n_runs),  # Standard of Care
  Exp = rep(NA, n_runs)   # Experimental treatment
)

# PSA LOOP FOR GAMMA:
# For each PSA iteration, run the model with curve_choice = "gamma"
# Use the SAME parameter samples (same row of df_PA_input) as Weibull
# This ensures fair comparison (only distribution changes, not parameters)
for(i_run in 1:n_runs){
  # Run model with Gamma distribution for this PSA iteration
  # curve_choice = "gamma" tells the function to use pgamma() for survival
  l_out_temp <- oncologySemiMarkov(
    l_params_all = df_PA_input[i_run, ],  # Same parameters as Weibull iteration
    n_wtp        = n_wtp,                  # Same WTP threshold
    curve_choice = "gamma"                 # Use Gamma distribution
  )

  # Store costs and QALYs for this iteration
  df_c_gamma[i_run, ] <- l_out_temp$Cost    # Costs for SoC and Exp
  df_e_gamma[i_run, ] <- l_out_temp$Effect  # QALYs for SoC and Exp

  # Display progress every 10% of simulations
  if(i_run %% (n_runs/10) == 0) {
    cat('\r', paste(round(i_run/n_runs * 100, 0), "% done (Gamma PSA)", sep = " "))
  }
}
cat("\n")

# CALCULATE PSA SUMMARY STATISTICS FOR GAMMA:
#
# Mean costs and QALYs (expected values across all PSA simulations)
gamma_cost_soc_mean <- mean(df_c_gamma$SoC)
gamma_cost_exp_mean <- mean(df_c_gamma$Exp)
gamma_qaly_soc_mean <- mean(df_e_gamma$SoC)
gamma_qaly_exp_mean <- mean(df_e_gamma$Exp)

# Calculate incremental outcomes
gamma_inc_cost_psa <- gamma_cost_exp_mean - gamma_cost_soc_mean
gamma_inc_qaly_psa <- gamma_qaly_exp_mean - gamma_qaly_soc_mean

# Calculate ICER from PSA means
gamma_icer_psa <- gamma_inc_cost_psa / gamma_inc_qaly_psa

# Calculate Net Monetary Benefit distribution for Gamma
gamma_incremental_costs <- df_c_gamma$Exp - df_c_gamma$SoC
gamma_incremental_qalys <- df_e_gamma$Exp - df_e_gamma$SoC
gamma_incremental_nmb <- (gamma_incremental_qalys * n_wtp) - gamma_incremental_costs

# Calculate 95% credible intervals for incremental outcomes
gamma_inc_cost_lower <- quantile(gamma_incremental_costs, probs = 0.025)
gamma_inc_cost_upper <- quantile(gamma_incremental_costs, probs = 0.975)
gamma_inc_qaly_lower <- quantile(gamma_incremental_qalys, probs = 0.025)
gamma_inc_qaly_upper <- quantile(gamma_incremental_qalys, probs = 0.975)
gamma_inc_nmb_mean <- mean(gamma_incremental_nmb)
gamma_inc_nmb_lower <- quantile(gamma_incremental_nmb, probs = 0.025)
gamma_inc_nmb_upper <- quantile(gamma_incremental_nmb, probs = 0.975)

# Display Gamma PSA results
cat("\n=======================================================\n")
cat("GAMMA PSA RESULTS (", country_name, ") - PSA-BASED\n", sep = "")
cat("=======================================================\n")
cat("Number of simulations:", n_runs, "\n\n")
cat("Mean Costs:\n")
cat("  SoC: €", round(gamma_cost_soc_mean, 2), "\n")
cat("  Exp: €", round(gamma_cost_exp_mean, 2), "\n\n")
cat("Mean QALYs:\n")
cat("  SoC:", round(gamma_qaly_soc_mean, 4), "\n")
cat("  Exp:", round(gamma_qaly_exp_mean, 4), "\n\n")
cat("Incremental Cost (Mean): €", round(gamma_inc_cost_psa, 2),
    " [95% CrI: €", round(gamma_inc_cost_lower, 2), " to €", round(gamma_inc_cost_upper, 2), "]\n")
cat("Incremental QALYs (Mean):", round(gamma_inc_qaly_psa, 4),
    " [95% CrI:", round(gamma_inc_qaly_lower, 4), "to", round(gamma_inc_qaly_upper, 4), "]\n")
cat("ICER (from PSA means): €", round(gamma_icer_psa, 2), " per QALY\n")
cat("Incremental NMB (Mean): €", round(gamma_inc_nmb_mean, 2),
    " [95% CrI: €", round(gamma_inc_nmb_lower, 2), " to €", round(gamma_inc_nmb_upper, 2), "]\n")
cat("=======================================================\n\n")


# ============================================================================
# STEP 3: CREATE PSA-BASED COMPARISON TABLE
# ============================================================================
#
# **PSA-BASED COMPARISON TABLE:**
# This table reports PSA means and 95% credible intervals for both distributions.
# All values are derived from the PSA results (not deterministic single-run values).
#
# This table is suitable for inclusion in the manuscript as it shows:
#   1. Mean costs and QALYs for each strategy under each distribution
#   2. Incremental costs and QALYs (with 95% CrIs)
#   3. ICERs calculated from PSA means
#   4. Incremental NMB (with 95% CrIs)
#
cat("Creating PSA-based Weibull vs Gamma comparison table...\n")

# Create comprehensive comparison table with PSA-based results
# This table has one row per distribution, showing all summary statistics
psa_comparison_table <- data.frame(
  Distribution = c("Weibull", "Gamma"),

  # Mean costs for each strategy
  SoC_Cost_Mean = c(weibull_cost_soc_mean, gamma_cost_soc_mean),
  Exp_Cost_Mean = c(weibull_cost_exp_mean, gamma_cost_exp_mean),

  # Mean QALYs for each strategy
  SoC_QALY_Mean = c(weibull_qaly_soc_mean, gamma_qaly_soc_mean),
  Exp_QALY_Mean = c(weibull_qaly_exp_mean, gamma_qaly_exp_mean),

  # Incremental outcomes (means)
  Inc_Cost_Mean = c(weibull_inc_cost_psa, gamma_inc_cost_psa),
  Inc_QALY_Mean = c(weibull_inc_qaly_psa, gamma_inc_qaly_psa),

  # ICER from PSA means
  ICER_PSA = c(weibull_icer_psa, gamma_icer_psa),

  # Incremental NMB (mean)
  Inc_NMB_Mean = c(weibull_inc_nmb_mean, gamma_inc_nmb_mean),

  # 95% Credible intervals for incremental cost
  Inc_Cost_Lower_CrI = c(weibull_inc_cost_lower, gamma_inc_cost_lower),
  Inc_Cost_Upper_CrI = c(weibull_inc_cost_upper, gamma_inc_cost_upper),

  # 95% Credible intervals for incremental QALYs
  Inc_QALY_Lower_CrI = c(weibull_inc_qaly_lower, gamma_inc_qaly_lower),
  Inc_QALY_Upper_CrI = c(weibull_inc_qaly_upper, gamma_inc_qaly_upper),

  # 95% Credible intervals for incremental NMB
  Inc_NMB_Lower_CrI = c(weibull_inc_nmb_lower, gamma_inc_nmb_lower),
  Inc_NMB_Upper_CrI = c(weibull_inc_nmb_upper, gamma_inc_nmb_upper),

  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Display the PSA-based comparison table
cat("\n=======================================================\n")
cat("WEIBULL VS. GAMMA COMPARISON TABLE (PSA-BASED)\n")
cat("=======================================================\n")
print(psa_comparison_table, row.names = FALSE)
cat("=======================================================\n\n")

# Save PSA-based comparison table to CSV for use in paper
# Filename dynamically includes country name from active country block
comparison_filename <- paste0("Weibull_vs_Gamma_", country_name, "_PSA.csv")
write.csv(
  psa_comparison_table,
  file = file.path("output", comparison_filename),
  row.names = FALSE
)

cat("PSA-based comparison table saved to: output/", comparison_filename, "\n\n", sep = "")


# ============================================================================
# STEP 4: INTERPRET PSA-BASED COMPARISON
# ============================================================================
#
# **INTERPRETATION OF PSA-BASED RESULTS:**
# Compare ICERs calculated from PSA means to assess structural uncertainty
#
icer_difference_psa <- gamma_icer_psa - weibull_icer_psa
icer_percent_change_psa <- (gamma_icer_psa - weibull_icer_psa) / weibull_icer_psa * 100

cat("=======================================================\n")
cat("INTERPRETATION OF PSA-BASED RESULTS:\n")
cat("=======================================================\n")
cat("ICER under Weibull (PSA): €", round(weibull_icer_psa, 2), " per QALY\n")
cat("ICER under Gamma (PSA):   €", round(gamma_icer_psa, 2), " per QALY\n")
cat("Absolute difference:      €", round(icer_difference_psa, 2), " per QALY\n")
cat("Relative change:          ", round(icer_percent_change_psa, 2), "%\n\n")

# Interpret the sensitivity based on the magnitude of change
# HEALTH ECONOMIC INTERPRETATION:
# - Small change (<10%): Results are robust to distributional choice
# - Moderate change (10-25%): Some structural uncertainty, but conclusions likely stable
# - Large change (>25%): Substantial structural uncertainty, may affect decision
#
# We also compare to the willingness-to-pay threshold for Ireland (€45,000/QALY)
# to see if the cost-effectiveness conclusion changes
wtp_ireland <- 45000

# Check if cost-effectiveness conclusion changes (using PSA-based ICERs)
weibull_cost_effective_psa <- weibull_icer_psa <= wtp_ireland
gamma_cost_effective_psa <- gamma_icer_psa <= wtp_ireland

if (weibull_cost_effective_psa == gamma_cost_effective_psa) {
  cat("COST-EFFECTIVENESS CONCLUSION: CONSISTENT\n")
  if (weibull_cost_effective_psa) {
    cat("The intervention is cost-effective under BOTH distributions\n")
    cat("(ICER < €", wtp_ireland, "/QALY in both scenarios)\n\n")
  } else {
    cat("The intervention is NOT cost-effective under EITHER distribution\n")
    cat("(ICER > €", wtp_ireland, "/QALY in both scenarios)\n\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("COST-EFFECTIVENESS CONCLUSION: **CHANGES WITH DISTRIBUTION**\n")
  cat("WARNING: The cost-effectiveness conclusion is sensitive to\n")
  cat("         distributional choice. This represents substantial\n")
  cat("         structural uncertainty that should be considered\n")
  cat("         in decision-making.\n\n")
}

# Provide interpretation guidance (using PSA-based percent change)
if (abs(icer_percent_change_psa) < 10) {
  cat("STRUCTURAL UNCERTAINTY: LOW\n")
  cat("The ICER changes by less than 10%, indicating that results are\n")
  cat("robust to the choice between Weibull and gamma distributions.\n")
} else if (abs(icer_percent_change_psa) < 25) {
  cat("STRUCTURAL UNCERTAINTY: MODERATE\n")
  cat("The ICER changes by 10-25%, indicating some structural uncertainty.\n")
  cat("The cost-effectiveness conclusion is likely stable, but the magnitude\n")
  cat("of cost-effectiveness varies with distributional choice.\n")
} else {
  cat("STRUCTURAL UNCERTAINTY: HIGH\n")
  cat("The ICER changes by more than 25%, indicating substantial structural\n")
  cat("uncertainty. Consider additional scenario analyses and potentially\n")
  cat("other survival distributions. The choice of distribution meaningfully\n")
  cat("affects the cost-effectiveness conclusion.\n")
}

# NOTE ON FURTHER ANALYSIS:
# If structural uncertainty is high, consider:
#   1. Testing additional distributions (log-normal, log-logistic, etc.)
#   2. Exploring alternative approaches (spline models, mixture models)
#   3. Obtaining longer-term follow-up data to reduce extrapolation uncertainty
#   4. Consulting clinical experts on plausibility of long-term extrapolations
#   5. Reporting a range of ICERs across plausible distributions

# ============================================================================
# METHODOLOGICAL NOTE: PSA-BASED RESULTS ARE THE REPORTED BASE CASE
# ============================================================================
#
# **CRITICAL CLARIFICATION FOR MANUSCRIPT:**
#
# All results reported in this analysis are PSA-BASED, not deterministic.
# This includes:
#   - The "base case" Weibull results: derived from PSA means, not single run
#   - The gamma scenario results: derived from PSA means, not single run
#   - All ICERs: calculated from PSA means (ΔCost_mean / ΔQALY_mean)
#   - All 95% CrIs: derived from PSA distributions
#
# This approach:
#   1. Aligns with reviewer feedback to treat PSA as the effective base case
#   2. Ensures internal consistency (all reported values reflect uncertainty)
#   3. Provides more transparent reporting of parameter uncertainty
#   4. Makes Weibull vs Gamma comparison methodologically rigorous
#
# For the paper:
#   - Table of base-case results → use PSA means from df_out_ce_PA
#   - Weibull vs Gamma comparison → use psa_comparison_table (saved to CSV)
#   - All reported ICERs → calculated from PSA means
#   - All uncertainty bounds → 95% CrIs from PSA distributions
#
cat("\n=======================================================\n")
cat("PSA-BASED GAMMA SCENARIO ANALYSIS COMPLETE\n")
cat("=======================================================\n")
cat("All results are PSA-based (means from", n_runs, "simulations)\n")
cat("Comparison table saved to: output/", comparison_filename, "\n", sep = "")
cat("=======================================================\n\n")
```

```{r}
# 09.1 Conduct probabilistic sensitivity analysis
#
# ============================================================================
# **CRITICAL METHODOLOGICAL NOTE - PSA AS BASE CASE:**
# ============================================================================
#
# This PSA analysis produces the "BASE CASE" results for the manuscript.
# All reported ICERs, costs, and QALYs are derived from PSA MEANS, not from
# deterministic single-run values.
#
# Key points:
#   1. This PSA uses Weibull distribution (curve_choice defaults to "weibull")
#   2. Results from this PSA (PSA means) = "base case" results
#   3. All ICERs are calculated from PSA means: ICER = ΔCost_mean / ΔQALY_mean
#   4. All uncertainty is quantified via 95% CrIs from PSA distributions
#   5. The gamma scenario (earlier in this file) is also PSA-based for consistency
#
# This approach aligns with reviewer feedback to treat PSA as the effective
# base case rather than reporting deterministic values with PSA as sensitivity.
#
# ============================================================================

# Running the probabilistic analysis :

# First we need to create data.frames to store the output from the PSA:

df_c <- df_e <- data.frame(
  SoC = rep(NA, n_runs),
  Exp = rep(NA, n_runs)
)

# As you'll see, first we make blank (repeat NA for the number of runs of the simulationn_runs) data.frames for costs (df_c) and effectiveness (df_e) for SoC and the experimental treatment:

head(df_c)

# > head(df_c)
#   SoC Exp
# 1  NA  NA
# 2  NA  NA
# 3  NA  NA
# 4  NA  NA
# 5  NA  NA
# 6  NA  NA

head(df_e)

# > head(df_e)
#   SoC Exp
# 1  NA  NA
# 2  NA  NA
# 3  NA  NA
# 4  NA  NA
# 5  NA  NA
# 6  NA  NA

# We run the Markov model for each set of parameter values from the PSA input dataset (a set of parameters here is the row of parameter values in the PSA data.frame from whatever run number of the nruns in the PSA dataset we are on, i.e. if we were doing this for run number 10 out of 10,000, we would be on row 10 in the data.frame (as each row refers to a run) and we would use all the values for costs and effect that appear in this row when running the Markov model. So, we would be using all the random draws for that PSA run in the Markov model).

# - I read a note indicating that this loop can be run in parallel to decrease the runtime, something to consider in the future if it takes a very long time...

for(i_run in 1:n_runs){

    # Evaluate the model and store the outcomes
  l_out_temp    <- oncologySemiMarkov(l_params_all = df_PA_input[i_run, ], n_wtp = n_wtp)
# The above is basically saying, apply the oncologySemiMarkov_function, where l_params_all in the function (i.e. the list of parameters the function is to be applied to) is equal to the parameters from the PSA data.frame for the run we are in, and the willingness to pay threshold is n_wtp.
  df_c[i_run, ] <- l_out_temp$Cost
  df_e[i_run, ] <- l_out_temp$Effect
# The above says, for the costs and effectiveness data.frames, store the value of costs and effects for each run that we are on in a row that reflects that run (remembering that [ROW,COLUMN], we are putting each cost and effect in a row that relates to the number of the run we are on, so if we are on run 1, i_run = 1 and we store the costs and effects for that run 1 in row 1. Remembering that our oncologySemiMarkov makes the "Cost" and "Effect" parameters at the end of the function, after applying the Markov cost-effectiveness model to all our input data for the cost-effectiveness model (so, things like, cost, utility and probability), so we are just pulling the ouputted Cost and Effect values calculated from a Markov cost-effectiveness model applied to our input data after the input data has been randomly drawn from a PSA (per the PSA input dataframe)).  

  
  # While we're doing this, we might like to display the progress of the simulation:
  if(i_run/(n_runs/10) == round(i_run/(n_runs/10), 0)) { # We've chosen to display progress every 10%
    cat('\r', paste(i_run/n_runs * 100, "% done", sep = " "))
  }
}
```

```{r}

# ============================================================================
# SECTION 09.1.1: CALCULATE INCREMENTAL OUTCOMES AND NET MONETARY BENEFIT
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC PURPOSE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This section analyzes the results of the Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis (PSA)
# to quantify the uncertainty in cost-effectiveness under parameter uncertainty.
#
# WHAT IS PROBABILISTIC SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PSA is the gold standard method for characterizing parameter uncertainty in health
# economic models. Unlike deterministic sensitivity analysis (which varies one or two
# parameters at a time), PSA varies ALL uncertain parameters SIMULTANEOUSLY by:
#
# 1. Defining probability distributions for each uncertain parameter
#    (e.g., gamma for costs, beta for probabilities, lognormal for hazard ratios)
#
# 2. Running the model thousands of times (typically 1,000-10,000 iterations)
#
# 3. For each iteration, drawing one random sample from each parameter's distribution
#
# 4. Recording the resulting costs and QALYs for each strategy
#
# The output is a DISTRIBUTION of possible cost-effectiveness outcomes, reflecting
# the joint uncertainty across all parameters.
#
# WHY IS PSA IMPORTANT?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PSA is critical for health economic evaluation because:
#
# 1. DECISION UNCERTAINTY: Quantifies the probability that each strategy is optimal
#    at a given willingness-to-pay threshold
#
# 2. EXPECTED VALUE OF INFORMATION: Enables calculation of the value of reducing
#    uncertainty through additional research
#
# 3. GUIDELINE REQUIREMENTS: Required by NICE, CADTH, PBAC, and other HTA agencies
#
# 4. REALISTIC REPRESENTATION: Jointly varying parameters captures correlations and
#    interactions that one-way sensitivity analysis misses
#
# WHAT IS NET MONETARY BENEFIT (NMB)?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Net Monetary Benefit is a decision-analytic metric that converts health economic
# outcomes into a single monetary value by valuing health gains at the societal
# willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold.
#
# FORMULA:
#   NMB = (Incremental QALY × WTP threshold) - Incremental cost
#
# INTERPRETATION:
#   - Positive NMB: The experimental strategy provides value for money
#                   (health benefits exceed additional costs when valued at WTP)
#   - Negative NMB: The experimental strategy does not provide value for money
#                   (additional costs exceed health benefits when valued at WTP)
#   - NMB = 0: Indifferent (on the cost-effectiveness acceptability frontier)
#
# ADVANTAGES OF NMB OVER ICER:
#   1. Linear scale (ICER has discontinuities when strategies are dominated)
#   2. Can be averaged across PSA simulations (ICER averaging can be misleading)
#   3. Directly interpretable as monetary value (ICER is a ratio)
#   4. Handles dominated and dominant strategies naturally
#
# WHAT ARE CREDIBLE INTERVALS?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# In Bayesian statistics and PSA, we use CREDIBLE INTERVALS rather than confidence
# intervals. A 95% credible interval (95% CrI) is defined as:
#
#   "The range containing 95% of the simulated values under parameter uncertainty"
#
# We calculate this using percentiles:
#   - Lower bound: 2.5th percentile (only 2.5% of simulations are below this)
#   - Upper bound: 97.5th percentile (only 2.5% of simulations are above this)
#
# INTERPRETATION:
# Given our current parameter uncertainty and chosen distributions, there is a 95%
# probability that the true value lies within this range.
#
# NOTE: This is subtly different from a frequentist confidence interval, which
# refers to repeated sampling properties rather than probability statements about
# the true value.
#
# PSA OUTPUT DATA STRUCTURES:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The PSA generates two key data frames (created earlier in the analysis):
#
# df_c (costs):
#   - Rows: PSA iterations (e.g., 10,000 simulations)
#   - Columns: Strategies (SoC = standard of care, Exp = experimental)
#   - Values: Total discounted lifetime costs for each strategy in each simulation
#
# df_e (effects):
#   - Rows: PSA iterations (e.g., 10,000 simulations)
#   - Columns: Strategies (SoC = standard of care, Exp = experimental)
#   - Values: Total discounted lifetime QALYs for each strategy in each simulation
#
# Each row represents ONE simulation where all uncertain parameters were sampled
# from their distributions and the model was run to completion.
#
# WHAT THIS SECTION DOES:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This section performs the following steps:
#
# STEP 1: Identify strategy column names (SoC vs experimental)
# STEP 2: Calculate incremental costs for each PSA simulation
# STEP 3: Calculate incremental QALYs for each PSA simulation
# STEP 4: Calculate incremental NMB for each PSA simulation
# STEP 5: Compute summary statistics (mean and 95% CrI) for each outcome
# STEP 6: Create formatted summary tables for reporting
# STEP 7: Save results to CSV files for manuscript preparation
#
# ALIGNMENT WITH BEST PRACTICES:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This approach is consistent with:
# - DARTH group tutorials on PSA analysis
# - dampack package PSA analysis workflow
# - ISPOR-SMDM Good Research Practices for PSA
# - NICE Decision Support Unit Technical Support Documents

# ============================================================================
# STEP 1: IDENTIFY STRATEGY COLUMN NAMES FROM PSA RESULTS
# ============================================================================
#
# DATA STRUCTURE VERIFICATION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Before we can calculate incremental outcomes, we need to identify which columns
# in our PSA results correspond to which strategies.
#
# The PSA data frames (df_c and df_e) contain columns for each strategy:
# - "SoC": Standard of Care (comparator)
# - Experimental strategy: May be named "Exp", "Bev", "Bevacizumab", etc.
#
# DEFENSIVE PROGRAMMING:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We don't hard-code the experimental strategy name because:
# 1. It may vary between analyses
# 2. Users may rename strategies in the model
# 3. This makes the code more robust and reusable
#
# Instead, we dynamically identify the column names and verify data integrity.

# Extract column names from the PSA output data frames
# -----------------------------------------------------
# colnames() returns a character vector of column names
# We check BOTH df_c (costs) and df_e (effects) to ensure consistency
#
# Health economic interpretation: Verifying that cost and effect data frames
# have matching structure (same strategies) before proceeding
strat_names_c <- colnames(df_c)
strat_names_e <- colnames(df_e)

# Display PSA results summary for verification
# ---------------------------------------------
# This console output helps verify that:
# 1. The PSA completed successfully (number of simulations matches expected)
# 2. Strategy names are correct and consistent between costs and effects
# 3. Data frames have the expected structure
#
# cat() is used instead of print() for more readable formatted output
# nrow(df_c) gives the number of PSA simulations (rows)
# paste() with collapse = ", " creates comma-separated list of strategies
#
# Health economic value: Transparent reporting of PSA structure for validation
cat("\nPSA Results Summary:\n")
cat("======================\n")
cat("Number of PSA simulations:", nrow(df_c), "\n")
cat("Cost strategies:", paste(strat_names_c, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Effect strategies:", paste(strat_names_e, collapse = ", "), "\n\n")

# VALIDATION CHECK (implicit):
# If cost and effect strategies don't match, subsequent code will fail,
# alerting the user to a data integrity problem

# Identify standard of care and experimental strategy columns
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# ASSUMPTION: One column is always named "SoC" (standard of care)
# This is enforced by the PSA code earlier in the analysis
#
# setdiff() finds elements in strat_names_c that are NOT in the set {"SoC"}
# This returns the experimental strategy column name(s)
# [1] extracts the first element (we assume only one experimental strategy)
#
# Mathematical interpretation: setdiff(A, B) = {x ∈ A : x ∉ B}
# Here: setdiff(strat_names_c, "SoC") = all strategies except SoC
#
# Health economic interpretation: Identifying the intervention being evaluated
soc_col <- "SoC"
exp_col <- setdiff(strat_names_c, "SoC")[1]  # The column that isn't "SoC"

# Display identified strategies for verification
# -----------------------------------------------
# This console output confirms that we've correctly identified:
# - The comparator (standard of care)
# - The intervention (experimental strategy)
#
# This is important for transparency: readers of the R console output can
# verify that the correct comparison is being made
#
# Health economic value: Clear documentation of which strategies are being
# compared (essential for interpreting cost-effectiveness results)
cat("Identified strategies for incremental analysis:\n")
cat("  Standard of Care (comparator):", soc_col, "\n")
cat("  Experimental (intervention):", exp_col, "\n\n")

# QUALITY ASSURANCE:
# If exp_col is NA or empty, this indicates a problem with the PSA data structure
# The subsequent code will fail with an informative error message

# ============================================================================
# STEP 2: CALCULATE INCREMENTAL OUTCOMES FOR EACH PSA SIMULATION
# ============================================================================
#
# INCREMENTAL ANALYSIS RATIONALE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# In cost-effectiveness analysis, we're interested in the ADDITIONAL (incremental)
# costs and effects of the new intervention compared to current practice.
#
# Incremental analysis answers the question:
#   "What extra resources are required, and what extra health benefits are gained,
#    by adopting the new intervention instead of continuing with standard care?"
#
# DATA EXTRACTION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# df_c contains costs for each PSA simulation (rows) and strategy (columns)
# df_e contains QALYs for each PSA simulation (rows) and strategy (columns)
# Each row corresponds to one PSA iteration (one complete model run)
#
# For example, in a PSA with 10,000 simulations:
#   - df_c has 10,000 rows × 2 columns (SoC and Exp)
#   - df_e has 10,000 rows × 2 columns (SoC and Exp)
#   - Row 1 = simulation 1 with one set of sampled parameters
#   - Row 2 = simulation 2 with a different set of sampled parameters
#   - ... and so on

# Calculate incremental costs for each PSA simulation
# ----------------------------------------------------
# FORMULA: Incremental Cost = Cost(Experimental) - Cost(Standard of Care)
#
# This is a VECTORIZED operation in R:
# - df_c[, exp_col] extracts all rows of the experimental strategy cost column
# - df_c[, soc_col] extracts all rows of the standard of care cost column
# - The subtraction happens element-wise across all simulations simultaneously
# - Result: a vector of length = number of PSA simulations
#
# INTERPRETATION:
# - Positive values: Experimental strategy costs MORE than SoC (additional cost)
# - Negative values: Experimental strategy costs LESS than SoC (cost saving)
# - Zero: No cost difference
#
# EXPECTED RESULT FOR THIS ANALYSIS:
# For bevacizumab in mCRC, we expect positive incremental costs because:
# - Bevacizumab is an expensive biologic therapy
# - It's added ON TOP OF standard chemotherapy (FOLFOX)
# - Therefore, total treatment costs should increase
#
# Health economic interpretation: Quantifying the additional healthcare expenditure
# required to provide the new intervention
incremental_costs <- df_c[, exp_col] - df_c[, soc_col]

# Calculate incremental QALYs for each PSA simulation
# ----------------------------------------------------
# FORMULA: Incremental QALY = QALY(Experimental) - QALY(Standard of Care)
#
# This is a VECTORIZED operation (same structure as incremental costs above)
#
# INTERPRETATION:
# - Positive values: Experimental strategy produces MORE QALYs (health gain)
# - Negative values: Experimental strategy produces FEWER QALYs (health loss)
# - Zero: No health difference
#
# EXPECTED RESULT FOR THIS ANALYSIS:
# For bevacizumab in mCRC, we expect positive incremental QALYs because:
# - Bevacizumab improves progression-free survival (delays cancer progression)
# - Extended PFS means more time in better health states
# - Even modest survival extensions translate to QALY gains
#
# Health economic interpretation: Quantifying the additional health benefit
# (in quality-adjusted life years) gained from the new intervention
incremental_qalys <- df_e[, exp_col] - df_e[, soc_col]

# ============================================================================
# STEP 3: CALCULATE NET MONETARY BENEFIT (NMB) FOR EACH PSA SIMULATION
# ============================================================================
#
# NET MONETARY BENEFIT EXPLAINED:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Net Monetary Benefit (NMB) is a LINEAR transformation of the cost-effectiveness
# decision that avoids the mathematical problems associated with ICER.
#
# FORMULA:
#   NMB = (Incremental QALY × WTP) - Incremental Cost
#
# WHERE:
#   - Incremental QALY: health gain from the intervention (calculated above)
#   - WTP: willingness-to-pay threshold (€/QALY) for the country
#     * Ireland: €45,000/QALY
#     * Germany: €78,871/QALY
#     * Spain: €30,000/QALY
#   - Incremental Cost: additional cost of the intervention (calculated above)
#
# INTERPRETATION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# NMB represents the NET VALUE (in monetary terms) of adopting the intervention:
#
#   Positive NMB: Benefits (valued at WTP) > Costs
#                 → The intervention provides value for money
#                 → Should be adopted (if WTP is societally appropriate)
#
#   Negative NMB: Benefits (valued at WTP) < Costs
#                 → The intervention does not provide value for money
#                 → Should not be adopted (at this WTP threshold)
#
#   NMB = 0: Benefits exactly equal costs
#            → Indifferent between intervention and standard care
#            → On the cost-effectiveness acceptability frontier
#
# WHY USE NMB INSTEAD OF ICER?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# ICER (Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio) has several technical problems:
#
# 1. DISCONTINUITIES: ICER is undefined or changes sign in quadrants where
#    interventions are dominated or dominant
#
# 2. AVERAGING PROBLEMS: Mean ICER ≠ ICER of mean costs and effects
#    This makes averaging across PSA simulations misleading
#
# 3. NON-LINEAR: ICER = ΔCost / ΔQALY is a ratio, making statistical analysis
#    complex (e.g., confidence intervals are difficult to interpret)
#
# NMB solves all these problems:
# - Linear in costs and effects (no discontinuities)
# - Can be averaged across PSA simulations (mean NMB is meaningful)
# - Normally distributed under PSA (facilitates statistical inference)
# - Directly interpretable as monetary value
#
# MATHEMATICAL RELATIONSHIP TO ICER:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# NMB and ICER are mathematically related:
#
#   NMB > 0  ⟺  ICER < WTP threshold
#   NMB < 0  ⟺  ICER > WTP threshold
#   NMB = 0  ⟺  ICER = WTP threshold
#
# So NMB provides the SAME decision as ICER, but with better statistical properties
#
# WTP THRESHOLD SELECTION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The WTP threshold (n_wtp) represents society's willingness to pay for one
# additional QALY. This is:
# - Country-specific (set in the active country block)
# - Policy-determined (based on HTA agency guidelines)
# - Potentially controversial (no objectively "correct" value exists)
#
# For this analysis:
# - Ireland: €45,000 (HIQA threshold)
# - Germany: €78,871 (empirically derived from previous decisions)
# - Spain: €30,000 (commonly referenced threshold)

# Calculate NMB for each PSA simulation
# --------------------------------------
# This is a VECTORIZED operation on the incremental outcomes:
#   1. incremental_qalys * n_wtp: Value health gains in monetary terms
#   2. Subtract incremental_costs: Net out the additional costs
#   3. Result: Net value in euros for each simulation
#
# EXAMPLE CALCULATION:
# If in one simulation:
#   - Incremental QALYs = 0.15 (3 month extension × 0.5 utility weight)
#   - Incremental Cost = €12,000 (bevacizumab cost + administration)
#   - WTP threshold = €45,000/QALY (Ireland)
#
# Then:
#   NMB = (0.15 × €45,000) - €12,000
#       = €6,750 - €12,000
#       = -€5,250
#
# Interpretation: At €45,000/QALY, this simulation suggests the intervention
# does NOT provide value for money (negative NMB)
#
# Health economic interpretation: Converting cost-effectiveness into a single
# monetary metric that directly shows whether benefits exceed costs at the
# societal WTP threshold
incremental_nmb <- (incremental_qalys * n_wtp) - incremental_costs

# AT THIS POINT WE HAVE THREE VECTORS:
# --------------------------------------
# Each vector has length = number of PSA simulations (e.g., 10,000)
# Each element represents one plausible outcome under parameter uncertainty
#
# incremental_costs: Distribution of possible additional costs
# incremental_qalys: Distribution of possible health gains
# incremental_nmb: Distribution of possible net monetary benefits
#
# These distributions form the basis for:
# - Summary statistics (mean and credible intervals) - calculated next
# - Cost-effectiveness planes (scatter plots of cost vs QALY)
# - Cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (probability of cost-effectiveness)
# - Expected value of perfect information (value of eliminating uncertainty)

# ============================================================================
# STEP 4: COMPUTE SUMMARY STATISTICS (MEAN AND 95% CREDIBLE INTERVALS)
# ============================================================================
#
# SUMMARIZING PSA DISTRIBUTIONS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The PSA produces DISTRIBUTIONS of outcomes (incremental costs, QALYs, NMB),
# not single point estimates. We summarize these distributions using:
#
# 1. MEAN: The expected (average) value across all simulations
#    - Represents the central tendency
#    - Used for decision-making under expected value criteria
#
# 2. 95% CREDIBLE INTERVAL (CrI): The range containing 95% of simulated values
#    - Quantifies uncertainty around the mean
#    - Defined by 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles
#    - Narrower intervals = less uncertainty
#    - Wider intervals = more uncertainty
#
# CREDIBLE INTERVAL CALCULATION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We use the quantile() function to find percentiles of the distribution:
#
#   quantile(x, probs = 0.025): 2.5th percentile (lower bound of 95% CrI)
#     → Only 2.5% of simulations produced values below this
#
#   quantile(x, probs = 0.975): 97.5th percentile (upper bound of 95% CrI)
#     → Only 2.5% of simulations produced values above this
#
#   Together: The interval [2.5th, 97.5th] contains the central 95% of the distribution
#
# INTERPRETATION OF CREDIBLE INTERVALS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Given our current parameter uncertainty and chosen distributions, there is
# a 95% probability that the true value lies within the credible interval.
#
# For example, if incremental cost has 95% CrI of [€10,000, €18,000]:
#   → We're 95% confident the true additional cost is between €10k and €18k
#   → There's a 2.5% chance it's below €10k (optimistic scenario)
#   → There's a 2.5% chance it's above €18k (pessimistic scenario)
#
# WHY NOT STANDARD DEVIATION OR STANDARD ERROR?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We report credible intervals rather than SD or SE because:
# 1. Credible intervals are easier to interpret for non-statisticians
# 2. They provide decision-relevant ranges (what outcomes are plausible?)
# 3. They're robust to non-normal distributions (PSA outputs may be skewed)
# 4. They align with HTA agency reporting requirements

# Calculate summary statistics for incremental costs
# ---------------------------------------------------
# mean(): Arithmetic mean of all PSA simulation results
# quantile(): Computes specified percentiles of the distribution
#
# Health economic interpretation: Expected additional cost and its 95% CrI
inc_cost_mean <- mean(incremental_costs)
inc_cost_lower <- quantile(incremental_costs, probs = 0.025)  # Lower 95% CrI bound
inc_cost_upper <- quantile(incremental_costs, probs = 0.975)  # Upper 95% CrI bound

# Calculate summary statistics for incremental QALYs
# ---------------------------------------------------
# Same structure as incremental costs above
#
# Health economic interpretation: Expected health gain and its 95% CrI
inc_qaly_mean <- mean(incremental_qalys)
inc_qaly_lower <- quantile(incremental_qalys, probs = 0.025)  # Lower 95% CrI bound
inc_qaly_upper <- quantile(incremental_qalys, probs = 0.975)  # Upper 95% CrI bound

# Calculate summary statistics for incremental NMB
# -------------------------------------------------
# Same structure as above
#
# Health economic interpretation: Expected net monetary benefit and its 95% CrI
# This is the KEY outcome for decision-making:
#   - Positive mean NMB suggests the intervention may be cost-effective
#   - If the entire 95% CrI is positive, we're very confident it's cost-effective
#   - If the CrI spans zero, there's substantial decision uncertainty
inc_nmb_mean <- mean(incremental_nmb)
inc_nmb_lower <- quantile(incremental_nmb, probs = 0.025)  # Lower 95% CrI bound
inc_nmb_upper <- quantile(incremental_nmb, probs = 0.975)  # Upper 95% CrI bound

# INTERPRETATION EXAMPLES:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example 1: NMB with 95% CrI entirely above zero
#   Mean NMB = €5,000, 95% CrI [€2,000, €8,000]
#   → Strong evidence of cost-effectiveness (95% confident NMB > 0)
#   → Low decision uncertainty
#
# Example 2: NMB with 95% CrI spanning zero
#   Mean NMB = €500, 95% CrI [-€3,000, €4,000]
#   → Weak evidence of cost-effectiveness (mean is positive but uncertain)
#   → High decision uncertainty (could be positive or negative)
#   → May warrant value of information analysis
#
# Example 3: NMB with 95% CrI entirely below zero
#   Mean NMB = -€10,000, 95% CrI [-€15,000, -€5,000]
#   → Strong evidence against cost-effectiveness (95% confident NMB < 0)
#   → Intervention should not be adopted at this WTP threshold

# ============================================================================
# STEP 5: CREATE SUMMARY TABLE FOR REPORTING
# ============================================================================
#
# TABLE PURPOSE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This table consolidates all PSA summary statistics into a single data frame
# suitable for:
# - Console display (immediate review of results)
# - Export to CSV (for manuscript tables)
# - Further analysis or plotting
#
# TABLE STRUCTURE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One row per country analysis with the following columns:
#
# 1. Country: Which country's parameters and WTP threshold were used
# 2. WTP_Threshold: The willingness-to-pay threshold (€/QALY)
# 3. Incremental_Cost_Mean: Expected additional cost
# 4. Incremental_Cost_Lower_CrI: Lower bound of 95% CrI for cost
# 5. Incremental_Cost_Upper_CrI: Upper bound of 95% CrI for cost
# 6. Incremental_QALY_Mean: Expected health gain
# 7. Incremental_QALY_Lower_CrI: Lower bound of 95% CrI for QALY
# 8. Incremental_QALY_Upper_CrI: Upper bound of 95% CrI for QALY
# 9. Incremental_NMB_Mean: Expected net monetary benefit
# 10. Incremental_NMB_Lower_CrI: Lower bound of 95% CrI for NMB
# 11. Incremental_NMB_Upper_CrI: Upper bound of 95% CrI for NMB
#
# ALIGNMENT WITH MANUSCRIPT:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This table format corresponds to Table 2 in the manuscript, which reports
# PSA-based cost-effectiveness results for each country.
#
# USAGE NOTES:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# - stringsAsFactors = FALSE: Ensures country_name stays as character, not factor
# - Numeric columns preserve full precision (rounding applied during display/export)
# - Column names use underscores for programmatic access (e.g., filtering, plotting)

# Create data frame with PSA summary statistics
# ----------------------------------------------
# data.frame() constructs a table where each named argument becomes a column
# All vector inputs must have the same length (here, length = 1 since we're
# summarizing results for one country at a time)
#
# Health economic interpretation: Tabulating the expected outcomes and uncertainty
# for cost-effectiveness decision-making
psa_summary_table <- data.frame(

  # Country and WTP context
  # -----------------------
  # Identifies which country's analysis this row represents
  # Important when combining results across multiple countries
  Country = country_name,

  # The WTP threshold used to calculate NMB
  # Different countries have different thresholds reflecting different societal
  # preferences or affordability constraints
  WTP_Threshold = n_wtp,

  # Incremental cost: mean and 95% CrI
  # -----------------------------------
  # Expected additional cost of the intervention
  Incremental_Cost_Mean = inc_cost_mean,

  # Lower bound: optimistic cost scenario (only 2.5% of simulations are cheaper)
  Incremental_Cost_Lower_CrI = inc_cost_lower,

  # Upper bound: pessimistic cost scenario (only 2.5% of simulations are costlier)
  Incremental_Cost_Upper_CrI = inc_cost_upper,

  # Incremental QALY: mean and 95% CrI
  # -----------------------------------
  # Expected health gain from the intervention
  Incremental_QALY_Mean = inc_qaly_mean,

  # Lower bound: pessimistic health scenario (only 2.5% of simulations show less benefit)
  Incremental_QALY_Lower_CrI = inc_qaly_lower,

  # Upper bound: optimistic health scenario (only 2.5% of simulations show more benefit)
  Incremental_QALY_Upper_CrI = inc_qaly_upper,

  # Incremental NMB: mean and 95% CrI
  # ----------------------------------
  # Expected net monetary benefit (KEY decision metric)
  Incremental_NMB_Mean = inc_nmb_mean,

  # Lower bound: pessimistic value-for-money scenario
  Incremental_NMB_Lower_CrI = inc_nmb_lower,

  # Upper bound: optimistic value-for-money scenario
  Incremental_NMB_Upper_CrI = inc_nmb_upper,

  # Prevent automatic conversion of strings to factors
  # This preserves country_name as character type for easier manipulation
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# ============================================================================
# STEP 6: DISPLAY SUMMARY RESULTS IN CONSOLE
# ============================================================================
#
# CONSOLE OUTPUT PURPOSE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This formatted console output provides immediate feedback on PSA results:
# - Allows quick verification that results are sensible
# - Helps identify data issues (e.g., unexpected signs or magnitudes)
# - Provides human-readable summary before creating formal tables/figures
#
# FORMATTING APPROACH:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We use cat() rather than print() to create custom-formatted output:
# - cat() allows precise control over line breaks and spacing
# - format() with big.mark = "," adds thousand separators (e.g., €10,000)
# - round() controls decimal precision (2 decimals for costs, 4 for QALYs)
#
# PRESENTATION STRUCTURE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Header: Identifies the analysis type and country
# Context: Shows WTP threshold and number of simulations
# Results: Displays mean and 95% CrI for each outcome
# Interpretation: Provides decision-relevant note based on NMB sign

# Display formatted PSA summary to console
# -----------------------------------------
# Horizontal rules (=======) visually separate the summary from other output
# This makes it easier to find results when scrolling through R console output
cat("\n=======================================================\n")
cat("PSA SUMMARY: Incremental Outcomes and Net Monetary Benefit\n")
cat("=======================================================\n\n")

# Display analysis context
# -------------------------
# country_name: Which country's parameters were used
# n_wtp: The WTP threshold for this country (determines NMB calculation)
# nrow(df_c): Number of PSA simulations (should match n_runs parameter)
cat("Country:", country_name, "\n")
cat("Willingness-to-pay threshold: €", format(n_wtp, big.mark = ","), "\n")
cat("Number of PSA simulations:", nrow(df_c), "\n\n")

# Display incremental cost results
# ---------------------------------
# round(, 2): Show costs to 2 decimal places (cent precision)
# format(, big.mark = ","): Add thousand separators for readability
# paste() with exp_col and soc_col: Show which comparison is being made
#
# Health economic interpretation: Expected additional cost and its uncertainty
cat("INCREMENTAL COST (", exp_col, " vs ", soc_col, "):\n", sep = "")
cat("  Mean: €", format(round(inc_cost_mean, 2), big.mark = ","), "\n")
cat("  95% CrI: €", format(round(inc_cost_lower, 2), big.mark = ","),
    " to €", format(round(inc_cost_upper, 2), big.mark = ","), "\n\n")

# Display incremental QALY results
# ---------------------------------
# round(, 4): Show QALYs to 4 decimal places (standard precision)
# No thousand separators needed for QALYs (values typically < 10)
#
# Health economic interpretation: Expected health gain and its uncertainty
cat("INCREMENTAL QALY (", exp_col, " vs ", soc_col, "):\n", sep = "")
cat("  Mean:", round(inc_qaly_mean, 4), "\n")
cat("  95% CrI:", round(inc_qaly_lower, 4), "to", round(inc_qaly_upper, 4), "\n\n")

# Display incremental NMB results
# --------------------------------
# Same formatting as costs (2 decimal places, thousand separators)
# NMB is the KEY outcome for interpreting cost-effectiveness
#
# Health economic interpretation: Expected net value of the intervention
cat("INCREMENTAL NET MONETARY BENEFIT (", exp_col, " vs ", soc_col, "):\n", sep = "")
cat("  Mean: €", format(round(inc_nmb_mean, 2), big.mark = ","), "\n")
cat("  95% CrI: €", format(round(inc_nmb_lower, 2), big.mark = ","),
    " to €", format(round(inc_nmb_upper, 2), big.mark = ","), "\n")
cat("=======================================================\n\n")

# Add interpretation note based on NMB sign
# ------------------------------------------
# DECISION RULE: Positive mean NMB suggests cost-effectiveness
#
# IMPORTANT CAVEAT: We say "may be" rather than "is" because:
# 1. This is based on expected values (mean), not the full distribution
# 2. Decision uncertainty exists if the 95% CrI spans zero
# 3. Cost-effectiveness depends on societal acceptance of the WTP threshold
#
# Health economic value: Translates statistical results into decision-relevant
# interpretation for stakeholders who may not be familiar with NMB
if (inc_nmb_mean > 0) {
  cat("NOTE: Positive mean NMB suggests the experimental strategy (", exp_col, ")\n", sep = "")
  cat("      may be cost-effective at the €", format(n_wtp, big.mark = ","), " WTP threshold.\n\n")
} else {
  cat("NOTE: Negative mean NMB suggests the experimental strategy (", exp_col, ")\n", sep = "")
  cat("      may not be cost-effective at the €", format(n_wtp, big.mark = ","), " WTP threshold.\n\n")
}

# Display the summary table in data frame format
# -----------------------------------------------
# print() shows the data frame in standard R tabular format
# This complements the cat() output above by showing all columns in one view
#
# Health economic value: Provides structured data format that can be
# copy-pasted into Excel or other tools for further analysis
print(psa_summary_table)

# ============================================================================
# STEP 7: SAVE RESULTS TO CSV FILES FOR MANUSCRIPT PREPARATION
# ============================================================================
#
# FILE OUTPUT PURPOSE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We save PSA summary results to CSV files for several reasons:
#
# 1. REPRODUCIBILITY: Permanent record of PSA results for each country
# 2. MANUSCRIPT PREPARATION: Can be imported into Word/LaTeX for Table 2
# 3. FURTHER ANALYSIS: Can be loaded into Excel, R, or other tools
# 4. VERSION CONTROL: Git can track changes to CSV files between analyses
# 5. STAKEHOLDER SHARING: Easy-to-share format for non-R users
#
# FILE ORGANIZATION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We use an "output/" subdirectory to:
# - Keep analysis outputs separate from code and input data
# - Make it easy to find all generated files
# - Allow adding output/ to .gitignore if desired (to avoid tracking large files)
#
# FILE NAMING CONVENTION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Format: PSA_Summary_NMB_<Country>.csv
# Examples:
#   - PSA_Summary_NMB_Ireland.csv
#   - PSA_Summary_NMB_Germany.csv
#   - PSA_Summary_NMB_Spain.csv
#
# This naming convention:
# - Clearly describes the content ("PSA_Summary_NMB")
# - Includes country context for organization
# - Uses consistent format for programmatic access

# Save the raw summary table to CSV
# ----------------------------------
# RAW TABLE FORMAT:
# This version contains numeric values without formatting:
# - Full precision for all numbers (no rounding artifacts)
# - Suitable for further statistical analysis
# - Can be imported into R and used for calculations
#
# file.path(): Constructs platform-independent file paths
#   - On Windows: "output\\PSA_Summary_NMB_Ireland.csv"
#   - On Mac/Linux: "output/PSA_Summary_NMB_Ireland.csv"
#
# paste0(): Concatenates strings without separator (same as paste with sep="")
#
# write.csv() parameters:
#   - file: where to save the file
#   - row.names = FALSE: Don't include row numbers (1, 2, 3...) in the CSV
#     This makes the CSV cleaner and easier to read
#
# Health economic value: Preserves full numerical precision for transparency
# and reproducibility of cost-effectiveness calculations
output_filename <- file.path("output", paste0("PSA_Summary_NMB_", country_name, ".csv"))
write.csv(psa_summary_table, file = output_filename, row.names = FALSE)

# Confirm successful save
# -----------------------
# Provides feedback to the user that the file was created
# Shows the exact file path for easy location
cat("\nSummary table saved to:", output_filename, "\n\n")

# ============================================================================
# STEP 8: CREATE AND SAVE FORMATTED VERSION FOR MANUSCRIPT
# ============================================================================
#
# FORMATTED TABLE PURPOSE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# While the raw table (above) preserves numerical precision, it's not ideal
# for direct inclusion in manuscripts because:
# - Numbers appear with many decimal places (not publication-ready)
# - No currency symbols or thousand separators
# - Mean and CrI are in separate columns (takes up more space)
#
# This formatted version addresses these issues by:
# - Combining mean and CrI into single columns (e.g., "€12,500 (€10,000 to €15,000)")
# - Adding currency symbols and thousand separators
# - Applying appropriate rounding (2 decimals for costs, 4 for QALYs)
# - Using human-readable column names with spaces
#
# TRADE-OFF:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The formatted version is BETTER for presentation but WORSE for analysis:
# + Easy to read and copy into manuscript tables
# + Matches journal formatting requirements
# - Cannot perform calculations on formatted text (e.g., "€12,500")
# - Loses some precision due to rounding
#
# Therefore, we save BOTH versions:
# - Raw version for analysis and transparency
# - Formatted version for manuscript preparation
#
# TABLE STRUCTURE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Each metric (cost, QALY, NMB) is represented by TWO columns:
# 1. Mean column: Shows the expected value with proper formatting
# 2. 95% CrI column: Shows the uncertainty range in "X to Y" format
#
# This matches common health economics manuscript table formats

# Create formatted summary table
# -------------------------------
# FORMATTING DECISIONS:
#
# For costs and NMB:
#   - paste0("€", format(round(x, 2), big.mark = ","))
#   - Adds € symbol
#   - Rounds to 2 decimal places
#   - Adds thousand separators (€12,345.67)
#
# For QALYs:
#   - round(x, 4): Standard precision for QALYs (0.1234)
#   - No currency symbol or separators needed
#
# For credible intervals:
#   - Combine lower and upper bounds with " to "
#   - Example: "€10,000 to €15,000"
#   - Example: "0.1234 to 0.5678"
#
# Health economic value: Publication-ready table following field conventions
psa_summary_formatted <- data.frame(

  # Country and WTP threshold (formatted with currency symbol)
  Country = country_name,
  WTP = paste0("€", format(n_wtp, big.mark = ",")),

  # Incremental cost: mean (formatted with € and separators)
  `Incremental Cost (Mean)` = paste0("€", format(round(inc_cost_mean, 2), big.mark = ",")),

  # Incremental cost: 95% CrI (formatted as range)
  # Example output: "€10,000.00 to €15,000.00"
  `Incremental Cost (95% CrI)` = paste0(
    "€", format(round(inc_cost_lower, 2), big.mark = ","),
    " to €", format(round(inc_cost_upper, 2), big.mark = ",")
  ),

  # Incremental QALY: mean (rounded to 4 decimal places)
  `Incremental QALY (Mean)` = round(inc_qaly_mean, 4),

  # Incremental QALY: 95% CrI (formatted as range)
  # Example output: "0.1234 to 0.5678"
  `Incremental QALY (95% CrI)` = paste0(
    round(inc_qaly_lower, 4), " to ", round(inc_qaly_upper, 4)
  ),

  # Incremental NMB: mean (formatted with € and separators)
  `Incremental NMB (Mean)` = paste0("€", format(round(inc_nmb_mean, 2), big.mark = ",")),

  # Incremental NMB: 95% CrI (formatted as range)
  # Example output: "€-5,000.00 to €2,500.00"
  `Incremental NMB (95% CrI)` = paste0(
    "€", format(round(inc_nmb_lower, 2), big.mark = ","),
    " to €", format(round(inc_nmb_upper, 2), big.mark = ",")
  ),

  # check.names = FALSE: Preserve column names with spaces and parentheses
  # Without this, R would convert "Incremental Cost (Mean)" to "Incremental.Cost..Mean."
  check.names = FALSE,

  # stringsAsFactors = FALSE: Keep text as character strings, not factors
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Display the formatted table to console
# ---------------------------------------
# This allows immediate review of how the table will appear in the manuscript
# Check that formatting looks appropriate (currency symbols, decimal places, etc.)
cat("\nFORMATTED SUMMARY TABLE (for manuscript):\n")
print(psa_summary_formatted, row.names = FALSE)

# Save the formatted table to CSV
# --------------------------------
# FILE NAMING: PSA_Summary_NMB_Formatted_<Country>.csv
# The "_Formatted" suffix distinguishes this from the raw version
#
# USAGE:
# - Open in Excel to copy-paste into manuscript Word document
# - Import into LaTeX using csvreader or similar packages
# - Share with co-authors who don't use R
#
# IMPORTANT: When opening in Excel, ensure it doesn't corrupt the formatting:
# - Use "Import Data" rather than double-clicking the CSV
# - Specify that columns are "Text" to preserve number formatting
#
# Health economic value: Streamlines manuscript preparation and reduces
# transcription errors by providing publication-ready formatted output
formatted_filename <- file.path("output", paste0("PSA_Summary_NMB_Formatted_", country_name, ".csv"))
write.csv(psa_summary_formatted, file = formatted_filename, row.names = FALSE)

# Confirm successful save
# -----------------------
cat("\nFormatted summary table saved to:", formatted_filename, "\n\n")

# ============================================================================
# SECTION COMPLETE: NMB CALCULATION AND REPORTING
# ============================================================================
#
# AT THIS POINT WE HAVE CREATED:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Three vectors of PSA outcomes (incremental costs, QALYs, NMB)
# 2. Summary statistics (mean and 95% CrI) for each outcome
# 3. Console output showing results in human-readable format
# 4. Raw CSV file with full numerical precision
# 5. Formatted CSV file ready for manuscript inclusion
#
# FILES CREATED (in output/ directory):
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# - PSA_Summary_NMB_<Country>.csv: Raw data with full precision
# - PSA_Summary_NMB_Formatted_<Country>.csv: Publication-ready formatted version
#
# NEXT STEPS IN THE ANALYSIS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The subsequent sections of the R Markdown file will use the PSA results to:
# - Create cost-effectiveness planes (scatter plots)
# - Generate cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs)
# - Calculate expected value of perfect information (EVPI) - if included
# - Create additional visualizations and summary tables
#
# TRANSPARENCY AND REPRODUCIBILITY:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The heavily commented code in this section ensures that:
# - Methods are transparent and can be peer-reviewed
# - Results can be reproduced by running the code
# - Future users can understand the health economic logic
# - The analysis follows best practices (DARTH, dampack, ISPOR-SMDM guidelines)

```

```{r}

# ============================================================================
# SECTION 09.1.2: CONSOLIDATE PSA RESULTS ACROSS ALL COUNTRIES
# ============================================================================
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC PURPOSE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This section creates a CONSOLIDATED summary table that combines PSA-based
# NMB and credible interval results from all three country analyses
# (Ireland, Germany, and Spain) into a single table for manuscript reporting.
#
# WHY CONSOLIDATE ACROSS COUNTRIES?
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The main analysis runs separately for each country because:
# 1. Different treatment costs (country-specific pricing and reimbursement)
# 2. Different adverse event costs (healthcare system differences)
# 3. Different WTP thresholds (societal preferences and affordability)
# 4. Different discount rates (national HTA agency requirements)
#
# However, for manuscript Table 2, we want a SINGLE table showing results
# for all countries side-by-side, allowing readers to compare:
# - Whether cost-effectiveness conclusions differ by country
# - How parameter uncertainty (CrIs) varies across healthcare systems
# - The impact of different WTP thresholds on NMB
#
# WORKFLOW:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Each country analysis (Ireland, Germany, Spain) must be run separately:
#
# STEP 1: Uncomment Ireland country block → Run PSA → Generates:
#   - output/PSA_Summary_NMB_Ireland.csv
#   - output/PSA_Summary_NMB_Formatted_Ireland.csv
#
# STEP 2: Uncomment Germany country block → Run PSA → Generates:
#   - output/PSA_Summary_NMB_Germany.csv
#   - output/PSA_Summary_NMB_Formatted_Germany.csv
#
# STEP 3: Uncomment Spain country block → Run PSA → Generates:
#   - output/PSA_Summary_NMB_Spain.csv
#   - output/PSA_Summary_NMB_Formatted_Spain.csv
#
# STEP 4: Run THIS chunk → Consolidates all country results into:
#   - output/PSA_Summary_NMB_All_Countries.csv (raw data)
#   - output/PSA_Summary_NMB_All_Countries_Formatted.csv (publication-ready)
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC INTERPRETATION:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The consolidated table allows assessment of:
#
# 1. TRANSFERABILITY: Do cost-effectiveness conclusions transfer across countries?
#    - If NMB is negative in all countries → robust evidence against adoption
#    - If NMB varies by country → need country-specific decision-making
#
# 2. UNCERTAINTY: How does parameter uncertainty differ across settings?
#    - Wider CrIs suggest more uncertain cost-effectiveness
#    - If CrI spans zero → high decision uncertainty (may need more research)
#
# 3. THRESHOLD SENSITIVITY: How does WTP threshold affect conclusions?
#    - Ireland (€45k) vs Spain (€30k) vs Germany (€79k)
#    - Higher WTP → more likely to have positive NMB
#
# DATA STRUCTURE REQUIREMENTS:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This chunk expects the following files to exist in the output/ directory:
# - PSA_Summary_NMB_Ireland.csv
# - PSA_Summary_NMB_Germany.csv
# - PSA_Summary_NMB_Spain.csv
#
# Each file should contain one row with columns:
# - Country, WTP_Threshold
# - Incremental_Cost_Mean, Incremental_Cost_Lower_CrI, Incremental_Cost_Upper_CrI
# - Incremental_QALY_Mean, Incremental_QALY_Lower_CrI, Incremental_QALY_Upper_CrI
# - Incremental_NMB_Mean, Incremental_NMB_Lower_CrI, Incremental_NMB_Upper_CrI
#
# If any files are missing, this chunk will display a warning and show
# results for available countries only.

# ============================================================================
# STEP 1: CHECK WHICH COUNTRY PSA RESULTS ARE AVAILABLE
# ============================================================================
#
# DEFENSIVE PROGRAMMING RATIONALE:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We cannot assume all three country analyses have been run. If this is someones first time using my code they could easily be:
# - Still be working through the countries sequentially
# - Have re-run one country after making changes
# - Be testing with a subset of countries
#
# Therefore, we check which files exist before attempting to load them.
#
# file.exists() FUNCTION:
# Returns TRUE if the file exists, FALSE otherwise
# Prevents errors from trying to read non-existent files
#
# file.path() FUNCTION:
# Constructs platform-independent file paths
# - Windows: "output\\PSA_Summary_NMB_Ireland.csv"
# - Mac/Linux: "output/PSA_Summary_NMB_Ireland.csv"

# Define file paths for each country's PSA summary
# -------------------------------------------------
# We use the raw (non-formatted) files because they contain full numerical
# precision needed for combining data and further calculations
#
# Health economic value: Ensures reproducibility by using unrounded values
file_ireland <- file.path("output", "PSA_Summary_NMB_Ireland.csv")
file_germany <- file.path("output", "PSA_Summary_NMB_Germany.csv")
file_spain <- file.path("output", "PSA_Summary_NMB_Spain.csv")

# Check which files exist
# -----------------------
# Creates logical (TRUE/FALSE) variables for each country
# These will be used to conditionally load data below
#
# Modelling approach: Graceful handling of missing data allows partial
# consolidation (e.g., if only Ireland and Germany have been run)
exists_ireland <- file.exists(file_ireland)
exists_germany <- file.exists(file_germany)
exists_spain <- file.exists(file_spain)

# Display which country results are available
# --------------------------------------------
# Console output informs the user which countries will be included
# in the consolidated table
#
# Health economic value: Transparency about which analyses contribute
# to the final consolidated results
cat("\n=======================================================\n")
cat("CONSOLIDATING PSA RESULTS ACROSS COUNTRIES\n")
cat("=======================================================\n\n")
cat("Checking for available PSA summary files...\n\n")

# Report availability status for each country
# --------------------------------------------
# ifelse() creates conditional text output:
# - If file exists: "✓ Available"
# - If file missing: "✗ Not yet generated"
cat("Ireland:", ifelse(exists_ireland, "✓ Available", "✗ Not yet generated"), "\n")
cat("Germany:", ifelse(exists_germany, "✓ Available", "✗ Not yet generated"), "\n")
cat("Spain:  ", ifelse(exists_spain, "✓ Available", "✗ Not yet generated"), "\n\n")

# ============================================================================
# STEP 2: LOAD AVAILABLE COUNTRY PSA RESULTS
# ============================================================================
#
# DATA LOADING STRATEGY:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We use a list to collect data frames for each country that has results.
# Lists in R are flexible containers that can hold multiple data frames
# of varying lengths and structures.
#
# ADVANTAGES OF USING A LIST:
# 1. Can dynamically add elements (countries) as we find them
# 2. Handles cases where only 1, 2, or 3 countries are available
# 3. Easy to combine into single data frame using do.call(rbind, list)
#
# HEALTH ECONOMIC RATIONALE:
# We load raw (non-formatted) files to preserve full numerical precision
# for any subsequent calculations or rounding decisions

# Initialize empty list to store country data frames
# ---------------------------------------------------
# list() creates an empty container
# We'll append each country's data frame to this list
#
# Modelling approach: Flexible data structure accommodates any number
# of available country results (1, 2, or 3)
psa_list <- list()

# Load Ireland data if available
# -------------------------------
# CONDITIONAL LOADING:
# if (exists_ireland) checks whether the Ireland file was found above
# Only executes the code block if TRUE (file exists)
#
# read.csv() PARAMETERS:
# - stringsAsFactors = FALSE: Keep text as character strings, not factors
#   This preserves country names and makes data manipulation easier
#
# LIST ASSIGNMENT:
# psa_list[["Ireland"]] adds the data frame to the list with name "Ireland"
# Named list elements allow us to track which country each data frame represents
#
# Health economic interpretation: Loading Ireland's PSA results including
# costs, QALYs, NMB at €45,000 WTP threshold
if (exists_ireland) {
  # Read the CSV file containing Ireland PSA summary
  # Each row contains mean and 95% CrI for incremental cost, QALY, and NMB
  psa_list[["Ireland"]] <- read.csv(file_ireland, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  # Console feedback confirms successful loading
  # Shows how many rows loaded (should be 1 for single-country file)
  cat("✓ Loaded Ireland results (", nrow(psa_list[["Ireland"]]), " row)\n")
}

# Load Germany data if available
# -------------------------------
# Same structure as Ireland loading above
#
# Health economic interpretation: Loading Germany's PSA results including
# costs, QALYs, NMB at €78,871 WTP threshold (higher than Ireland/Spain)
if (exists_germany) {
  # Read the CSV file containing Germany PSA summary
  psa_list[["Germany"]] <- read.csv(file_germany, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  # Console feedback
  cat("✓ Loaded Germany results (", nrow(psa_list[["Germany"]]), " row)\n")
}

# Load Spain data if available
# -----------------------------
# Same structure as Ireland and Germany loading above
#
# Health economic interpretation: Loading Spain's PSA results including
# costs, QALYs, NMB at €30,000 WTP threshold (lowest of the three countries)
if (exists_spain) {
  # Read the CSV file containing Spain PSA summary
  psa_list[["Spain"]] <- read.csv(file_spain, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

  # Console feedback
  cat("✓ Loaded Spain results (", nrow(psa_list[["Spain"]]), " row)\n")
}

# ============================================================================
# STEP 3: COMBINE COUNTRY RESULTS INTO CONSOLIDATED TABLE
# ============================================================================
#
# COMBINING DATA FRAMES:
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We use do.call(rbind, list) to stack country data frames vertically.
#
# WHAT IS do.call()?
# do.call(function, list_of_arguments) applies a function to a list of arguments
# Example: do.call(rbind, list(df1, df2, df3)) is equivalent to rbind(df1, df2, df3)
#
# WHAT IS rbind()?
# rbind() stands for "row bind" - it stacks data frames vertically
# Requirements: All data frames must have the same columns
# Result: A single data frame with rows from all input data frames
#
# EXAMPLE:
# If Ireland data has 1 row, Germany has 1 row, Spain has 1 row:
```
